afternoon.name: An afternoon
afternoon.line: One sitting, or two. Nothing here needs weeks.
afternoon.after: Done in a day, and it stays done. The room it lives in has more like it.

weeks.name: A few weeks
weeks.line: A little most days, and it is yours before the month is out.
weeks.after: That is the whole ladder. If it caught you, the room it lives in has more.

months.name: A few months
months.line: About three months of a little most days. Every ladder in the school stops around there.
months.after: That is where the ladder stops — about three months in, at something real you can actually do. Nothing in the school runs for years, because a chain you cannot finish stops being a chain. Past here it is yours to carry on, on your own or with your facilitator or with the group.

groups.name: Your body
groups.line: Moving it, making it strong, and what it can do in water.

groups.name: The outdoors
groups.line: Fire, weather, wild things, and everything above your head.

groups.name: Your mind
groups.line: Numbers, words, memory, seeing properly, and saying what you mean.

groups.name: Making things
groups.line: With your hands, with a tune, and with a bit of misdirection.

groups.name: Everyday life
groups.line: Feeding people, earning, fixing, caring, and keeping your head.

categories.name: Body and movement
categories.line: Juggling, skipping, upside down, breath, strength, speed.

tracks.name: Juggling
tracks.line: Three balls in the air, eventually.

steps.test: Throw one ball from hand to hand ten times without dropping it.
how: One ball only. A rolled sock works.
Throw it from your right hand to your left, up to about eye height.
Aim for the same arc every time rather than for speed.
Ten throws without dropping it.

steps.test: Throw one ball twenty times, and have every throw peak at the same height.
steps.note: Pick a spot on the wall at eye height. Every throw should touch it. Boring, and it is the whole thing.

steps.test: Throw one ball twenty times with your eyes on the top of the arc, not on your hands.
steps.note: You catch by feel, not by looking. This is the step that makes three balls possible later.

steps.test: Throw one ball twenty times starting with your weaker hand.
steps.note: Whichever hand you have been avoiding. Both hands have to learn this or three balls never comes.

steps.test: Do the two-ball exchange five times, drops allowed.
steps.note: One ball in each hand. Throw the right; when it reaches the top, throw the left. Catch what you can. Drops are expected here.

steps.test: Do the two-ball exchange ten times in a row, catching both.
Do the two-ball exchange twenty times, starting with your weaker hand.
Do the two-ball exchange twenty times without your feet moving.
steps.note: If you are chasing the balls, the throws are going forward. Throw straight up in front of your face instead.

steps.test: Hold three balls, throw all three once, and catch at least one.
steps.note: It will go everywhere. That is the step. Everybody looks foolish here and everybody gets through it.

steps.test: Do a three-ball cascade for three catches.
steps.note: A cascade means they cross over in the middle, not round in a circle.

steps.test: Do a three-ball cascade for five catches.
Do a three-ball cascade for ten catches.
Do a three-ball cascade for twenty catches.
Juggle three balls for thirty seconds with no drop.
Practise for ten minutes without stopping, however many times you drop them.
steps.note: Ten minutes on the clock. Pick them up and carry on. Everybody who can juggle dropped several hundred times first.

steps.test: Juggle three balls for a full minute.
Juggle three balls for two whole minutes.
Juggle two balls in one hand, twenty throws.
steps.note: Both balls in the SAME hand, going round in a circle. Harder than the cascade — a flourish, not a step backwards.

steps.test: Juggle while walking twenty steps.
Teach somebody their first ten throws, until they can do it without you.

tracks.about: Three balls in the air is a month of a few minutes a day, and almost nobody who tries it properly fails. It teaches the hands and the eyes to work without you, and it is the clearest proof there is that a thing you could not do last month is now yours. Three rolled socks will do to start.

tracks.name: Skipping
tracks.line: Stepping over a rope to running a game of it.

steps.test: Step over a rope lying still on the ground, ten times.
Swing the rope over your head and let it land in front of your feet, ten times.
steps.note: No jumping yet. Just get the rope round and stop it there.

steps.test: Swing it over and step across it, ten times.
Skip three times in a row.
Skip ten times in a row without stopping.
Skip twenty-five in a row.
Skip for one whole minute, however many times you trip.
Skip fifty in a row.
Skip one hundred in a row.
Skip ten times on one foot, then ten on the other.
Skip one hundred with the rope crossed over at least once.
Run a skipping game for other people.

tracks.about: Skipping is the quickest fitness there is and it feels like play. From stepping over a rope on the ground to a hundred in a row and tricks, in a few weeks. A rope costs a few pounds; a length of washing line will do to begin.

tracks.name: Upside down
tracks.line: Rolls, cartwheels, handstands.

steps.test: Do a forward roll and come back up on your feet.
Do three forward rolls in a row, in a straight line.
Do a backward roll.
Kick your legs up against a wall and hold for five seconds.
steps.note: Hands a little way from the wall, arms straight, look at the floor between them.

steps.test: Hold a wall handstand for fifteen seconds.
Hold a wall handstand for thirty seconds.
Do a cartwheel, any shape at all, and land on your feet.
Do a cartwheel with your legs straight.
Cartwheel cleanly in both directions.
Walk your feet up a wall until your chest touches it, and hold for ten seconds.
Come out of a handstand into a roll, on purpose.
steps.note: Learn the way out before you need it. This is the step that makes the rest safe.

steps.test: Kick up away from the wall and hold for one second.
Hold a free handstand for three seconds.
Hold a free handstand for five seconds.
Hold a free handstand for ten seconds.
Hold ten seconds three separate times in one go.
Take one step on your hands.
Walk three steps on your hands.
Walk five steps on your hands.
Show somebody how to kick up safely, and hold their legs while they try.

tracks.name: Breath
tracks.line: From ten slow breaths to two minutes held, calmly, and teaching it to somebody.

steps.test: Take ten slow breaths through your nose, with your mouth shut.
how: Sitting up, shoulders down, mouth closed the whole time.
In through the nose to a count of four, out through the nose to a count of six.
Feel your stomach move rather than your chest.
steps.note: Breathing through your nose warms, filters and slows the air. Most of us mouth-breathe all day without noticing, and simply closing your mouth is a real change.

steps.test: Breathe out for twice as long as you breathe in, twenty times.
how: In for four, out for eight. Count it in your head.
Do not force the out-breath — let it be long and loose.
Twenty rounds is about four minutes.
steps.note: The long out-breath is the switch. It is the one thing that reliably slows a racing heart, and it works within about a minute.

steps.test: Breathe in for four, hold four, out for four, hold four — ten rounds.
how: Square, even counts. Sitting up, eyes closed if you like.
If four is a struggle, use three.
Ten rounds is about three minutes.
steps.note: This is the pattern soldiers and divers are taught for staying steady under pressure, and it is simple enough that a child of seven can use it in a dentist's chair.

steps.test: Hold your breath for thirty seconds, sitting still.
how: Sitting down, on dry land, never in or near water.
Two or three slow breaths first, then a normal breath in, then hold.
Stop the moment it is genuinely unpleasant. This is not a competition.
steps.note: On land, a breath hold is completely safe and simply uncomfortable. In water it is dangerous, and people have drowned practising exactly this. Never in water.

steps.test: Use the slow breathing before something you are nervous about.
how: Twenty long out-breaths, in the five minutes before the thing.
A phone call, a talk, a test, a difficult conversation, a needle.
Then go and do the thing.
steps.note: Here is where this stops being an exercise and becomes a tool. Having something to actually do with your hands and your lungs while you wait is half the battle.

steps.test: Hold your breath for forty-five seconds.
how: Sitting still, on dry land, timer running.
Relax your face and shoulders. Tension burns air.
The first urge to breathe is not the end — it comes far earlier than you need to stop.
steps.note: Most of the improvement here is not lung capacity, it is learning that the first strong urge to breathe can be sat through calmly. That transfers to a lot of things.

steps.test: Do the slow breathing every day for a week.
how: Five minutes, same time each day. First thing or last thing.
Any of the patterns you have learned.
Seven days, ticked off.
steps.note: Practising when you are calm is what makes it available when you are not. Nobody can learn a new way of breathing in the middle of a panic.

steps.test: Hold your breath for one minute.
how: Sitting or lying, never in water.
A few slow breaths first, then a full but not stuffed breath in.
Let it out slowly when you finish rather than gasping.
steps.note: A minute sounds impossible before you have done thirty seconds and easy afterwards. Almost everybody gets there within a fortnight of trying every few days.

steps.test: Slow your own pulse down on purpose, and count it before and after.
how: Find your pulse at your wrist or your neck and count the beats for thirty seconds. Double it.
Three minutes of long out-breaths, four in and eight out.
Count it again.
steps.note: Watching a number you thought was out of your control move because you decided it should is the moment this ladder lands. Ten or fifteen beats is a normal change.

steps.test: Hold your breath for ninety seconds.
how: Dry land, sitting still, somebody nearby if you like.
Stay loose. Swallowing once is normal and buys you time.
Never do this standing at the edge of anything, or in a bath.
steps.note: By now the hold is almost entirely a mental job. The lungs are not the limit; the willingness to be uncomfortable calmly is.

steps.test: Hold your breath for two minutes.
how: Lying down, warm, still, on a day you are rested.
Slow breathing for two minutes first, then the hold.
Stop whenever you want to. Nothing here is worth pushing into feeling unwell.
steps.note: Two minutes is the end of this ladder and it is a genuinely surprising thing to own. Longer than this is a thing for trained people with trained supervision, not for an app.

steps.test: Teach somebody the slow breathing until they can do it without you.
how: The long out-breath first. That is the one that works.
Do it with them rather than describing it.
Give them one moment to use it for: before bed, before a test, when they are angry.
steps.note: A child who is given this at six has it for life, and it is the single most useful thing on this ladder. Give them the out-breath and one moment to use it, and nothing else.

tracks.about: Your breathing is the one part of your body that runs itself and that you can also take hold of, which makes it the fastest way there is to calm yourself down on purpose. This ladder is half calm and half capacity: slow breathing that you can use before anything frightening, and breath holds that climb to two minutes. One safety rule runs through all of it, and it is not negotiable: never practise any of this in water, or near water, ever.

tracks.name: Carrying
tracks.line: From two heavy bags to a person on your back.

steps.test: Carry a full bag in each hand the length of your street.
how: Two shopping bags, two full water containers, two bags of books.
Stand tall, shoulders back, walk normally. Do not lean to one side.
If you have to stop, they are too heavy — go a bit lighter and walk the whole way.
steps.note: Two even loads are the easiest way to carry weight and the best place to start. The goal is always to walk normally, not to survive.

steps.test: Carry something heavy in one hand the same distance, then swap.
how: One bag, one side, the whole length, then the same on the other side.
Do not lean away from it — stay upright and let your middle do the holding.
Shorter distance if you find yourself tipping.
steps.note: One-sided carrying is what really trains the sides of your middle, and it is what most of real life is: one heavy bag and a door to open.

steps.test: Carry something awkward up a full flight of stairs.
how: A box, a laundry basket, a bag of sand, a bedside table.
High and close to your chest so you can see the steps.
One step at a time. No rushing the last three.
steps.note: Stairs with something awkward is where carelessness costs most. Slow is not weakness here; it is the skill.

steps.test: Carry two heavy bags for a hundred metres without setting them down.
how: Count the distance out — about a minute and a half of ordinary walking.
Set your grip properly before you start rather than adjusting on the move.
Breathe. People hold their breath when carrying and it is why they stop.
steps.note: A hundred metres is roughly a car park to a front door. This is the rung that makes a big shop a non-event.

steps.test: Carry something heavy on one shoulder for fifty metres.
how: A sack of compost or coal, a heavy holdall, a rolled carpet.
Up to the chest first, then onto the shoulder, one hand steadying it.
Swap sides halfway if it is comfortable.
steps.note: The shoulder carry is how heavy things were moved for most of history, and it is far easier than it looks once the load is properly settled.

steps.test: Carry a full rucksack for a solid hour's walk.
how: Ten to fifteen kilos: water containers, books, tins, whatever is to hand.
Straps tight, load high and close to your back.
An hour, one walk, no sitting down. Rain is fine.
steps.note: A loaded walk is the single best bit of training in this whole ladder and it doubles as a day out. Take it somewhere worth looking at.

steps.test: Carry something heavy in each hand for two hundred metres.
how: Twice the distance of rung four, same load or heavier.
Pick a landmark and walk to it rather than counting steps.
Set down once and finish, if you must — then do it unbroken next time.
steps.note: Grip usually fails before the rest of you does. That is normal, it improves fast, and it is worth having for its own sake.

steps.test: Carry a child on your shoulders for a mile.
how: Hands holding their shins, their hands on your head, both of you agreeing to the plan.
Duck under branches early rather than late.
No child to hand? A rucksack with fifteen kilos in it for the same mile.
steps.note: This is the carrying that everybody actually wants to be able to do. It is also fifteen or twenty kilos for twenty minutes, which is real work.

steps.test: Carry two heavy bags up two flights of stairs without setting them down.
how: Steady pace from the first step. Do not start fast.
Even loads, upright, eyes on the steps.
If your grip is going, that is the rung for another fortnight.
steps.note: Stairs with a load are about three times as hard as flat ground and are exactly what a house move consists of.

steps.test: Carry half your own bodyweight for fifty metres.
how: Split across two hands, or a loaded rucksack plus a bag.
Set up properly, walk tall, breathe.
Do not chase this one if your back complains — go back a rung.
steps.note: Half your bodyweight is a serious carry and it is the point where people start volunteering you for things.

steps.test: Carry somebody your own size ten metres on your back.
how: They climb on from a step or a wall so you are not lifting them from the ground.
Arms under their thighs, lean forward a little, walk tall.
Agree how they get off before you start.
steps.note: A piggyback is a ridiculous amount of fun and a genuinely heavy carry. Ten metres is enough to find out how heavy a person is.

steps.test: Do the carries on three separate days in one week.
how: Two or three carries a session: two bags, one shoulder, one loaded walk.
Ten or fifteen minutes is plenty.
Write the three days down and tick them off.
steps.note: Carrying builds quickly because it is the kind of work your body was built for. Three sessions a week is a month of noticeable change.

steps.test: Carry somebody your own size twenty-five metres.
how: On your back, arms under the thighs, upright rather than bent over.
Short steps, steady breathing, no rushing.
Put them down properly rather than dropping them.
steps.note: Twenty-five metres with a person on your back is the distance that turns this from a game into a thing you could do if you had to.

steps.test: Carry a loaded rucksack up a hill without stopping.
how: Ten to fifteen kilos, any decent hill, all the way to the top.
Short steps and a slow steady pace beat charging and stopping.
No hill nearby? Two flights of stairs, five times over, with the pack on.
steps.note: Hills with weight are the oldest training there is. It also happens to be how you end up at the top of somewhere worth seeing.

steps.test: Carry two full water containers a mile.
how: Ten litres a side is twenty kilos. Five litres a side if that is too much.
Set down as many times as you need the first time, fewer the next.
Water is free and you can pour it out at the end.
steps.note: The cheapest heavy training in the world, and the load gets exactly as heavy as you decide. A mile with it is a proper morning's work.

steps.test: Carry somebody your own size fifty metres.
how: Fifty metres, on your back, no setting them down.
Find your rhythm in the first ten steps and keep it.
Somebody else nearby, just in case.
steps.note: Fifty metres is far enough to get somebody out of a field, off a beach or to the end of a road. That is the reason this rung exists.

steps.test: Carry a heavy load for half an hour over rough ground.
how: A loaded rucksack, a field, a beach, a forest path.
Uneven ground makes everything harder and it is the point.
Watch your feet and slow down on the descents.
steps.note: Rough ground works your ankles, your balance and your attention all at once. Flat pavements never will.

steps.test: Move a household with somebody for a whole day, and still be useful at the end.
how: Offer before you are asked, turn up early, bring gloves.
Take the awkward end and keep your technique when you are tired.
The rung is the last hour, not the first.
steps.note: Everything on this ladder was built for this day. The person who is still careful and cheerful at six o'clock is the one everybody remembers.

steps.test: Carry a loaded pack for a full day's walk.
how: Ten kilos or so, six or seven hours of walking, food and water in the pack.
Start slower than you want to. Eat before you are hungry.
Any long marked path, any decent hill day.
steps.note: A day under a pack is where carrying stops being training and becomes a way of getting somewhere. This is the rung that opens the outdoors.

steps.test: Teach somebody how to lift and carry without hurting themselves.
how: Close to you, back straight, legs doing the work, no twisting under load.
Watch them do it and correct the back before the weight goes up.
Show them the awkward-end rule and the agree-the-plan-first rule.
steps.note: Almost nobody is ever taught this and almost everybody hurts their back at some point. Half an hour of your time can spare somebody that entirely.

tracks.about: Strength that goes somewhere. Lifting is getting a load off the ground; carrying is moving it down a street, up a hill or up two flights of stairs, and it is the sort of strength that actually shows up in a life — shopping, moving house, a child asleep on your shoulder, somebody who has turned an ankle. No equipment: bags, water containers, sacks, and people.

tracks.name: Running
tracks.line: From one minute without stopping to five kilometres.

steps.test: Run for one minute without stopping.
how: Slower than you think — a pace you could hold a conversation at.
One minute on the clock, then walk.
Any shoes that do not hurt. Any pavement, path or field.
steps.note: If one minute is hard, you are going too fast, not too unfit. Halve the speed and try again — it works every time.

steps.test: Run one minute and walk one minute, eight times over.
how: Sixteen minutes in all. Clock or phone timer running.
The running minutes stay slow; the walking minutes are proper walking, not shuffling.
Finish feeling like you could have done another.
steps.note: Run-walk is not a beginner's compromise, it is how nearly every runner is actually built. Do not skip it because it feels too easy.

steps.test: Run for three minutes without stopping.
how: Same slow pace. Breathing through your nose is a good check.
Three minutes, then walk as long as you like.
Two or three of these in one outing is a good session.
steps.note: Three minutes usually arrives within a week of the run-walks. Nothing has got fitter yet — you have just stopped sprinting.

steps.test: Go running three times in one week.
how: Three outings, twenty minutes each, mostly walking at first if you need it.
A day off between where you can.
Write the three days down and tick them off.
steps.note: Three a week is the whole thing. Everything from here is built on it, and one long run on a Sunday builds far less than three short ones.

steps.test: Run for five minutes without stopping.
how: Still slow. If you cannot talk, slow down.
Five minutes, walk five, five more.
Rain is fine. Rain is usually better.
steps.note: Almost everybody can run for five minutes if they go slowly enough, and almost everybody tries to go too fast and learns they cannot.

steps.test: Run for eight minutes without stopping.
how: Pick a route you know so you are not guessing the distance.
Steady. Boring is the correct feeling.
Walk as much as you like afterwards.
steps.note: Eight minutes is where the legs stop being the limit and breathing takes over. Steady breathing in a rhythm is what carries you from here.

steps.test: Run for ten minutes without stopping.
how: Out for five, turn round, back for five.
Same slow pace the whole way, including the last minute.
Get it twice before you move on.
steps.note: Ten minutes without stopping is roughly a mile for most beginners, which means the next rung is already nearly yours.

steps.test: Run a mile without walking any of it.
how: Measure it on a phone map, or use a known lap.
Start slower than you want to. Almost everybody goes out too fast.
Finish it, however slowly.
steps.note: A mile is the first real milestone and the first one worth telling somebody about. It is also a distance you now have for good.

steps.test: Go out and run in the rain on purpose, and finish.
how: Wait for the rain, put your shoes on, go.
You will be wet in the first two minutes and then it stops mattering.
Dry clothes and something warm waiting for you at home.
steps.note: This is the rung that makes you a person who runs, because the weather stops being a decision. It is also more enjoyable than anybody expects.

steps.test: Run for fifteen minutes without stopping.
how: Pace it so the last three minutes are the same speed as the first three.
Steady breathing, easy shoulders, short steps.
Walk home afterwards rather than stopping dead.
steps.note: Fifteen minutes is where a run becomes a thing you can think during. That is when people start looking forward to it.

steps.test: Run three times a week for a fortnight.
how: Six runs in fourteen days. Two short, one longer, each week.
Write the six down first and tick them off.
Miss one? Do it the next day. Do not restart the fortnight.
steps.note: This fortnight is the whole difference between someone who has been for a run and someone who runs. Nothing else on this ladder matters as much.

steps.test: Run for twenty minutes without stopping.
how: Out ten, back ten, at a pace you could talk at.
Take a drink of water beforehand rather than carrying one.
Slow down rather than stopping if it gets hard.
steps.note: Twenty minutes is about two miles for most people and it is the point where fitness starts to show up in the rest of your day.

steps.test: Run two miles without walking.
how: Measure the route, run it, no walking breaks.
Start slow enough that the second mile is the same speed as the first.
It should take twenty to twenty-five minutes.
steps.note: Doubling the mile is mostly patience rather than fitness. Go out slower than feels right and it does itself.

steps.test: Run up a hill without walking any of it.
how: Short steps, lean in slightly, arms working.
Slow right down — the rung is not stopping, not going fast.
No hill nearby? A long steady road bridge, or twenty flights of stairs.
steps.note: Hills are where the actual fitness gets built, and where a slow pace is not embarrassing but correct. One hill a week is plenty.

steps.test: Run for twenty-five minutes without stopping.
how: A new route is easier than a known one at this length.
Take the first five minutes far slower than the rest.
Eat something small an hour or two before.
steps.note: Past twenty minutes the run becomes the easy part of the day rather than the hard part. Most people find this stretch the most enjoyable.

steps.test: Run for thirty minutes without stopping.
how: Fifteen out, fifteen back, steady the whole way.
Walk for five minutes first as a warm-up.
Water afterwards, and something to eat.
steps.note: Half an hour of continuous running is a properly fit adult by any ordinary standard, and it is about three kilometres to four for most people.

steps.test: Run four kilometres without stopping.
how: Measure the route rather than guessing it.
Even pace, no heroics in the first kilometre.
Finish with something left.
steps.note: Four is the last rung before the one everybody has heard of, and by now the distance is a pacing job rather than a fitness one.

steps.test: Run five kilometres without stopping.
how: Measured route, or a parkrun on a Saturday morning, which is free everywhere.
Start at your talking pace and stay there until the last kilometre.
Whatever the time is, the rung is finishing without walking.
steps.note: Five kilometres from a start of one minute, in about three months, with no money spent on anything but shoes. This is the rung the whole ladder was built for.

steps.test: Run five kilometres faster than the first time you did it.
how: Same route, timed, at least a fortnight later.
Hold back for the first two kilometres and spend it in the last one.
Any improvement counts, by a second or by five minutes.
steps.note: Beating your own old number is a cleaner satisfaction than beating anybody else's, and it is available to you for the rest of your life.

steps.test: Run beside somebody doing their first mile, and finish at their pace.
how: Their pace, not yours, the whole way. Talk to them.
Tell them the run-walk method and that going slowly is the trick.
Finish together and make a proper fuss of it.
steps.note: Running somebody else's first mile with them costs you an easy twenty minutes and gives them the thing you have. It is the best use of this ladder there is.

tracks.about: Running from nothing to five kilometres, the way it actually works: slowly. Almost everybody who says they cannot run is simply running too fast, and the whole first half of this ladder is about going slow enough to keep going. It needs shoes that do not hurt and a road. Three times a week for about three months takes most people from a minute to five kilometres without stopping.

tracks.name: Balance
tracks.line: A log to a slackline.

steps.test: Walk the length of a log or a low wall without falling off.
Stand on one foot for thirty seconds.
steps.twist: The foot you would never choose.

steps.test: Stand on one foot for a full minute.
steps.twist: The foot you would never choose.

steps.test: Stand on one foot for thirty seconds with your eyes closed.
steps.note: Much harder than it sounds. Balance is mostly your eyes until you train the rest.

steps.test: Stand on one foot for a minute with your eyes closed.
Walk heel to toe along a straight line for twenty steps.
Walk heel to toe for twenty steps with your eyes closed.
Walk a kerb the length of a street without stepping off.
Stand on one foot and pick something up off the floor.
steps.twist: The foot you would never choose.

steps.test: Go down on one leg holding something, and stand back up.
Stand up on a slackline or a beam and stay there for ten seconds.
Stand on it for thirty seconds.
Take three steps along it.
Walk two metres along it.
Walk five metres along it.
Stop halfway, stand still for five seconds, and carry on.
Kneel down on it and stand back up.
Turn round on it.
Turn round on it and come back.
Hold somebody steady while they cross theirs for the first time.

tracks.name: Riding
tracks.line: Balance bike to a long road.

steps.test: Sit on a bike and push yourself along with your feet.
Push off and freewheel with both feet up for three seconds.
Freewheel for ten seconds, steering as you go.
Ride ten metres pedalling, with nobody holding on.
Start off on your own from standing still.
Stop exactly where you meant to stop, three times.
Steer around three things without putting a foot down.
Ride up a hill without getting off.
Look over your shoulder and keep riding straight.
steps.note: This is the one that keeps you alive on a road. Practise it somewhere with no traffic.

steps.test: Signal with one hand and keep riding straight.
Ride two miles without stopping.
Ride on a road with the signals and the road sense, with an adult beside you.

tracks.name: Hopping and balancing
tracks.line: From four, beside you. One foot, two feet, a straight line and a roll.

steps.test: Stand on one foot while somebody counts to five. Then the other foot.
Stand on one foot while they count to ten.
Hop three times on one foot.
steps.twist: The foot you would never choose.

steps.test: Hop five times on one foot without putting the other one down.
steps.twist: The foot you would never choose.

steps.test: Jump with both feet together, ten times.
Jump over a line with both feet together, ten times.
Jump off a low step and land on two feet without wobbling.
Walk along a line without stepping off it.
Walk along the line heel to toe.
Do a forward roll on something soft.
Hop all the way across the room on one foot.
steps.twist: The foot you would never choose.

steps.test: Hop across the room, swap feet halfway, and land the last one still.
steps.twist: Start on the foot you would never choose.

categories.name: Outdoors and wild
categories.line: Fire, finding your way, shelter, weather, tracks, wild food.

tracks.name: Out the door, part one
tracks.line: From an hour's walk without a phone to a whole day outside.

steps.test: Walk for an hour with the phone in your pocket the whole time.
steps.note: Anywhere: streets count. Notice what you look at when there is nothing to look at.

steps.test: Say which way is north from where you stand, then check.
steps.note: The sun, the time, moss, a landmark. Then a compass or a map to see how you did.

steps.test: Watch the sky at dusk until the first star, and name it if you can.
steps.note: The first "star" is often a planet. A free sky app will tell you which.

steps.test: Go out in the rain on purpose, dressed for it, for twenty minutes.
steps.note: Proper coat, hood up. Nobody else is out; that is what makes it good.

steps.test: Name five trees or plants on one walk.
steps.note: A street, a park, a verge. An app can name them; you have to remember them.

steps.test: Read tomorrow's weather from tonight's sky and wind, write it down, and check.
steps.note: Red sky, wind direction, the kind of cloud. Then see in the morning. Wrong is fine; the looking is the rung.

steps.test: Walk somewhere new with a paper map, or no map at all.
steps.note: Pick a point a mile off and find a way there you have never used.

steps.test: Light a candle with one match.
steps.note: A fire where you have somewhere to make one; a candle where you do not. One match, no second go.

steps.test: Watch the sunrise, out of doors.
steps.note: Look up the time, be outside ten minutes before. Once a year would change most people.

steps.test: Walk ten thousand steps in one day.
steps.note: About five miles. The phone counts them; the legs do the rest.

steps.test: Find the moon, say what phase it is, and where it will be tomorrow.
steps.note: Later each night, by about fifty minutes. Check tomorrow.

steps.test: Sit outside for thirty minutes and write down everything alive you saw.
steps.note: Birds, insects, a cat, a dog, people. A doorstep or a balcony will do.

steps.test: Eat one meal outside.
steps.note: A sandwich on a bench, a flask on a wall. Weather permitting is not a rule; dressing for it is.

steps.test: Walk for two hours in one go.
steps.note: Six or seven miles. Water, a snack, no hurry.

steps.test: Spot three birds and name them.
steps.note: Pigeon, gull and crow count at first. A robin, a blackbird, a wren next.

steps.test: Go for a walk at night with a torch you do not switch on.
steps.note: Twenty minutes. Eyes adjust in about ten. Streets count; somewhere darker is better.

steps.test: Get yourself to somewhere five miles away and back, on foot or by bike.
steps.note: Ten miles in the day. Plan it, pack water, go.

steps.test: Pack a bag for a day out with everything you would need, and go.
steps.note: Water, food, a layer, a waterproof, a map, a plaster. Then a day out with it.

steps.test: Find the highest point you can walk to within an hour of home, and go up it.
steps.note: A hill, a tower, a multi-storey car park roof, a church that lets you climb. Look at your town from above.

steps.test: A whole day outside, dawn to dusk.
steps.note: Sunrise from rung nine, dusk from rung three, and everything between. Part two is the wild proper.

tracks.about: Out the door, wherever you live: an hour without the phone in your hand, north found and checked, the first star, rain on purpose, a sunrise, ten thousand steps, a walk at night with the torch off, and a whole day outside at the end. Every rung works from a town street.

tracks.name: Fire
tracks.line: Gathering sticks to teaching somebody else.

steps.test: Gather a bundle of dry sticks that would actually burn.
steps.note: Snap them. If they bend instead of snapping they are wet and they will not light.

steps.test: Gather three sizes: tinder, kindling, and wood, in three piles.
Lay a fire properly so that it would light.
Light it with matches, first go.
Put it out so completely that nobody could tell it was there.
steps.note: Water, stir, water again, and feel it with your hand. Warm is not out.

steps.test: Keep one going for half an hour without it needing rescuing.
Light one in the wind.
Cook something on a fire you laid and lit.
Light one with a single match.
Light one with a spark and no flame — a striker or a flint.
Light one when everything around you is damp.
Teach two other people to lay and light one safely.

tracks.name: Finding your way
tracks.line: Pointing north to leading a route.

steps.test: Point which way is north, and be right.
Name three landmarks you can see and say which way home is.
Find north from the sun, and check it against a compass.
Hold a map the right way round for where you are standing.
steps.note: Turn the map, not your head. Almost everybody gets lost because they never do this.

steps.test: Point out three things on the map that you can see in front of you.
Follow a marked path on a map for a mile without being told.
Read the contours and say which way the ground rises.
Walk to a spot you picked on the map and arrive at it.
Take a bearing with a compass and walk it for two hundred metres.
Walk a bearing to something you cannot see from the start.
Navigate a mile with a map and a compass.
Work out how long a walk will take before you set off, and be close.
Navigate three miles across country.
Find your way in poor visibility, slowly and safely.
Say where you are on the map at any moment, all the way round a walk.
Plan a route yourself, on paper, with the timings.
Lead the group along it and get everybody there.
Change the route halfway because of the weather, and say why.
Leave a route plan with somebody at home before you go.
Lead a route that takes a whole day, and bring everybody back on time.

tracks.name: Shelter
tracks.line: A den to a night out in it.

steps.test: Build a den big enough to sit inside.
Build one that two people fit in.
Choose a spot properly — not in a dip, not under a dead branch.
Build one with a frame that stands up on its own.
Thatch it so that daylight barely gets through.
Build one that keeps you dry through ten minutes of rain.
Get the door out of the wind, and say how you knew where the wind was.
Insulate the floor so the ground does not take your heat.
steps.note: The ground steals more warmth than the air does. This one step is the difference between a night and a miserable night.

steps.test: Build one you would be warm in overnight, and prove it with a thermometer.
Sit in your own shelter for two hours in bad weather.
Sleep a whole night in a shelter you built.
Build one with a group and get everybody through the night dry.

tracks.name: Weather and tide
tracks.line: Reading the day before it happens.

steps.test: Dress yourself right for the weather that is actually outside.
Read a forecast and say what everybody should bring.
Look at the sky and say whether the forecast looks right.
Know what wind chill is and dress for it, not for the number.
Pack a bag for a day out where the weather might turn.
Read a tide table and say when the beach will be gone.
Know which way the tide is going right now, by looking.
Plan a beach walk around the tide and get it right.
Say what time it gets dark today, without looking it up.
Plan a walk that finishes before dark, and finish before dark.
Spot weather coming in and say how long you have.
Turn back early, on purpose, and be glad you did.
Change or call off a plan because of the weather, and explain why.
steps.note: Calling it off is the hardest and most useful of these. Anybody can go anyway.

steps.test: Get somebody warm and dry again who got cold and wet.
Know the signs of somebody getting too cold, and what to do first.
Carry the right kit for the day without carrying everything.
Lead a short walk in weather that was not ideal, and keep it cheerful.
Read a shipping or mountain forecast and say what it means for tomorrow.
Make the call on a day out for other people, and be right.
Keep a group safe and cheerful through genuinely bad weather.

tracks.name: Trees and birds
tracks.line: Five leaves to leading a nature walk.

steps.test: Find five different kinds of leaf and lay them out.
Name three trees from their leaves alone.
Name five trees from their leaves alone.
Name three trees in winter, with no leaves on them at all.
Find the oldest tree near you and say how you can tell.
Name three birds on sight, outdoors, not from a book.
Sit still outside for ten minutes and count how many birds come.
Name five birds on sight.
Name three birds from their call with your eyes shut.
Name ten birds on sight.
Name ten birds from their call with your eyes shut.
Name ten wild plants where you walk.
Say which month each of five plants flowers, and be there when one does.
Name twenty wild plants and say which are useful.
Find a nest, a burrow or a den without disturbing it.
Keep a list of everything you name for a whole month.
Notice one thing changing with the season and follow it for a month.
Name what lives in one hedge, top to bottom.
Take one person out and name ten things for them.
Lead a walk and name what you pass as you go.

tracks.name: Wild food
tracks.line: One berry to a whole meal.

steps.test: Pick and eat one wild food with somebody who knows it.
steps.note: Never eat anything on this ladder without a person who is certain. Certain, not fairly sure.

steps.test: Learn the rule: if you are not certain, you do not eat it.
Identify one safe wild food on your own and have it checked.
Identify three safe wild foods without being told.
Name three things near you that would poison you, and how to know them.
Learn which of them has a lookalike, and what tells them apart.
Pick enough of something to bring home.
Wash it, prepare it and cook it.
Pick only what you need and leave the rest standing.
Find out whose land you are on and whether you may pick there.
Identify six safe wild foods without being told.
Name five things that would poison you, and why.
Follow one plant through a season until it is ready.
Pick something in each of three different months.
Make a meal where one ingredient came from the wild.
Make a meal where three ingredients came from the wild.
Preserve something you picked so it keeps.
Give some of what you picked to somebody else.
Say no to something you were not sure about, out loud.
Take somebody else foraging and keep them safe.

tracks.name: Tracking
tracks.line: A footprint to following an animal.

steps.test: Find an animal footprint and say what made it.
Find your own footprint and say which way you were going.
Follow your own tracks backwards for fifty metres.
Find three different sets of prints in one place.
Name three animals from their prints.
Find a run or a path an animal uses regularly.
Name three animals from their droppings.
Find where something has been eating, and say what it was.
Name five animals from their prints or droppings.
Say whether a track is fresh or old, and why you think so.
Follow an animal trail for a hundred metres.
Follow one for two hundred metres.
Read a trail and say what the animal was doing.
Read one and say roughly when it passed.
Find a print, make a cast of it, and keep it.
Sit still outdoors for twenty minutes without moving.
Sit still for forty minutes and write down everything that happened.
Move through woodland without being heard for fifty metres.
Sit still long enough that a wild animal comes close on its own.
Take somebody out and find them a track they can read themselves.

tracks.name: Camping
tracks.line: The garden to a wild night.

steps.test: Sleep a whole night in a tent in the garden.
Put a tent up with somebody helping.
Put a tent up on your own.
Take it down, dry it and pack it properly.
Pack for a night away from a list and forget nothing.
Choose a pitch — flat, dry, out of the wind — and say why.
Camp a night away from the house and cook your own tea.
Keep everything you own dry through a wet night.
Leave a pitch so that nobody could tell you were there.
Camp a night carrying everything you need on your back.
Camp two nights carrying everything you need.
Take a younger child on their first night out and get them home happy.

categories.name: Water and boats
categories.line: Swimming, cold water, rowing, sailing, fishing, rock pools.

tracks.name: Swimming
tracks.line: From your face in the water to fifty metres without stopping.

steps.test: Put your face in the water and blow bubbles, ten times.
how: Shallow end, hold the side, take a breath, face in, blow out slowly through your nose and mouth.
Ten times, each one a little longer.
Breathing out under the water is the whole foundation. Nobody swims well while holding their breath.
steps.note: This is the rung that adults skip and then wonder why swimming feels like a panic. Blowing out under water is what makes everything above it calm.

steps.test: Hold the side and kick your legs for thirty seconds.
how: Arms straight, holding the rail or the edge, body flat on the surface.
Kick from the hips with straight-ish legs and loose ankles, small and fast.
Small splashes, not big ones — big splashes mean the knees are doing it.
steps.note: The kick does less than people think for moving you and a lot for keeping you flat. Flat is what makes swimming easy.

steps.test: Push off the side and glide with your face in, as far as you can.
how: Feet on the wall, arms stretched out in front, head between your arms, face down.
Push off and go — no kicking, no pulling. Just hold the shape.
See how far the glide takes you before you need to stand up.
steps.note: A good glide is the whole of good swimming. Everything you learn from here is about keeping that shape while you add the arms and legs.

steps.test: Float on your front for five seconds, then stand back up.
how: Face in, arms out, let your legs come up behind you.
Relax — tension sinks and calm floats.
To stand: tuck your knees to your chest, put your feet down, lift your head last.
steps.note: Being able to stop and stand up calmly is what takes the fear out of the deep bit. Practise the standing-up as much as the floating.

steps.test: Float on your back for ten seconds.
how: Head back so your ears are in the water, hips up, arms out to the sides.
Look straight up at the ceiling. Looking at your feet sinks you.
Somebody's hand under your back at first if it helps.
steps.note: Floating on your back is the single most useful thing in the water: it is how anybody in trouble rests. Worth having for its own sake.

steps.test: Push off and glide with a leg kick, three metres.
how: Same glide shape, then add the small fast kick you practised at the side.
Face down, breathing out slowly the whole way.
Three metres, then stand up calmly.
steps.note: Glide plus kick is already swimming — you simply have no arms in it yet. Getting this bit right makes the arms easy.

steps.test: Swim five metres any way you like, without touching the bottom.
how: Doggy paddle, breaststroke, anything. Five metres, feet off the bottom.
Along the shallow end, so you can stand whenever you want.
Calm and slow beats fast and thrashing.
steps.note: Any five metres is a proper milestone: you are now swimming, and everything after this is refinement.

steps.test: Swim ten metres on your front.
how: Face in, breathing out under water, lifting your head only when you must.
Long slow arms rather than fast short ones.
Ten metres is usually about half a short pool.
steps.note: The temptation is to lift your head and rush. Long and slow gets you further with half the effort — that is true for the whole of swimming.

steps.test: Swim ten metres on your back.
how: Ears in the water, hips up, small kick, arms brushing past your ears one at a time.
Look straight up. Glance at the wall behind you as you approach it.
On your back you can always breathe, which is why it is the restful one.
steps.note: Front and back both means you always have a way to keep going when one of them tires. It also means you can rest without touching the bottom.

steps.test: Turn your head to the side, take one breath, and keep swimming.
how: Breathe out under the water first, then turn your head — do not lift it.
One ear stays in the water as you breathe. The head turns, the body stays flat.
Take one breath, put your face back, keep going.
steps.note: This one movement is the difference between swimming ten metres and swimming as far as you like. Practise it at the side of the pool before you swim with it.

steps.test: Swim ten metres taking a breath every three or four strokes.
how: Steady rhythm: stroke, stroke, breathe, stroke, stroke, breathe.
Breathing out continuously between breaths, never holding.
Slow the arms down until the rhythm works.
steps.note: Once the breathing has a rhythm, distance stops being a fitness question. Most people double their distance the week this clicks.

steps.test: Jump in from the side and swim back to it.
how: Water you know the depth of, with somebody watching.
Jump feet first, let yourself come back up, turn and swim to the side.
Do it a second time straight away — the second is far easier.
steps.note: Going under and coming back up without panic is the safety skill hiding inside swimming, and it is worth practising deliberately rather than by accident.

steps.test: Swim fifteen metres without stopping.
how: Long strokes, steady breathing, face in.
Count your strokes — fewer strokes for the same distance means better shape.
Stop calmly at the end rather than lunging for the side.
steps.note: Counting strokes is the swimmer's trick for improving without going faster. Fewer strokes, same distance, is always progress.

steps.test: Pick something up off the bottom in water up to your chest.
how: A diving toy, a coin, anything that sinks.
Breathe out as you go down, eyes open, take it, push off the bottom.
Three or four goes. It gets easy quickly.
steps.note: Going down on purpose and coming back up teaches your body that under the water is a place you can visit, which takes a surprising amount of fear away.

steps.test: Tread water for thirty seconds.
how: Out of your depth, or deep enough that you cannot stand.
Slow circles with your hands, gentle cycling with your legs. Calm and small.
Somebody watching, and the side within reach.
steps.note: Treading water is almost entirely about relaxing. Everybody's first attempt is far too frantic and the second one is easy.

steps.test: Tread water for a full minute.
how: Same slow small movements, breathing normally.
Lie back into a float for a few seconds if you need a rest, then carry on.
Time it rather than guessing.
steps.note: A minute of treading water plus a back float means you could look after yourself in deep water long enough for help to reach you.

steps.test: Swim twenty-five metres on your front without stopping.
how: A full length of most pools. Steady breathing rhythm all the way.
Start slower than you want to — the second half is where people stop.
Finish calmly and hold the side for a moment before standing.
steps.note: A full length is the milestone everybody recognises and the point at which you can call yourself a swimmer without qualifying it.

steps.test: Swim twenty-five metres on your back without stopping.
how: Ears in, hips up, long arms past your ears.
Count strokes so you know when the wall is coming.
Straight line — one arm usually pulls harder and drifts you across.
steps.note: Having a second full length in a different stroke means you can now rest by changing stroke rather than by stopping.

steps.test: Swim there and back with one rest in the middle.
how: Twenty-five metres, a short rest at the wall, twenty-five back.
Same steady rhythm both ways.
Breathe properly before you push off for the second length.
steps.note: This is the rung that turns one length into two, and two into as many as you like. The rest at the wall is a technique, not a weakness.

steps.test: Swim fifty metres without stopping, and climb out unaided.
how: Two lengths, no touching the bottom, no holding the wall at the turn.
Steady from the first stroke. Slow is what finishes it.
Then out at the side on your arms, not up the steps.
steps.note: Fifty metres unbroken from a start of blowing bubbles, in about three months. From here, open water and the cold water ladder are both open to you.

tracks.warn: Never on your own, and never in open water on this ladder. Every step happens at a pool or a lifeguarded beach with somebody beside you who can already swim.
tracks.about: Swimming is the one thing on this list that is a safety skill as well as a fitness one, and the water is patient: it takes almost everybody from blowing bubbles to fifty metres inside a few months. It needs a pool, which is the only cost here — most council leisure centres are a few pounds and many have free or cheap family sessions. Nothing else in the school trains your breathing and your whole body at once like this.

tracks.name: Cold water
tracks.line: From thirty seconds at the end of a shower to a calm four minutes in the sea.

steps.test: Finish a shower with thirty seconds of cold.
how: Normal warm shower, then turn it to full cold for the last thirty seconds.
Head and shoulders under it, not just your feet.
Breathe out slowly and steadily. Do not hold your breath.
steps.note: Thirty seconds, in your own bathroom, costing nothing. The gasp lasts about ten seconds and then it is simply cold, which is a very different thing.

steps.test: Finish a shower with a full minute of cold, three days running.
how: Same routine, longer. A minute is not twice as hard as thirty seconds.
Slow long out-breaths all the way through.
Three days, ticked off.
steps.note: By the third morning you will notice that the dread beforehand is bigger than the cold itself. That gap is the lesson this ladder is really teaching.

steps.test: Stand in the sea or a lough up to your ankles for one minute.
how: Somewhere you know, with somebody with you.
Shoes off, trousers rolled. A minute on the clock.
Any beach, any weather. Free everywhere in this country.
steps.note: Cold feet on a cold day is worse than people expect and is the honest start. The sea is a different thing from a shower and deserves its own first rung.

steps.test: Stand in up to your knees for a minute.
how: Walk in slowly rather than dashing.
Long out-breaths from the moment the water touches you.
Dry socks and shoes waiting on the sand.
steps.note: The cold moves up your body in stages and each stage has its own gasp. Taking them one at a time is exactly how the whole ladder is climbed.

steps.test: Get in up to your waist and stay calm for a minute.
how: This is the one that makes people squeal. Go slowly and keep breathing out.
Hands out of the water at first — hands and wrists feel it worst.
Somebody with you on the shore.
steps.note: Waist deep is the real test of the breathing, because this is where the gasp reflex is strongest. Slow out-breaths beat it every time.

steps.test: Get in up to your shoulders and control your breathing.
how: Lower yourself in rather than jumping. Never dive into cold water.
The first thirty seconds are the worst and then it settles.
Out as soon as the breathing is under control — this rung is not about staying in.
steps.note: Cold water shock is a real thing and it is at its worst in the first thirty seconds. Getting in slowly and breathing out is what makes it safe.

steps.test: Get warm again properly afterwards, and write down how you did it.
how: Dry off completely and dress from the top down, hat on early.
Something warm to drink, and move about — walk, do not sit in the car.
No hot shower straight away; warm up from the inside first.
steps.note: Getting warm again is the part people get wrong, and the cold keeps coming for twenty minutes after you are out. Plan this before you get in, not after.

steps.test: Stay in up to your shoulders for one full minute.
how: Timer on the shore. Somebody watching.
Still, calm, breathing slowly. Not swimming about.
Out on the minute, whatever it feels like.
steps.note: A minute in properly cold water is a real thing to have done. Get out on time rather than proving anything — the people who get into trouble are the ones who stay longer than they planned.

steps.test: Go in on a day you did not feel like it.
how: Decide the night before and go, regardless of the weather or the mood.
Do not renegotiate with yourself at the car park.
Same routine: in slowly, breathe out, warm up properly.
steps.note: This is the rung the whole ladder exists for. Doing the thing you had decided to do, on a day you did not fancy it, is a skill that has nothing to do with water.

steps.test: Stay in for two minutes and get properly warm again afterwards.
how: Two minutes, timed, then straight out and into the warming routine you wrote down.
Watch for shivering that will not stop — that is the point to stop for the day.
Never alone, and never after a drink.
steps.note: Longer is not better in cold water. Two minutes with a good warm-up afterwards is worth far more than five minutes and an afternoon of shivering.

steps.test: Go in once a week for a month, whatever the weather.
how: Four dips, one a week, written in the calendar in advance.
Same place, with the same person, so it needs no arranging.
Whatever the weather does.
steps.note: A month of this changes how you meet cold, rain and discomfort generally. It also tends to become the thing you look forward to most in the week.

steps.test: Take somebody else through their first cold dip, safely.
how: Tell them about the gasp before it happens so it does not frighten them.
In slowly, never diving, long out-breaths, and out on an agreed time.
Their warm clothes, hat and hot drink ready before they get in.
steps.note: Talking somebody through their first thirty seconds is a genuinely useful thing to be able to do, and safety is the whole of it: slow in, breathe out, agreed time, warm afterwards.

tracks.about: Getting into cold water is the shortest route there is to finding out that you can do something you do not want to do, and it takes two minutes. It starts in your own shower, which costs nothing, and moves out to the sea or a lough. The whole skill is the breathing: cold water makes you gasp, and everything else here is learning to take hold of that. Never get into open water alone, never after drinking, and always have dry warm clothes waiting.

tracks.name: Rowing and paddling
tracks.line: Getting in to crossing a lough.

steps.test: Get into a boat and sit safely without wobbling it.
Put a buoyancy aid on properly and check somebody else's.
Move a boat twenty metres under your own power.
Move it in a straight line for a hundred metres.
Steer around a marker and come back.
Stop the boat where you meant to stop it.
Turn it round on the spot.
Come alongside a jetty and get out without help.
Paddle one kilometre.
Paddle into the wind for ten minutes and keep your line.
Paddle five kilometres with a group.
Take a beginner out and bring them back confident.

tracks.name: Sailing
tracks.line: Naming the parts to sailing a course.

steps.test: Name the parts of a small boat and what each one does.
Put a buoyancy aid on properly and say what you would do if you went in.
Say which way the wind is coming from, without being told.
Rig a small boat and check it over before it goes in.
Sit in the right place and hold the tiller and the rope at once.
Sail a straight line across the wind.
Sail out and come back to where you started.
Let the sail out and pull it in to change your speed on purpose.
Tack — turn through the wind — without stopping.
Tack three times in a row and keep going.
Gybe safely, with your head down.
Sail a triangle around three marks.
Sail in a stronger wind and stay in control.
Right a capsized dinghy and get back in.
steps.note: Everybody capsizes. Doing it on purpose, with somebody watching, is how it stops being frightening.

steps.test: Sail a full course with buoys.
Come alongside and stop the boat exactly where you wanted.
Take somebody out as your crew and tell them what to do.
Crew properly for somebody else and be useful.
Sail a race, wherever you finish.
Take somebody on their first ever sail and hand them the tiller.

tracks.name: Fishing
tracks.line: A rock pool to your own supper.

steps.test: Catch something in a rock pool with a net and put it back.
Set up a rod with a line and a hook, on your own.
Tie the knot that holds the hook on, three times, until it holds.
Cast and land the line roughly where you meant it to go.
Cast ten times and land eight of them where you aimed.
Sit and fish for a whole hour without needing anything to happen.
steps.note: This is the part of fishing that is actually fishing.

steps.test: Find out what is legal to catch where you are, and when.
Catch a fish.
Get the hook out and put a fish back unharmed.
Catch three in one outing.
Catch, prepare and cook a fish you caught.
Teach somebody else to cast and land one.

tracks.name: Rock pools and shore
tracks.line: Five creatures to reading the shore.

steps.test: Find five different creatures in a rock pool.
Name five of them correctly.
Turn a stone over, look under it, and put it back the way it was.
Explain what the tide does to everything living there.
Find the high tide line and say how you know.
Find and name ten seashore species.
Do a proper shore survey and write down what you found.
Lead a rock pool hunt for younger children.

categories.name: Fitness and strength
categories.line: Press-ups, sit-ups, pull-ups, the plank, lifting, sprinting.

tracks.name: Press-ups
tracks.line: From two to thirty in one go.

steps.test: Do two proper press-ups. Hands on a table or a step if you need to.
how: Body one straight line from heels to head, hands a little wider than your shoulders.
Chest down to a fist's width from the surface, elbows going back at forty-five degrees, then all the way up.
Raise your hands until two are honest: table, then a chair, then a step, then the floor.
steps.note: Two real ones beat ten half ones and always will. If you are already past two on the floor, start at the rung that is actually hard for you and count the ones below as done.

steps.test: Do five in a row at the height where five is hard.
how: Pick the height where the fifth one is a struggle — table, sofa arm, bottom step.
Five with no rest at the top.
Same depth every rep. When the depth goes, the set is over.
steps.note: The height is your dial. You lower it when five becomes easy, and every time you lower it you are lifting more of yourself.

steps.test: Do ten in a row at that height.
how: Two seconds down, one second up, no bouncing off the bottom.
If you stall at seven, rest ten seconds and finish — then go for ten unbroken next time.
When ten is comfortable, drop the height one notch.
steps.note: Ten at a raised height is the strength that makes the first floor press-up possible. Do not skip ahead; people who do spend a month stuck at one.

steps.test: Do one press-up on the floor, chest all the way down.
how: Hands under your shoulders, heels to head in one line, backside squeezed.
Down until your chest is a fist's width off the floor, then all the way up.
One. Properly. That is the whole rung.
steps.note: This is the moment people remember. If it will not come yet, go back a rung for a fortnight — the bottom step is not a failure, it is the training.

steps.test: Do three in a row on the floor.
how: Fresh, at the start of a session, not the end.
No resting at the top. Three continuous.
If you get two, do two, rest a minute, and do two more.
steps.note: From here on, every number is bought with sets on the days in between, not with heroics on the day.

steps.test: Do five in a row on the floor.
how: Build it with three sets of three, twice a week, with a minute between sets.
Then try five unbroken on a fresh day.
Chest to the floor every single rep.
steps.note: Two to five is usually about a fortnight. This is also where the easiest mistake shows up: chasing the number and letting the depth go.

steps.test: Do press-ups on three separate days in one week.
how: Monday, Wednesday, Friday, or whatever three days suit, with a day off between.
Three or four sets each day, stopping two short of failure every set.
Write the three days down and tick them off.
steps.note: This rung is the engine of the whole ladder. Everything from here is built on three sessions a week; without them the numbers stop moving at about eight.

steps.test: Do eight in a row.
how: Sets of five on your three days, then go for eight on a fresh one.
Breathe in on the way down, out on the way up.
Do not let your hips lead. Shoulders and hips move together.
steps.note: If your back is sagging by the sixth, your middle is the limit, not your arms — squeeze your backside hard and the shape holds.

steps.test: Do ten in a row.
how: Three sets of six or seven on your training days is what buys ten.
Fresh, first thing in the session.
Get it twice in one week before you call it yours.
steps.note: Ten proper press-ups is already more than most adults can do. It is also the halfway house: from here the method changes from more reps to harder reps.

steps.test: Do five slowly — three seconds down, three seconds up.
how: Count it out. Three full seconds each way, no cheating at the top.
Five of these is thirty seconds of unbroken work and it is brutal.
If you collapse at four, that is the rung for another week.
steps.note: Time under strain is what actually builds muscle. This one rung is why your normal number jumps a fortnight later without you trying.

steps.test: Do fifteen in a row.
how: Sets of ten on your three days, then fifteen fresh.
Pace it — the first five should feel too slow.
Depth to the last one or it does not count.
steps.note: The middle of a long set is where you find out whether you can stay calm while something is uncomfortable. That is a skill worth more than the press-ups.

steps.test: Do thirty across one day, in as many sets as you like.
how: Five here, five there — every time you walk past a clear bit of floor.
Spread them across the whole day. Nothing has to be hard.
Count as you go so you know when you are done.
steps.note: Total volume is the quiet ingredient in all of this. A day of easy sets does more for next month's number than one heroic set does.

steps.test: Do twenty in a row.
how: Build with three sets of thirteen to fifteen, twice a week.
Fresh, first, with a proper warm-up: twenty squats and some arm swings.
Twenty unbroken, chest to the floor.
steps.note: Twenty is two thirds of the way there, and it is the number where people start noticing your shoulders. Keep the depth honest and the last ten come faster than you expect.

steps.test: Do ten with your feet up on a chair.
how: Feet on a chair or the second step, hands on the floor, one straight line.
More weight goes through your arms, so ten here is worth about fifteen flat.
Chest all the way down, every rep.
steps.note: This is how you keep getting stronger without weights: raise the feet instead of adding reps. It is also the fastest way to add five to your flat number.

steps.test: Do press-ups every other day for a fortnight.
how: Seven sessions in fourteen days, three or four sets each, never to complete failure.
Alternate: one day flat, next session feet up.
Miss one and do it the next day rather than starting the fortnight again.
steps.note: Press-ups recover fast, which is why they take well to every other day where most training does not. This fortnight is usually worth five reps on its own.

steps.test: Do twenty-five in a row.
how: Sets of eighteen to twenty on your training days.
Slow the middle of the set down deliberately — rushing is what ends it early.
Fresh, first thing, properly warmed up.
steps.note: Twenty-five is where the set becomes a mental job as much as a physical one. Pick a spot on the floor, breathe, and keep the rhythm identical from the first to the last.

steps.test: Do fifty across one day, in as many sets as you like.
how: Ten sets of five, or five sets of ten, or anything in between.
Spread across the whole day so nothing is ever hard.
Count them and stop at fifty.
steps.note: The same trick as rung twelve with a bigger number. Do this in the week before you go for thirty and the thirty will feel lighter.

steps.test: Do ten with your feet up on a chair, slowly — two seconds down, two up.
how: Feet up, flat hands, count the seconds out.
Forty seconds of work. This is the hardest rung on the ladder.
Nine honest ones beats ten with the last three rushed.
steps.note: If you can do this, thirty flat is already in you — it is now only a question of pacing the long set. This is the rung that quietly finishes the job.

steps.test: Do thirty press-ups in one go.
how: Fresh, first thing, properly warmed up, on a day you have slept.
Start slower than feels right. A steady rhythm all the way is what gets you past twenty-five.
Chest to the floor every rep, no resting at the top.
Missed at twenty-seven? That is a very good day. Go again in three days.
steps.note: That is the ladder. Thirty proper press-ups in one go, from two, with no equipment and no money spent — for most people about three months of a few minutes three times a week. Very few adults can do this.

steps.test: Get somebody else from none to their first proper one.
how: Start them on a table, exactly as you started.
Five hard ones at the right height, three days a week. Lower the height when five is easy.
Do the sessions with them rather than telling them about them.
Warn them about depth before they learn it wrong.
steps.note: Teaching it is how you find out you actually know it, and the person you teach remembers it for the rest of their life. This costs you four weeks of five-minute sessions.

tracks.about: Thirty press-ups in one go is a real undertaking and it is not an overwhelming one. It needs no equipment, no gym and no money, it takes about five minutes a session three times a week, and the whole path from two to thirty is a few simple steps repeated. Almost nobody who does the sets fails to get there. It is the clearest proof in the school that a thing you could not do last month is now yours.

tracks.name: Sit-ups
tracks.line: From five to fifty, and straight legs to the ceiling.

steps.test: Do five sit-ups, all the way up and all the way down.
how: Knees bent, feet flat, hands on your chest rather than behind your head.
Up until your chest is near your knees, down until your shoulders touch.
Feet lifting? Tuck them under a sofa while you build the strength.
steps.note: Hands behind the head is how people end up pulling on their own neck. Crossed on the chest from day one saves you that.

steps.test: Do ten without stopping.
how: Steady, no bouncing off the floor at the bottom.
Breathe out on the way up.
All the way down every rep — half sit-ups are where the cheating starts.
steps.note: If you are already well past ten, start at the rung that is actually hard and count the ones below as done.

steps.test: Hold yourself halfway up for twenty seconds.
how: Sit up halfway, lean back until you feel it, and stop there.
Arms out in front, back rounded slightly, breathing.
Shaking is normal. Falling back is the end of the hold.
steps.note: This is the position every sit-up passes through. Holding it teaches your middle to do the work that momentum was doing.

steps.test: Do fifteen without stopping.
how: Same shape, same depth.
Slow the last five down rather than speeding them up.
Neck relaxed — if it aches, you are pulling with it.
steps.note: Fifteen is where sit-ups stop being about learning the movement and start being training.

steps.test: Do sit-ups on three separate days in one week.
how: Three sets each day, a day off between where you can.
Stop two or three short of failure every set.
Write the three days down and tick them off.
steps.note: As with everything physical, how often beats how hard. Three short sessions a week moves the number; one long one on a Sunday does not.

steps.test: Do twenty without stopping.
how: Build with sets of twelve to fifteen on your training days.
Fresh, at the start of a session.
Full range to the last one.
steps.note: Twenty is more than most people manage properly, and it is about the point where you feel it in how you get out of bed.

steps.test: Do ten slowly — three seconds up and three seconds down.
how: Count it out. Sixty seconds of unbroken work.
No rest at the bottom and no flopping down.
Six honest slow ones beat ten rushed ones.
steps.note: Slow is where the strength is. This rung is why your ordinary number jumps a fortnight later without you chasing it.

steps.test: Lie on your back and lift both straight legs up to vertical, ten times.
how: Hands under your backside, legs straight, lift until your feet point at the ceiling.
Lower slowly. Do not let your lower back arch off the floor — if it does, bend your knees a little.
Ten controlled ones.
steps.note: This is the lower half of your middle, which sit-ups barely touch and which is the half that protects your back.

steps.test: Do thirty without stopping.
how: Find a rhythm and hold it. Count in tens.
Breathe out up, in down, every rep.
Shoulders to the floor at the bottom.
steps.note: Thirty takes about a minute. The second half is a test of staying steady rather than a test of strength.

steps.test: Hold yourself halfway up for a full minute.
how: Timer on. Arms out in front, leaning back, breathing.
Break it into two thirties if you must, then close the gap.
Stop the second your back arches or your feet lift.
steps.note: A minute here is a stronger middle than forty fast sit-ups, and it is kinder to your neck and your back.

steps.test: Do forty without stopping.
how: Pace it from the first rep, not the twentieth.
Full range or it does not count.
If you stop at thirty-four, that is the number — go again in three days.
steps.note: Forty is roughly the end of what more reps can teach you. From here the ladder turns to harder movements instead.

steps.test: Lift both straight legs to vertical twenty times.
how: Slower on the way down than on the way up.
Lower back stays flat on the floor the whole way.
Hands under your backside for support if you need them.
steps.note: Twenty of these is a genuinely strong lower middle, and it is what stops a long day of lifting turning into a sore back.

steps.test: Do a hundred across one day, in as many sets as you like.
how: Twenty every time you pass the living room floor.
Nothing has to be hard. Spread them wide.
Count as you go.
steps.note: Volume across a day builds without leaving you sore. This is the week before you go for fifty.

steps.test: Hold a hollow position for thirty seconds: legs and shoulders both off the floor.
how: On your back, lower back pressed flat, legs straight out just off the floor, shoulders and arms lifted.
Lower back flat is the whole exercise. The moment it arches, bring your legs higher.
Knees bent makes it easier while you learn it.
steps.note: Gymnasts build everything on this one position. Thirty seconds of it is worth more than a hundred sit-ups and takes half a minute.

steps.test: Do fifty sit-ups without stopping.
how: Fresh, first thing, at a rhythm you could keep up for eighty.
Full range to the very last one.
Neck loose, hands on your chest, breathing out on the way up.
steps.note: Fifty unbroken is the number end of this ladder. Everything after it is about making the movement harder rather than doing more of it.

steps.test: Do twenty sit-ups holding something heavy on your chest.
how: A full rucksack, a bag of rice, a heavy book held against your chest.
Same shape, same range, slower.
Nothing to hand? Fill a bag with books.
steps.note: Adding weight is how you keep this useful once fifty is easy, and it is a far better use of five minutes than a hundred fast ones.

steps.test: Hold a hollow position for a full minute.
how: Timer on, lower back flat, breathing normally.
Lower your legs a little each week as it gets easier — lower is harder.
Break the line and the hold is over.
steps.note: A minute of hollow with your legs low is a very strong middle, and unlike a long plank it carries straight over into everything else.

steps.test: Hang from a bar and lift your knees to your chest ten times.
how: A park bar, a beam, a door frame bar. Hang with straight arms, feet off the ground.
Knees up to your chest, then lower slowly. No swinging.
Free option: almost every play park has a bar you can hang from.
steps.note: Hanging leg work is the hardest thing you can do for your middle and it builds grip at the same time. Ten with no swing is a real rung.

steps.test: Do sit-ups every other day for a fortnight.
how: Seven sessions in fourteen days, three sets each, never to complete failure.
Mix them: sit-ups, leg lifts, a hollow hold, every session.
Miss one and do it the next day rather than restarting.
steps.note: Two clean weeks is what turns this from something you did into something you do.

steps.test: Hold a hollow position for a minute, then do fifty sit-ups, in the same session.
how: Hollow first, rest two minutes, then the fifty.
Both to full range, both honest.
That is the ladder.
steps.note: Strong in a hold and strong in a movement, in the same five minutes on a floor, with no equipment bought. That is as much as this part of you needs.

tracks.about: The front of your middle, trained on a floor with nothing else. This one stops at fifty in one go and turns to harder movements instead of bigger numbers, because a hundred fast sit-ups teaches your neck more than your stomach. Do it alongside the plank, not instead of it: one is moving, one is holding, and a middle needs both.

tracks.name: Pull-ups
tracks.line: From hanging on for ten seconds to five in a row.

steps.test: Hang from a bar with your feet off the ground for ten seconds.
how: Hands a little wider than your shoulders, palms facing away, arms straight.
Feet off the ground. Let your shoulders stretch up at first.
Free option: almost every play park and outdoor gym has a bar at the right height.
steps.note: Grip is usually what gives out first, and it is the quickest thing to improve. Ten seconds becomes thirty within a fortnight of trying.

steps.test: Hang for twenty seconds.
how: Same hold, relaxed shoulders, breathing.
If your hands hurt, that is the skin, not the strength — it toughens in a week.
Two hangs of fifteen with a rest is fine on the way there.
steps.note: A daily hang is also the best thing there is for shoulders that have spent the day at a desk.

steps.test: Hang and pull your shoulders down away from your ears, five times.
how: Start hanging loose, then without bending your arms, pull your shoulder blades down.
You rise an inch or two. Hold for two seconds, then let back down.
Five slow ones. Arms stay straight throughout.
steps.note: This tiny movement is the first inch of a pull-up and the piece nearly everybody is missing. Learn it before you ever bend an elbow.

steps.test: Hang for thirty seconds.
how: One hang, thirty seconds, feet off the ground.
Shoulders pulled down rather than up by your ears.
Chalk not required. Dry hands are enough.
steps.note: Thirty seconds of dead hang means grip is no longer the thing stopping you, which matters because it is about to stop being the easy part.

steps.test: Do five rows under a low bar or a sturdy table, feet on the floor.
how: Lie underneath, grab the edge, body straight, arms straight at the bottom.
Pull until your chest touches, then lower all the way down.
Knees bent and feet flat makes it easier; legs straight makes it harder.
steps.note: A row is a pull-up you can already do, at whatever angle suits you. This is where the pulling strength is actually built.

steps.test: Do ten rows.
how: Same shape, chest to the edge every rep.
Slower on the way down than on the way up.
Straighten your legs out if ten is comfortable.
steps.note: If you only ever did rows you would end up with a strong back and no pull-up. They are the base, not the goal — but the base has to be there.

steps.test: Do fifteen rows with your legs straight.
how: Heels on the floor, body one straight line, chest to the bar every time.
Fifteen in a row, controlled.
Heels on a chair when this gets easy — that is almost a horizontal pull-up.
steps.note: Fifteen straight-legged rows is roughly the strength a first pull-up sits on. Most people who cannot do a pull-up cannot do this either.

steps.test: Jump to the top of a pull-up and hold your chin over the bar for five seconds.
how: Jump, or step off a bench, so your chin starts above the bar.
Hold there — elbows in, chest up to the bar, shoulders down.
Five seconds, then lower yourself rather than dropping.
steps.note: The top is the position you are trying to reach, so it is worth learning what it feels like before you can get there on your own.

steps.test: Hold your chin over the bar for ten seconds.
how: Same jump to the top, ten seconds of holding on.
