Chest towards the bar, not chin craned over it.
Two holds of seven with a rest is fine on the way.
steps.note: Ten seconds at the top is worth about three ordinary pull-ups' worth of work and you can do it today.

steps.test: Jump to the top and lower yourself as slowly as you can, three times.
how: Get to the top, then take as long as you can to come down to straight arms.
Five seconds is good. Ten is excellent.
Rest a full minute between each. Three is plenty.
steps.note: You can lower far more than you can lift, which is exactly why this is how a first pull-up is built. This rung is the single most useful one on the ladder.

steps.test: Lower yourself over a slow count of five, five times.
how: Five seconds down, every time, all the way to straight arms.
No dropping the last bit — control to the end is the rung.
A minute's rest between each one.
steps.note: If the fifth one is as slow as the first, you are close. Most people find the first pull-up appears within three weeks of doing these twice a week.

steps.test: Do the slow lowerings twice a week for a fortnight.
how: Four sessions in fourteen days: five slow lowerings, plus fifteen rows, plus a thirty-second hang.
Never more than twice a week — this is hard on the arms and needs the recovery.
Write the four sessions down and tick them off.
steps.note: This is the fortnight where the pull-up is actually bought. Everything before it was preparation and everything after it is counting.

steps.test: Do five pull-ups with one foot resting on a chair.
how: Chair or bench under the bar, one foot on it, using the leg just enough to keep going.
Chin over the bar every rep, lower all the way down.
Use less leg each week.
steps.note: The foot on the chair is a dial you can turn down a fraction at a time, which is far better than failing at nothing repeatedly.

steps.test: Do five pull-ups with somebody holding your feet, or with a band.
how: A hand under each foot, taking just enough weight that you can finish the set.
Ask them to help less on each rep.
No band needed, and no band is better — a person can give you exactly what you need.
steps.note: This is also a good way to get somebody else onto the bar, since they will want a go once they have held your feet.

steps.test: Do one pull-up on your own, chin clearly over the bar.
how: Fresh, first thing, dead hang to start — no swinging, no kipping.
Pull your shoulders down first, then bend your arms.
Chin clearly over. All the way down after.
steps.note: This is one of the few things in life you genuinely cannot fake, and the day it arrives is a day you remember. A good many adults will never do one.

steps.test: Do one pull-up on three separate days in one week.
how: One is plenty per session — do three or four singles with long rests.
Strict every time. Never let the form slip to get a number.
Rows and hangs on the days in between.
steps.note: Three separate days proves it was not a fluke and is also exactly how the second one is built.

steps.test: Do two in a row.
how: Dead hang, up, all the way down, up again without dropping off.
Rest three minutes and try again rather than grinding sets.
Keep doing the slow lowerings on the other days.
steps.note: The second one is the hardest jump on the ladder. From two onwards the numbers come much faster.

steps.test: Do three in a row.
how: Fresh, dead hang, full range.
Build with singles and doubles, four or five sets, plenty of rest.
Never train these to complete failure.
steps.note: Three is where people stop asking whether you can do a pull-up and start asking how many.

steps.test: Do five across a day, in singles.
how: One every time you pass the bar. Five by bedtime.
Strict every time, no rushing.
Great to do on a day at a park with the family.
steps.note: Little and often is how this whole ladder works, and it is also how you stay fresh enough to keep adding.

steps.test: Do five in a row, and show somebody the slow lowering.
how: Dead hang, five strict pull-ups, all the way down each time.
Then put somebody else on the bar and teach them the slow lowering.
Tell them the honest timescale: a couple of months, twice a week.
steps.note: Five strict pull-ups is a strong adult by any standard, from a start of hanging on for ten seconds. Teaching the lowering is the whole ladder in one gift.

tracks.about: The hardest thing in the school to get the first one of, and the most satisfying. It is the one ladder here that needs something to hang from — a park bar, a beam, a strong branch, a door frame bar — and nothing else. The path is not more pull-ups, because you cannot do any yet: it is hanging, then rows under a table, then lowering yourself slowly from the top. Do those three and the first one arrives on its own.

tracks.name: The plank
tracks.line: Twenty seconds, up to a solid two minutes and a side plank.

steps.test: Hold a plank for twenty seconds with your hips level.
how: Elbows under your shoulders, forearms flat, feet back, one straight line from heels to head.
Squeeze your backside and your stomach — that is what stops the sag.
When the line breaks, the hold is over. That is your number.
steps.note: A sagging plank does nothing for you and can hurt your back. Twenty honest seconds is worth more than a minute of hanging off your spine.

steps.test: Hold it for thirty seconds, breathing normally the whole time.
how: Timer on so you are not guessing.
In through the nose, out through the mouth, steadily.
If you are holding your breath, come down and try again.
steps.note: Breathing is the rung here, not the time. A plank you cannot breathe in is a plank you are bracing rather than holding.

steps.test: Hold it for forty-five seconds.
how: Look at the floor just in front of your hands — your neck follows your back.
Heels pushing back, crown of your head pushing forward.
Break at thirty-five? Come down, rest a minute, do two more thirties.
steps.note: Little and often beats one long hold. Three short honest planks in a session build more than one sagging long one.

steps.test: Hold it for one minute.
how: Pick a spot on the floor and stay with it.
Squeeze harder rather than waiting it out — that is what buys the last fifteen seconds.
Get it twice before you move on.
steps.note: A minute is the standard most people never need to beat for ordinary life. Everything past it is optional.

steps.test: Hold a side plank for twenty seconds on each side.
how: On one forearm, elbow under your shoulder, feet stacked or one in front of the other.
Hips lifted so you are a straight line from ankle to head.
Knee down on the floor makes it easier while you learn it.
steps.note: The sides of your middle are what a normal plank misses entirely, and they are what actually hold your back steady when you carry something in one hand.

steps.test: Hold a plank three separate times in one session, a minute each.
how: A minute on, a minute off, three times.
The third one is the rung. The first two are the warm-up.
Keep the shape identical in the third as in the first.
steps.note: Three honest minutes of work in five minutes of your life. This is the rung that makes the longer holds possible.

steps.test: Hold it for ninety seconds.
how: Timer, level hips, steady breathing.
Squeeze your backside hard — it is the one cue that works past a minute.
Break at seventy? Hold seventy twice and come back in two days.
steps.note: Past a minute this becomes a test of staying calm while something is uncomfortable. That is worth practising for its own sake.

steps.test: Hold a side plank for forty-five seconds on each side.
how: Feet stacked, hips high, top arm straight up or on your hip.
The weaker side goes first and gets an extra set.
Do not let your hips drift backwards — stay in one flat plane.
steps.note: One side being clearly worse is normal and worth knowing about. Give that side the extra work until they match.

steps.test: Hold a plank with one foot off the floor, twenty seconds each side.
how: Normal plank, then lift one foot a few inches. Do not let your hips twist.
Twenty seconds, swap, twenty seconds.
Steady, small lift. This is about not moving, not about lifting high.
steps.note: Taking one point of contact away is how you make a plank harder without making it longer. Twenty seconds here is worth two minutes flat.

steps.test: Hold it for two minutes.
how: Fresh, at the start of a session.
Count in blocks of fifteen so the number stays small.
The shape holds or it does not count.
steps.note: Two minutes is the honest end of the ordinary plank. If you have it, stop adding time and start taking feet off the floor instead.

steps.test: Hold a side plank for a full minute on each side.
how: Both sides in the same session, a minute's rest between.
Hips high the whole way.
Lift the top leg for the last ten seconds once a minute is easy.
steps.note: A minute a side is a strong middle by any measure, and it shows up as carrying a bag on one shoulder without leaning.

steps.test: Hold a two-minute plank with one foot off the floor for thirty seconds of it.
how: Two minutes in total: thirty normal, thirty left foot up, thirty right foot up, thirty normal.
No twisting at the hips through the swaps.
That is the end of this ladder.
steps.note: Harder, not longer, is the rule from here. If you want more, go to the sit-up ladder or hang from a bar and lift your knees.

tracks.about: The plank trains the part of you that stops your back hurting, and it needs a patch of floor and nothing else. This one stops at two minutes on purpose: past that it is a party trick, and a side plank or a one-foot plank buys far more for the same time. A few weeks of a minute a day is enough to feel it in how you stand.

tracks.name: Squats
tracks.line: From ten to a hundred, and one on one leg.

steps.test: Do ten squats with your heels flat and your thighs level at the bottom.
how: Feet about shoulder width, toes turned out a little, chest up.
Sit back and down as if a chair were behind you, then stand all the way up.
Heels lifting? Stand with them on a folded towel or a thin book and go again.
steps.note: Nearly everybody can already do ten of something they call a squat. The rung is ten where the thighs actually reach level — it is a different exercise and you will feel it.

steps.test: Sit at the bottom of a squat for thirty seconds.
how: All the way down, heels flat, and stay there.
Hold onto a door frame at first if you tip backwards.
Relax into it rather than fighting it. Breathe.
steps.note: This is the position half the world rests in and most of us have lost. Getting it back is what makes every squat above it easy, so it comes early on purpose.

steps.test: Do twenty in one go.
how: Steady pace from the first rep, not fast.
Depth on the last one the same as the first.
Knees push out over your toes, never caving inwards.
steps.note: Twenty is where you start breathing. Breathe out on the way up, every rep, and the whole thing gets easier.

steps.test: Do thirty in one go.
how: Keep the last five as clean as the first five.
Shaking legs are normal, caving knees are not.
If depth goes at twenty-six, stop at twenty-six — that is the number.
steps.note: Thirty good squats a few days a week is enough on its own to change how stairs and hills feel. Most people notice that before they notice anything else.

steps.test: Do squats on three separate days in one week.
how: Three sets each day, a day off between where you can.
Never to complete failure — stop two or three short.
Write the three days down and tick them off.
steps.note: This is the rung that makes the rest happen. Legs answer to how often, not how hard.

steps.test: Sit at the bottom of a squat for a full minute.
how: Heels down, back reasonably straight, nothing to hold on to.
Shift about, look around, breathe — it is a rest position, not a hold.
Split into two thirties if you need to, then close the gap.
steps.note: A minute at the bottom without holding anything means your ankles and hips have opened up properly. From here the deep end of every squat stops being a fight.

steps.test: Do fifty in one go.
how: Pace it like a run. The first twenty should feel too easy.
Breathe in down, out up, every rep.
Break it as twenty-five and twenty-five, then close the gap over a fortnight.
steps.note: Fifty in one go puts you past almost everybody you know. It is also the point where squats become a lungs exercise as much as a legs one.

steps.test: Do ten slowly — four seconds down and four seconds up.
how: Count it out. Eighty seconds of unbroken work.
No pause at the top to shake it off.
If you cannot hold the count, do six and build up.
steps.note: Slow reps are where the strength comes from. Ten of these is harder than fifty normal ones and does more for your next number.

steps.test: Do twenty holding something heavy at your chest.
how: A full rucksack, a bag of potatoes, a water container, a small child who thinks it is a game.
Held against your chest with both arms, elbows in.
Nothing to hand? Fill a rucksack with books and wear it on your front.
steps.note: Adding weight is how a squat keeps getting harder once the reps get silly. Everything you need is already in the house and none of it costs anything.

steps.test: Do seventy in one go.
how: Rhythm is everything now. Find one and do not change it.
Small pauses at the top are allowed. Stopping is not.
Depth to the last one.
steps.note: Seventy takes about two and a half minutes and it is mostly a test of whether you will keep going when it is boring and burning. That is the useful part.

steps.test: Do a hundred across one day, split however you like.
how: Twenty every time you boil the kettle, or ten an hour.
Nothing has to be hard. Spread them wide.
Count as you go.
steps.note: Volume across a day builds legs beautifully and costs nothing in recovery. Do this in the week before you go for a hundred in one go.

steps.test: Do ten jump squats, landing quietly.
how: Down to level, then jump, then land soft with bent knees and go straight into the next.
Quiet landings are the rung. Loud landings mean you are crashing through your knees.
Sore knees? Skip this rung and do thirty holding something heavy instead.
steps.note: Power is a different quality from strength and it is the first one that goes with age. Ten quiet jumps a week keeps it.

steps.test: Do thirty holding something heavy.
how: Same load as before, or heavier if twenty became easy.
Depth first, number second.
Set it down between sets rather than dropping it.
steps.note: Thirty loaded squats is a real bit of work and the closest this school gets to a gym without you ever going near one.

steps.test: Do a hundred in one go.
how: Start absurdly slow. A hundred is about four minutes of work.
Count in tens so the number stays small in your head.
Breathe every rep and keep the depth honest to the end.
steps.note: A hundred unbroken squats is the far end of what reps alone can give you. From here the ladder turns to one leg, which is a harder and more useful thing.

steps.test: Stand on one leg and go down as far as you can, holding onto a door frame.
how: One foot flat, the other leg held out in front, both hands on a door frame or a chair back.
Down slowly, as far as you can control, then pull yourself back up.
Use as much arm as you need at first.
steps.note: This is the start of the one-leg squat and it is more balance and ankle than strength. Nearly everybody tips over on the first attempt. That is the exercise.
steps.twist: The leg you would never choose first.

steps.test: Go halfway down on one leg without holding anything.
how: Arms straight out in front to balance, other leg held out.
Halfway is thigh at about forty-five degrees. Come back up under control.
Practise both legs — one will be noticeably worse and it needs the extra sets.
steps.note: Balance improves within days of trying this, and it is the single thing that keeps people on their feet in old age.
steps.twist: The leg you would never choose first.

steps.test: Go down on one leg onto a low seat and stand back up.
how: Sit down onto a low chair, stool or the second step with one leg out in front.
Touch down, do not flop, then stand up on the same leg without rocking.
Lower the seat over a few weeks until it is nearly the floor.
steps.note: The seat is your dial: the lower it goes, the closer you are to the full thing. This is exactly how the full one gets built.

steps.test: Do one squat on one leg, all the way down and back up.
how: Other leg out in front and off the ground the whole way.
All the way down, backside near the heel, then up without touching down.
Hold a small weight out in front — it acts as a counterbalance and makes it easier.
steps.note: Very few adults can do this. It is the best single test there is of leg strength, balance and ankle range together, and it needs nothing but a floor.

steps.test: Do three on one leg, on both legs.
how: Three in a row on each side, without touching down between them.
The weaker side gets twice the practice until it catches up.
Rest a full minute between sides.
steps.note: Three each side means it was not a fluke and both legs actually own it. That is the difference between a trick and a skill.

steps.test: Do a hundred and fifty across one day, and walk properly the next.
how: Spread them right across the day in sets of fifteen or twenty.
The rung is the next morning: stairs without wincing.
Walk, and get your legs moving the day after rather than sitting still.
steps.note: Being able to do a big day's work and be fine the next morning is what fitness actually is. That is the ladder finished.

tracks.about: Legs are the muscles you use every single day and the first ones people lose. This ladder goes from ten honest squats to a hundred in one go and a squat on one leg, which almost nobody can do. It needs no equipment and no space beyond a patch of floor, and it is the quickest thing in the school to notice in ordinary life: stairs, hills, getting off the ground, carrying a child upstairs.

tracks.name: Lifting
tracks.line: Picking a heavy thing up properly, and putting it up high.

steps.test: Pick something heavy up off the floor with a straight back, and put it down again.
how: Stand close to it, feet apart, bend at the hips and knees rather than rounding your back.
Grip it, take the slack out of your arms, then stand up by pushing the floor away.
Set it down the same way. Lowering carelessly is how most backs go.
steps.note: Close to you, back straight, legs doing the work. That is the whole technique and it does not change however heavy the object gets.

steps.test: Do that ten times without your back rounding once.
how: Watch yourself in a window or a mirror, or have somebody watch your back.
Stop the set the moment your back rounds — that is the number, not a failure.
Reset your feet and your grip before every single rep.
steps.note: Ten in a row is where technique either holds or shows itself up. Practising with something light and getting it perfect is the point.

steps.test: Lift something the weight of your own head straight up overhead.
how: A full kettle, a heavy book, a bag with a few tins in it. About four or five kilos.
Press it straight up until your arms are locked out beside your ears.
Ribs down, backside squeezed — do not lean back to get it up.
steps.note: Overhead is the range most adults quietly lose first, and losing it is why high shelves become somebody else's job.

steps.test: Lift something heavy from the floor onto a table in one smooth movement.
how: A crate, a box of books, a bag of compost.
Straight back down, stand up with it, step in and set it down — no dropping, no swinging.
If you have to jerk it, it is too heavy. Go lighter and do it properly.
steps.note: Smooth is stronger than fast. A lift that has to be snatched is a lift that is about to go wrong.

steps.test: Put something heavy on a high shelf without wobbling.
how: Lift to your chest first, then press it up and onto the shelf.
Get your feet under you before the weight goes overhead.
Both hands stay on it until it is resting.
steps.note: The dangerous moment is never the lifting — it is the half second when you are reaching and the weight is out in front of you.

steps.test: Carry something awkward up a full flight of stairs.
how: A box, a full laundry basket, a bag of sand — something with no good handles.
Hold it high and close to your chest so you can see your feet.
Go slowly. One step at a time, no rushing the last few.
steps.note: Awkward beats heavy for causing injuries. Everything in real life is awkward, so it is worth practising on purpose.

steps.test: Lift something heavy from the floor to your shoulder in one go.
how: A sack of potatoes or compost, a heavy holdall, a bag of coal.
Floor to chest, then roll it onto your shoulder and stand tall.
Both hands on it, back straight, legs doing the work.
steps.note: Floor to shoulder is the old test of everyday strength, and it is the one movement that covers almost everything a working day asks for.

steps.test: Move ten heavy things with somebody, taking the awkward end every time.
how: A wardrobe, a sofa, a washing machine, boxes, a bed frame.
Take the end that is harder to hold or has to go backwards up the stairs.
Agree the plan out loud before you lift: where it is going, who steps first.
steps.note: Lifting with somebody is a skill of its own: the talking matters more than the strength, and the person who takes the awkward end is the one who gets asked back.

steps.test: Lift something half your own weight off the floor, ten times.
how: A well-packed rucksack, two water containers tied together, a heavy case.
Straight back, close to you, legs pushing the floor away.
Stop at the first rounded back rather than at ten.
steps.note: Half your bodyweight lifted ten times is a genuinely strong back and hips, and every bit of it was built with household objects.

steps.test: Lift something your own bodyweight off the floor.
how: A very full case, a heavy person on a chair with two of you, a loaded sack barrow.
One clean lift, an inch off the ground is enough, straight back throughout.
If you cannot keep your back straight, it is too heavy. That is not a rung worth forcing.
steps.note: Your own bodyweight off the floor is a proper benchmark. It is also the rung to be sensible on: nothing here is worth a hurt back.

steps.test: Lift something the weight of a small child overhead, five times.
how: Fifteen kilos or so — a full rucksack, a water container, a bag of coal.
Chest first, then press up, arms locked out beside your ears.
Ribs down, no leaning back.
steps.note: Being able to put something heavy over your head is what keeps you independent in a house with high shelves, lofts and roof boxes.

steps.test: Help somebody move house for a whole day, and still be useful at the end of it.
how: Offer before you are asked. Turn up early with gloves.
Take the awkward end, pace yourself, and keep your technique when you are tired.
The rung is the last hour, not the first.
steps.note: Technique when you are fresh is easy. Technique in the last hour, when everybody is tired and careless, is what this ladder was actually for.

tracks.about: Getting something heavy off the floor and up onto a shelf, without hurting yourself. This is the least glamorous and most useful physical skill there is: almost every bad back in the world came from one careless lift. Everything you need is already in the house — bags, boxes, water containers, sacks of coal or compost. Carrying it any distance is its own ladder.

tracks.name: Bending and stretching
tracks.line: From reaching past your knees to both palms flat on the floor.

steps.test: Stand with straight legs and reach past your knees.
how: Feet together, knees locked but not jammed back.
Fold from the hips rather than curling your shoulders down.
Wherever your hands get to, stop and breathe there for twenty seconds.
steps.note: This is a measurement, not a competition. Wherever you reach today is the honest start, and it moves faster than anything else in this school.

steps.test: Sit on the floor with your legs straight out and reach towards your ankles.
how: Sit up tall first, then hinge forward from the hips.
Knees pressed down, toes pointing up.
Sitting on the edge of a cushion makes it much easier at the start.
steps.note: Sitting takes your balance out of the equation so you feel the stretch where it actually is: the backs of your legs.

steps.test: Hold a hamstring stretch for a full minute on each leg.
how: Lie on your back, one leg straight up, hands behind the thigh, other leg flat on the floor.
Straight knee on the lifted leg matters more than how high it goes.
Breathe out and let it sink a little further every few breaths.
steps.note: A minute is where a stretch stops being a stretch and starts being a change. Thirty seconds feels nice and does much less.

steps.test: Stretch for five minutes every morning for five days running.
how: Same five minutes: standing fold, sitting fold, one minute a leg on your back.
Set it right after something you already do — the kettle, the shower.
Five days, ticked off.
steps.note: Stretching answers to how often more than any other kind of training. Five minutes daily beats an hour on a Sunday by a distance.

steps.test: Touch your toes with your knees slightly bent.
how: Soft knees, fold from the hips, let your head hang heavy.
Hold for thirty seconds rather than bouncing at it.
Bend as much as you need to reach — this rung is about the fold, not the legs.
steps.note: Bent knees take the backs of your legs out of it and let your lower back open. It is the honest halfway house to the real thing.

steps.test: Hold a deep squat with your heels down for thirty seconds.
how: All the way down, heels flat, backside near your ankles.
Hold a door frame at first if you fall backwards.
Heels lifting? Stand them on a folded towel and lower it over the weeks.
steps.note: This is the position half the world still rests in. Getting it back opens your ankles and hips, which is most of what stops people touching their toes.

steps.test: Reach one hand over your shoulder and the other up your back, and touch your fingers.
how: One arm up and over, elbow pointing at the ceiling; the other arm up behind your back.
Walk the fingers towards each other.
Hold a tea towel between your hands and climb it if they do not meet.
steps.note: Shoulders quietly close up from years of desks and phones. The tea towel is how you measure the gap closing week by week.

steps.test: Do the same with the other arm on top.
how: Swap which arm goes over the shoulder.
One side will be clearly worse. That side gets twice the practice.
Tea towel again if needed.
steps.note: Everybody is lopsided here and almost nobody notices until they try it. Evening the two sides up is worth more than making the good side better.

steps.test: Hold the deep squat for a full minute.
how: Nothing to hold on to, heels flat, back reasonably straight.
Move about, look around, breathe — it is a rest, not a hold.
Two thirties with a rest is fine on the way there.
steps.note: A minute at the bottom with nothing to hold means your ankles and hips have genuinely opened. Everything below gets easier from here.

steps.test: Stretch every day for two weeks without missing one.
how: Ten minutes: the folds, a minute a leg, a deep squat, both shoulders.
Fourteen days in a row, written down and ticked off.
Miss one and do it that evening rather than restarting.
steps.note: This fortnight is where the change becomes yours rather than borrowed. Range you stop using goes away again within a month, which is the whole reason for the habit.

steps.test: Touch your toes with your legs completely straight.
how: Feet together, knees locked, fold from the hips.
Come up slowly rather than snapping up.
Warm first — after a walk or a bath is far easier than cold.
steps.note: This is the one everybody has heard of, and most adults cannot do it. If you have it already, hold your toes for thirty seconds and move on.

steps.test: Hold your toes for thirty seconds with your legs straight.
how: Get down there, take hold, and stay.
Breathe out and let it sink on each breath.
Straight knees the whole time or it is a different exercise.
steps.note: Touching and holding are two different things. Holding is what actually moves the range.

steps.test: Sit with your legs wide and lean forward until your elbows reach the floor.
how: Legs as wide as is comfortable, toes up, sit tall first.
Hinge from the hips, not from your back.
Sit on a cushion to tip your hips forward if you cannot sit up straight.
steps.note: The insides of the legs are the piece that the toe-touch never reaches and the piece that makes sitting on the floor comfortable again.

steps.test: Lie on your back and pull one straight leg up until it points at the ceiling.
how: Other leg flat on the floor, both knees straight.
Hands behind the thigh or a towel round the foot to pull gently.
Hold a minute each side.
steps.note: Straight up with the other leg flat is a proper hamstring, and having it on both sides is what makes running and lifting safe.

steps.test: Kneel, lean back and hold your heels for twenty seconds.
how: Kneel with your feet behind you, hips pushed forward, reach back for your heels.
Hips forward is the rung — do not just fold backwards from the waist.
Hands on a low chair behind you instead, if the heels are too far.
steps.note: This opens the fronts of your hips and thighs, which shorten from sitting more than any other part of you.

steps.test: Hold a lunge stretch for a minute on each side.
how: One foot forward, back knee on the floor, hips pushed forward and down.
Chest up and back straight — do not lean over the front leg.
A folded towel under the back knee makes it bearable.
steps.note: The front of the hip is the quiet cause of most sore lower backs. A minute a side, daily, is a remarkably good trade.

steps.test: Put your knuckles on the floor with your legs straight.
how: Fold from the hips, straight knees, reach for the floor with loose fists.
Warm up first. Cold, this rung will not come.
Hold for twenty seconds once you get there.
steps.note: Knuckles down is the last stop before palms, and the point at which strangers start commenting on it.

steps.test: Hold a bridge — hands and feet down, hips up — for twenty seconds.
how: Lie on your back, hands by your ears, push up onto your hands and feet.
Hips as high as they go, arms pushing you away from the floor.
Too hard? Push up onto the top of your head first, then to straight arms over a few weeks.
steps.note: The bridge is everything this ladder has opened, all at once: shoulders, hips and back. It is also the most fun thing here.

steps.test: Put both palms flat on the floor with your knees a little bent.
how: Small bend in the knees, fold from the hips, both palms flat.
Then try straightening the knees a fraction at a time.
Warm, at the end of the day, is when this will come.
steps.note: Palms flat with soft knees means you already have the range. The last rung is simply the same thing with the knees locked.

steps.test: Put both palms flat on the floor with your legs straight, and hold it for ten seconds.
how: Feet together, knees locked, both palms flat, ten seconds.
Come up slowly.
Do it again two days later to be sure it was not a warm-day fluke.
steps.note: That is the ladder. Most adults cannot do this, most assume it is a thing you are born with, and it took you ten minutes a day and no money at all.

tracks.about: Getting back the range you had as a child. Palms flat on the floor with straight legs is a genuinely hard thing that most adults cannot do, and it takes five or ten minutes a day for a few months rather than any talent. It needs no equipment, no space and no money, and unlike almost everything else physical, it is easiest to do at the end of the day in front of the fire. Everything else in the Fitness path works better once you have it.

tracks.name: Sprinting
tracks.line: From ten seconds flat out to a hundred metres you have beaten twice.

steps.test: Sprint flat out for ten seconds.
how: Warm up first: five minutes of walking and jogging, then a few faster runs.
Ten seconds at about nine tenths, not a hundred per cent, the first time.
Grass or a track is kinder than pavement.
steps.note: Never sprint cold. Pulled hamstrings almost always happen on the first sprint of the day, and five minutes of warming up prevents nearly all of them.

steps.test: Sprint ten seconds, walk a minute, and do it five times.
how: Five sprints, full walking recovery between each.
If the fifth is much slower than the first, your rests are too short.
The whole session is about eight minutes plus the warm-up.
steps.note: Long rests feel like cheating and are the entire method. Sprinting trains speed, and speed is only trained when you are fresh.

steps.test: Run a hundred metres without slowing down at the end.
how: Pace out a hundred metres, or use a football pitch — it is about one and a bit lengths.
Build up over the first twenty metres rather than exploding off the line.
Run through the finish, not to it.
steps.note: Nearly everybody slows in the last twenty metres. Holding the speed to the line is the skill and it is worth more than a fast start.

steps.test: Time your hundred metres and write the number down.
how: Get somebody to time you, or use a phone stopwatch on a wall.
Warm up properly, then one honest run.
Write it down with the date, whatever it is.
steps.note: Whatever the number, it is your number and it is about to get smaller. Nobody else ever sees it.

steps.test: Sprint from a standing start ten times, resting properly between each.
how: Thirty to forty metres each, walk back slowly, go again when your breath is back.
Two full minutes between sprints is not too long.
Stop the session the moment they start getting slower.
steps.note: The standing start is where the power is. Stopping while you are still fast is how you get faster, which is the opposite of how most training feels.

steps.test: Sprint uphill five times.
how: A short steep hill, twenty or thirty metres, walk down between each.
Drive the arms, short steps, lean into the hill.
No hill? A steep set of steps or a long ramp.
steps.note: Hill sprints are the safest kind — the hill slows you down just enough that hamstrings almost never complain — and they build power quickly.

steps.test: Beat your hundred metre time.
how: Same stretch of ground, same timing method, a fresh day.
Warm up longer than last time. It is worth a tenth of a second on its own.
Write the new number under the old one.
steps.note: The first improvement is usually large and is mostly technique: warming up, building speed properly, and running through the line.

steps.test: Sprint on two separate days in one week.
how: Two sessions, five or six sprints each, long rests.
Never on back-to-back days — this needs the recovery.
Write the two days down and tick them off.
steps.note: Twice a week is the most sprinting anybody needs. Any more and the sessions get slower, which trains the opposite of what you want.

steps.test: Run a hundred metres in under twenty seconds.
how: Full warm-up, one honest run, timed.
Relaxed face and shoulders — tension is slow.
Run through the line.
steps.note: Twenty seconds is a comfortable jog for a sprinter and a real effort for most adults. It is the first proper marker on the way down.

steps.test: Run a hundred metres in under eighteen seconds.
how: Warm up thoroughly, then two attempts at most, with a long rest between.
Drive the first twenty metres, then relax and hold it.
Grass costs you a second or so against a proper track — do not let that put you off.
steps.note: This is where your hill sprints and standing starts show up. From here the improvements get smaller and harder, which is fine.

steps.test: Run a hundred metres in under sixteen seconds.
how: Only on a day you are fresh and properly warm.
One good run beats four tired ones.
Have somebody time you rather than doing it yourself.
steps.note: Under sixteen is a genuinely quick hundred metres for an adult who is not training for it. That is the number end of this ladder.

steps.test: Race somebody, and beat your own old time doing it.
how: Anybody — a friend, a brother, one of the children with a head start.
Time the race as well as running it.
The rung is your own old number, not theirs.
steps.note: Racing somebody makes you faster than any session will, because you forget to hold anything back. It is also the most fun this ladder gets.

tracks.about: Flat-out running is a different quality from distance running, it is the first one to go with age, and it is almost never practised after school. This ladder is short on purpose: a handful of sprints with long rests, once or twice a week, on grass if you can. It costs nothing and it makes you feel about fifteen.

tracks.name: Getting strong, part one
tracks.line: Three honest numbers, then a round of three moves, up to ten proper press-ups.
tracks.about: This is the way in to everything physical in the school, and it needs nothing at all: no gym, no weights, no clothes you do not own, no money. Three moves — a squat, a press-up and a plank — done as one short round, a few days a week. You write down what you can do on day one, and at the end you write the same three numbers again underneath. Most people are somewhere around ten proper press-ups by the end of it, from nothing, in about three months. It takes six or seven minutes a session, and the reason it works is that it is small enough that you keep doing it.

steps.test: Write down three numbers: press-ups you can do in one go, squats in one go, seconds of a plank.
how: Do the three one after the other, with a good rest in between. This is a measurement, not a session.
Knees on the floor counts for the press-ups. Stop each one when your shape goes, not when it burns.
Write the three numbers down with today's date — paper, or a note on your phone.
Put it where you will find it again in three months.
steps.note: This is the rung everything else is measured against, so be honest — nobody else ever sees it. If the answer is none, write nought. Nought is a perfectly good starting number and it does not stay nought.

steps.test: Do ten squats with your heels flat on the floor and your thighs level at the bottom.
how: Feet about shoulder width, toes turned out a little.
Sit back and down as if there were a chair behind you, chest up, heels glued down.
Go until your thighs are level with the floor, then stand all the way up.
If your heels lift, stand with them on a folded towel or a book and go again.
steps.note: This is the move most people already own and do badly: they stop halfway and lean forward. Ten honest ones beat thirty half ones. If ten is easy, do them slower — three seconds down — and count that as the rung.

steps.test: Do five press-ups with your hands on a table or a windowsill.
how: Hands on the edge, a little wider than your shoulders, feet back so you are a straight plank.
Lower your chest to the edge, elbows going back at about forty-five degrees, not out sideways.
Push all the way up. Your hips move with your shoulders, never ahead of them.
Too easy? Use something lower — the arm of a sofa, the third step of the stairs.
steps.note: Raised hands are not a lesser press-up, they are the same press-up with less of you to lift. Everybody starts at the height where five are honest. If five on a table is easy, find the height where five is hard and stay there.

steps.test: Hold a plank for twenty seconds with your hips level.
how: Elbows under your shoulders, forearms flat, feet back, body in one straight line.
Squeeze your backside and your stomach. That is what stops your hips sagging.
Breathe normally the whole time. If you are holding your breath, come down.
Twenty honest seconds. When your hips drop, the hold is over — that is the number.
steps.note: A sagging plank does nothing for you and hurts your back. Come down the second the line breaks. If twenty seconds is easy, hold it until it is not, and write down what you got.

steps.test: Do all three back to back in one go: ten squats, five press-ups, twenty seconds of plank.
how: Squats first, straight into the press-ups, straight into the plank.
Rest as long as you like between the three if you need to, but do all three in one sitting.
It should take about two minutes.
That is one round. The rest of this ladder is that round, getting heavier.
steps.note: Here is the whole programme in one rung. From now on there is nothing new to learn — the three moves you have just done are the three moves for the next three months. The work is turning up, not learning.

steps.test: Do the round on three separate days in one week.
how: Three days, with a day off between them where you can — Monday, Wednesday, Friday is the classic.
Same round each time: ten squats, five press-ups, twenty seconds of plank.
Do it at the same point in the day, so it hangs off something you already do.
Tick the three days off somewhere you can see them.
steps.note: This is the most important rung in the ladder and the least impressive. Three sessions in one week is the thing that turns an afternoon of good intentions into a body that changes. If you already train three days a week, do these rounds inside that and count it.

steps.test: Do twenty squats in one go.
how: Same shape as before: heels down, thighs level, all the way up.
Slow down rather than bounce when it gets hard near the end.
If your form goes at seventeen, stop at seventeen and try again in two days.
Add these to your round from now on.
steps.note: Your round is now twenty squats, five press-ups, twenty seconds. The numbers change, the round does not.

steps.test: Do ten press-ups with your hands on a table.
how: Same table, same shape. Chest to the edge every time.
Do not rush. Two seconds down, one second up.
If you stall at seven, rest ten seconds and finish the last three. Next time, get all ten.
Then lower the height: sofa arm, or a chair against a wall.
steps.note: Doubling the reps is easier than it sounds because your shape is now honest. If ten on a table came easily, move to something lower before you move on — the rung is ten hard ones, not ten easy ones.

steps.test: Hold a plank for forty seconds.
how: Set a timer so you are not counting and guessing.
Squeeze everything from your heels to your shoulders. A plank is a squeeze, not a hang.
If the line breaks at thirty, come down, rest a minute, and hold twice more for twenty.
Two short honest holds beat one long sagging one.
steps.note: Forty seconds is roughly where the plank stops being about your arms and starts being about your middle. If your lower back aches, your hips are too low — lift them a fraction and squeeze harder.

steps.test: Do five press-ups with your hands on the bottom step of the stairs.
how: The lower your hands, the more of you there is to lift. The stairs are the dial.
Same shape: straight line, elbows back, chest to the step.
No stairs? Stack two thick books, or use the edge of a bed frame or a low sturdy box.
When five on the bottom step is comfortable, the floor is next.
steps.note: This is the rung where the programme starts to feel like real training. You are not learning anything new — you are turning the dial down one notch and doing the same five.

steps.test: Do two rounds back to back, with a minute between them.
how: Round one: twenty squats, five press-ups on the step, forty seconds of plank.
One minute of standing about, then round two, the same.
It should take about six minutes in all.
Two rounds is your session from now on.
steps.note: Volume is the quiet ingredient. Two rounds three times a week is six times as much work as one round once, and it still costs you six minutes.

steps.test: Do thirty squats in one go.
how: Thirty is where squats become breathing as much as legs. Let yourself breathe out on the way up.
Keep the last five as clean as the first five.
Legs shaking is normal. Knees caving inwards is not — push them out over your toes.
If thirty is easy, do them with a four-second lowering instead and count that.
steps.note: Thirty good squats a few days a week is enough on its own to change how stairs, hills and getting off the floor feel. Most people notice that before they notice anything in the mirror.

steps.test: Do two press-ups on the floor, chest all the way down.
how: Hands under your shoulders, body one straight line from heels to head.
Down until your chest is a fist's width from the floor, then all the way up. Nothing half-way counts.
Two is the rung. Two proper ones, not five bad ones.
Cannot get one? Go back to the bottom step for another week — it will come.
steps.note: This is the rung people remember. The first real press-up off the floor is a moment, and almost everybody who does the rounds three times a week gets there within a few weeks of starting. If you could already do two on day one, the rung is two slow ones: three seconds down, three seconds up.

steps.test: Hold a plank for one minute.
how: Timer on, hips level, breathing.
Break it into thirty and thirty with a rest if you must, then try the full minute two days later.
Look at the floor, not up — your neck should follow the line of your back.
One honest minute is a real thing to own.
steps.note: A minute is the standard most people will never need to go past for ordinary life. If it is easy, lift one foot off the floor for the last fifteen seconds rather than holding for five minutes.

steps.test: Do ten rows: lie under a sturdy table, grab the edge, and pull your chest up to it.
how: Heels on the floor, body straight, arms straight at the bottom.
Pull until your chest touches the underside of the table edge, then lower all the way down.
Too hard? Bend your knees and put your feet flat — that takes weight off.
No table you trust? A bannister, a low bar in a park, or a broom handle across two chairs.
steps.note: Everything so far has been pushing. This is the first pulling, and it is the half of the body that a floor programme normally forgets. Do it and your shoulders will thank you; skip it and press-ups slowly round your back.

steps.test: Do five press-ups on the floor without stopping.
how: Same shape. Five in a row, no resting at the top.
If you get three, rest twenty seconds and do two more. Next session, go for four in a row.
Add floor press-ups into your round now, even if it is only three.
Chest all the way down, every time.
steps.note: Two to five is usually about two weeks. This is also the point where the easiest mistake appears: chasing the number and letting the depth go. Half press-ups do not build anything. Count only the ones that go all the way down.

steps.test: Do forty squats in one go.
how: Pace yourself from the first one. Steady, not fast.
Breathe in on the way down, out on the way up, every rep.
If your heels lift near the end, that is fatigue — stop there and call it the number.
Split into twenty and twenty if you must, then try the forty again in two days.
steps.note: Forty in one go is a genuine bit of fitness, not a beginner's number. If you are already past forty, do twenty with something heavy held at your chest — a bag of potatoes, a full rucksack, a child — and count that.

steps.test: Do the round three days a week for a fortnight, without missing one.
how: Six sessions in fourteen days. Two rounds each session.
Write the six days down before you start and tick them off.
A session missed gets made up the next day — it does not get skipped.
Anything is better than nothing: one round, half a round, five squats in the kitchen all count as turning up.
steps.note: This is the rung that makes the rest of your life easy. After a fortnight of not missing, the sessions stop needing a decision. If you miss one anyway, do not start the fortnight again — just do the next one.

steps.test: Do ten press-ups on the floor without stopping.
how: Ten in a row, chest to the floor every time, no rest at the top.
Get there by doing more sets of fewer: six, six, six is how you get to ten.
Fresh, at the start of a session, not at the end of it.
When you have it, do it again two days later to be sure it was not a one-off.
steps.note: Ten proper press-ups from a standing start of none is the end of this ladder and it is a real thing. Most people who do the rounds three times a week are here inside three months. Thirty is part two and the press-up ladder; you are now well on the way to both.

steps.test: Write the three numbers again, underneath the first three.
how: Same three: press-ups in one go, squats in one go, seconds of plank.
Same conditions — fresh, with a rest between each.
Write them under the old ones with today's date, so you can see the two sets together.
Then read the first line again.
steps.note: This is the whole point of rung one. Numbers you wrote before you believed anything would happen are the only proof that cannot be argued with. Keep the paper: part two starts by setting the next three.

tracks.name: Getting strong, part two
tracks.line: From ten press-ups to twenty, two minutes of plank, and a body used outside the room.
tracks.about: Part one built the round. Part two makes it heavier and then takes it outdoors: the same three moves going up, pulling added properly, a walk that turns into a run, and something heavy carried down the street. It ends by asking you to pick the one ladder you want to push a long way — press-ups to thirty, squats to a hundred, a first pull-up, five kilometres — because by then you will know which one you actually want.

steps.test: Write down the three you are going for: twenty press-ups, sixty squats, two minutes of plank.
how: Under the two sets of numbers from part one.
Add the date you expect to have them. Be generous: about three months.
These are the ends of this ladder, not a hope.
If you are already past one of them, write the next number up instead and aim there.
steps.note: Named targets beat good intentions because you can tell whether you hit them. Everything in this ladder walks towards these three.

steps.test: Do the round twice through on three days in one week, at part one's finishing numbers.
how: Forty squats, ten floor press-ups, one minute of plank, ten rows. Twice through.
Three days, a rest day between where you can.
About twelve minutes a session now.
Get this week done before you chase any new number.
steps.note: Part one ended at these numbers once. This rung makes them your ordinary Tuesday. If that feels like a step backwards, it is not — comfortable is exactly what it is meant to become.

steps.test: Do twelve press-ups in one go.
how: Fresh, at the start of the session.
Chest down to a fist's width from the floor each time.
Get there with sets of eight: eight, eight, eight with a minute between beats one all-out set.
Twelve in a row, no resting at the top.
steps.note: From here on, the press-up number climbs two at a time and every climb is bought with sets you do on the days between.

steps.test: Walk for forty-five minutes without stopping.
how: Out the door, one direction, twenty-two minutes, then turn round.
Proper walking pace — enough that you could talk but would rather not sing.
Phone in your pocket, not in your hand.
Rain is fine. Rain is usually better.
steps.note: A long walk is the base everything else sits on, and it is the one piece of training nobody is too unfit or too tired for. If you already walk this much, do it somewhere you have never walked before and count that.

steps.test: Do fifty squats in one go.
how: Steady from the first rep. This is now a breathing exercise as much as a leg one.
Thighs level every time — the last ten are where depth quietly disappears.
Break as twenty-five and twenty-five with ten seconds between, then close the gap over a fortnight.
Shaking legs afterwards is normal and passes in a minute.
steps.note: Fifty in one go puts you past almost everybody you know. It is also where you stop needing a warm-up for ordinary life.

steps.test: Hold a plank for ninety seconds.
how: Timer on. Hips level the whole way or it does not count.
Squeeze your backside hard — that is the trick that buys the last twenty seconds.
Breathe in a steady rhythm rather than gritting your teeth.
If you break at seventy, hold seventy twice with a minute's rest and go again in two days.
steps.note: Past a minute the plank is mostly a test of whether you will stay calm while something is uncomfortable. That is worth practising on its own.

steps.test: Do ten press-ups slowly — three seconds down, three seconds up.
how: Count it out loud or in your head. Three full seconds each way.
That is sixty seconds of work. It is much harder than ten normal ones.
If you fail at seven, that is the rung for another week.
Do not let the last few speed up. Slow is the whole point.
steps.note: Time under strain, not the number of reps, is what actually builds the muscle. This one rung is why your normal press-up number jumps a fortnight later.

steps.test: Do twenty rows under a table.
how: Body straight, chest all the way to the table edge, arms straight at the bottom.
Twenty in one go. Legs straight out makes it harder, knees bent makes it easier.
Rest your heels on a chair to make it harder still, once twenty is easy.
Keep these in every round — pulling is half of a body.
steps.note: Twenty honest rows is roughly the strength that a first pull-up is built on. If you want the pull-up ladder later, this is the rung that pays for it.

steps.test: Carry something heavy in each hand the length of your street, without putting it down.
how: Two full shopping bags, two water containers, a bag of coal, two full buckets.
Stand tall, shoulders back, walk normally. Do not lean.
If you have to stop, the load is right — pick something slightly lighter and go again.
No heavy things at home? Fill two bags with books, or two containers with water from the tap.
steps.note: This is the strength that actually shows up in a life: shopping, moving house, carrying a child who has fallen asleep. It costs nothing and no gym machine trains it better than two heavy bags.

steps.test: Do fifteen press-ups in one go.
how: Fresh, first thing in the session.
Ten, then breathe at the top without dropping your hips, then five more if you must — but aim for fifteen straight.
Depth over number, every single time.
Do it once, then get it again two days later.
steps.note: Fifteen is three quarters of the way to this ladder's target and about half way to the press-up ladder's thirty.

steps.test: Hang from a bar with your feet off the ground for thirty seconds.
how: A park bar, a beam, a strong door frame bar, a low tree branch.
Hands a little wider than your shoulders, arms straight, feet off the ground.
Let your shoulders stretch at first, then pull them down away from your ears and hold that.
Free option: almost every play park and outdoor gym in the country has a bar.
steps.note: A hang decompresses everything that sitting compresses, and it builds the grip that pull-ups, carrying and lifting all need. Thirty seconds is a lot the first time and easy within a fortnight.

steps.test: Hold a plank for two minutes.
how: Timer, level hips, steady breathing.
Pick a spot on the floor and stay with it.
If the line breaks, come down — the two minutes only count if the shape holds.
Once you have it, stop chasing plank time and make it harder instead: lift one foot, then the other.
steps.note: Two minutes is the honest end of the plank for ordinary strength. Anything past it is a party trick, and the side plank and the one-foot version buy you far more.

steps.test: Do sixty squats in one go.
how: Pace it like a run, not a sprint. The first thirty should feel too easy.
Breathe every rep. Holding your breath is what makes fifty feel like a hundred.
Depth to the last one.
Too easy? Hold something heavy at your chest and do thirty instead.
steps.note: That is one of your three targets reached. Write it down next to the date you guessed at the start.

steps.test: Do the round three days a week for a fortnight, without missing one.
how: Six sessions in fourteen days, at your current numbers, two rounds each.
Write the six dates down first, tick them off.
Missed one? Do it the next day. Do not restart the fortnight.
Short and done beats long and skipped.
steps.note: This is the same rung as part one's, and it is here again on purpose: consistency is not a thing you learn once. Two clean fortnights is what makes the rest of this a habit instead of a project.

steps.test: Do ten press-ups with your feet up on a chair.
how: Feet on a chair or the second step, hands on the floor, body in one straight line.
More of your weight goes through your arms, so ten here is worth about fifteen flat.
Chest all the way to the floor, as always.
Higher feet, harder press-up — that is the dial from now on.
steps.note: Now that the floor is comfortable, this is how you keep getting stronger without ever needing weights. Feet up is the same move with the dial turned.

steps.test: Run for five minutes without stopping.
how: Slow. Slower than you think — a pace you could hold a conversation at.
Five minutes, clock running, no walking breaks.
Any shoes that do not hurt. Any road, path or field.
Already a runner? Run five minutes at a pace that makes talking impossible instead.
steps.note: Almost everybody can run for five minutes if they go slowly enough, and almost everybody tries to go too fast and finds out they cannot. Slow it right down and it is yours today.

steps.test: Do twenty press-ups in one go.
how: Fresh, first thing, chest all the way down.
Build it with sets of twelve to fifteen on the days between.
Twenty in a row, no rest at the top.
Get it twice in one week before you call it yours.
steps.note: That is the second of your three targets. Twenty proper press-ups is more than most adults will ever do in one go, and it came from a windowsill.

steps.test: Lower yourself slowly from the top of a pull-up, three times.
how: Jump or step up so your chin is over the bar, then lower yourself as slowly as you can.
Five seconds is good, ten is excellent. Stay in control all the way to straight arms.
Rest a full minute between each one. Three is plenty.
Step off a bench or a low wall to get to the top if you cannot jump there.
steps.note: You can lower far more than you can lift, which is why this is how a first pull-up is built. Three of these twice a week is the whole secret, and it is where the pull-up ladder begins.

steps.test: Do something physical with somebody else, twice in one week.
how: A walk, a swim, a kickabout, a bike ride, a climb up a hill, a game in the garden.
It does not have to be hard. It has to be with somebody.
Ask — most people say yes and nobody ever asks them.
Free option: a walk costs nothing and is the easiest thing in the world to say yes to.
steps.note: Training on your own works until the week it does not. Somebody expecting you is the strongest thing there is for keeping this going, and it turns exercise into time with people, which is a better deal than it sounds.

steps.test: Write your three numbers again, and pick the one ladder you want to push a long way.
how: Press-ups, squats, plank — under the two earlier sets.
Then read the Fitness path and pick one: press-ups to thirty, squats to a hundred, a first pull-up, five kilometres, a hundred metres flat out.
One, not four. The point is to take one thing a long way.
Keep doing the round while you climb it — the round is now your base, not your project.
steps.note: Two programmes, three sets of numbers, and a body that can do things it could not do at the start. From here the single-move ladders go much further than these rounds ever will, and you now know which of them you actually want.

categories.name: Air and sky
categories.line: Kites, rockets, planes, stars, weather in the sky.

tracks.name: Kites
tracks.line: Flying one to making one that flies.

steps.test: Get a kite into the air and keep it there for a minute.
Work out which way the wind is going before you launch.
Launch it on your own, with nobody holding it.
Land it on your own without it crashing.
Fly it for ten minutes without it coming down.
Make a kite from scratch that actually flies.
Change one thing about it — the tail, the bridle — and fly it better.
Teach two younger children to launch and land.

tracks.name: Rockets
tracks.line: A bottle rocket to a two-stage one.

steps.test: Make a paper rocket and launch it off a straw.
Make three with different fins and see which goes furthest.
Make a water bottle rocket that leaves the ground.
Launch it safely — everybody back, nobody over it.
steps.note: A pressurised bottle is a real thing. Set the rules before the first launch, every time.

steps.test: Get one ten metres up, measured.
Change one thing, test it, and say whether it helped.
Get one twenty metres up, measured.
Work out how much water gives the best flight, by trying it.
Build one with a nose cone that stays on.
Build one with a parachute that comes back down safely.
Launch three in a row that all work.
Run a rocket launch afternoon for other people.

tracks.name: Stars and planets
tracks.line: One constellation to knowing the sky.

steps.test: Find the Plough and the North Star.
Use the Plough to find north, and check it against a compass.
Name three constellations and find them on your own.
Go out on a clear night and just look up for ten minutes.
Find Orion, and the three stars of his belt.
Find Cassiopeia.
Tell the difference between a star and a planet by eye.
steps.note: Stars twinkle. Planets hold steady. Once you have seen it you cannot unsee it.

steps.test: Find a planet with your own eyes and know which one it is.
Watch the moon on five nights and draw what it looked like.
Know what the moon will look like tomorrow, and be right.
Spot a satellite crossing the sky.
Find the Milky Way from somewhere dark.
Watch a meteor shower and count what you see.
Find five constellations without help.
Look at the moon through binoculars and find one crater.
Find the Andromeda galaxy.
Know which constellations belong to which season, and say why they move.
Find eight constellations without help.
Take somebody out and show them three things in the sky.
Run a stargazing night and show people what is up there.

tracks.name: Things that fly
tracks.line: Paper wings to something with a motor.

steps.test: Fold a paper aeroplane that flies across the room.
Fold three different ones and see which flies furthest.
Fold one that flies ten metres, measured.
Bend the back edge of the wings up a little and see what it does.
steps.note: Those are elevators. You have just found out how a real aeroplane is steered.

steps.test: Make one that turns in a circle on purpose.
Fold one that flies thirty feet, measured, with somebody watching.
Make one that glides slowly instead of fast, and say why it does.
Explain what keeps an aeroplane up, in your own words.
Build a card or balsa glider from a plan.
Get it to fly level instead of diving, by moving the weight.
Make it fly twenty metres.
Build a glider of your own design that flies.
Make a paper helicopter and time how long it takes to fall.
Change the blades and make it fall slower.
Build something with elastic or a motor that leaves the ground.
Get it to fly the same way twice.
Fly something with a controller and land it on purpose.
Fly it round a marker and back.
Build or fly a small helicopter or drone that lifts and lands where you meant.
Run a flying afternoon and get everybody something in the air.

tracks.name: Wind and weather watching
tracks.line: Which way to keeping records.

steps.test: Say which way the wind is blowing without looking at anything.
Say roughly how hard it is blowing, and check it against a forecast.
Make something that shows wind direction and put it up outside.
Watch it for a week and write down which way the wind came from each day.
Name three cloud types on sight.
Name five cloud types on sight.
Say what each of those five usually means for the next few hours.
Spot rain coming before anybody else does, and be right.
Predict tomorrow from the sky alone, and check whether you were right.
Do that on five days and count how many you got.
Explain what a front is, and spot one arriving.
Read a pressure reading and say what it means.
Keep a weather record every day for a fortnight.
Keep it every day for a month.
Work out from your own record which wind brings the rain here.
Get three forecasts right in a row and explain how.
Know when the sun sets today without looking it up, to within ten minutes.
Call the weather for a day out, and be right enough that nobody got caught.
Get five forecasts right in a row and explain how.
Teach somebody to read the sky well enough that they get one right.

tracks.name: Throwing
tracks.line: Hitting a target to hitting it every time.

steps.test: Scrunch a sheet of paper into a ball and throw it into a bin from five paces.
Do that five times out of five.
Hit a target the size of a bin lid from ten paces.
Hit it five times out of five.
Hit it from twenty paces.
Throw with your other hand and hit it from five paces.
Throw something as far as you can, then beat it by five metres.
steps.twist: Other hand, then beat that too.

steps.test: Catch ten in a row thrown at you.
Skim a stone three bounces.
Skim a stone six bounces.
Skim one ten bounces.
Teach somebody else to skim one properly.

categories.name: Mind and numbers
categories.line: Tables, the cube, chess, memory, codes, puzzles.

tracks.name: Learning to learn, part one
tracks.line: From one thing you wondered about to thinking for half an hour with a pen.

steps.test: Look up one thing you have wondered about and read until you could explain it.
steps.note: Why the sky is blue, how a lock works, where a word comes from. Explain it to the wall if nobody is there.

steps.test: Read for twenty minutes with your phone in another room.
steps.note: Anything on paper. Twenty minutes is longer than it sounds the first time.

steps.test: Write ten lines by hand, slowly and neatly.
steps.note: Copy them from a book. The point is the hand, not the words.

steps.test: Learn five words of a language you do not speak and say them out loud.
steps.note: Hello, thank you, please, yes, no. Pick the language of a place you would like to go.

steps.test: Memorise ten things and say them back an hour later.
steps.note: A shopping list, a poem's first verse, ten capitals. Picture each one somewhere in your house.

steps.test: Do twenty sums in your head, no paper.
steps.note: Adding prices, doubling numbers, splitting a bill. Say the answers out loud.

steps.test: Explain one thing you know well to somebody in three sentences.
steps.note: If it takes more than three, you do not know it as well as you thought. Try again tomorrow.

steps.test: Read one chapter of a book that is a bit too hard for you.
steps.note: Look up nothing. Let the hard words go by and see how much you still got.

steps.test: Find an answer without a screen.
steps.note: A library, a reference book on a shelf, or three people who might know. Slower, and you will remember it.

steps.test: Learn the times table you never quite learned.
steps.note: The sevens, the eights, the twelves. Out loud, forwards and backwards. Have them all? Squares to twenty.

steps.test: Take one bad argument you hear this week and say, kindly, what is wrong with it.
steps.note: "Everybody knows…", "you would say that", two things happening together being called cause. Name the move.

steps.test: Learn twenty words of that language.
steps.note: The five from rung four and fifteen more. Numbers to ten count as ten.

steps.test: Read a whole book, cover to cover.
steps.note: Any book, any length. Finishing is the rung.

steps.test: Write one page about what you learned this month.
steps.note: By hand or typed. What surprised you, what you got wrong, what you want next.

steps.test: Learn one poem by heart and say it to somebody.
steps.note: Short is fine. Four lines said properly beats twenty stumbled.

steps.test: Solve a puzzle that takes more than an hour.
steps.note: A hard crossword, a cube, a logic problem, a jigsaw. Sit with it; do not look up the answer.

steps.test: Teach somebody one thing you learned on this ladder.
steps.note: The sums trick, the poem, the words. Teaching it is how you find out you know it.

steps.test: Hold a short conversation in that language.
steps.note: With a person, or with a recording you answer out loud. Two minutes. Mistakes and all.

steps.test: Read a book written more than a hundred years ago.
steps.note: Old does not mean hard. A short one, all the way through, and notice what has not changed.

steps.test: Sit and think about one question for thirty minutes with nothing but a pen.
steps.note: Write the question at the top. No phone, no book. Whatever you write underneath is yours. Part two goes deeper.

tracks.about: How to learn anything, practised on a few things at once: a language, a poem, sums in your head, a book that is a bit too hard. The rungs are short and the last one is thirty minutes of thinking with only a pen. Nothing to buy; a library card helps.

tracks.name: Times tables
tracks.line: Counting in twos to sixty seconds flat.

steps.test: Count in twos up to twenty.
Count in fives up to fifty, and in tens up to a hundred.
Say the two times table with no mistakes.
Say the five and ten times tables with no mistakes.
Say the three times table.
Say the four times table.
Answer twenty mixed questions from the tables you know, all correct.
Say the six times table.
Say the seven times table.
Say the eight times table.
Say the nine times table, and spot the trick in it.
steps.note: Add the two digits of any answer in the nine times table. They come to nine every time.

steps.test: Say the eleven and twelve times tables.
Say every table up to twelve correctly, with no time limit.
Answer thirty mixed questions in a row, all correct.
Say every table up to twelve in under three minutes.
Answer any single table question in under two seconds.
Say every table up to twelve in under two minutes.
Say every table up to twelve in under ninety seconds.
Say every table up to twelve in under sixty seconds.
Teach somebody else one whole table until they have it.

tracks.name: The cube
tracks.line: One face to under a minute.

steps.test: Name the pieces and turn the cube twenty times without losing track of a colour.
steps.note: Centres never move. Whatever colour is in the middle is that face, always.

steps.test: Learn what the letters mean — R, L, U, D, F, B — and turn each one.
Follow a written sequence of six turns without a mistake.
Make one whole face a single colour, with nobody helping you.
Solve the white cross — four white edges round the white centre.
Solve the white cross with the sides matching their centres too.
Put one white corner in, on your own.
Solve the whole white layer, corners and all.
Solve the white layer again in under two minutes.
Learn the sequence that puts a middle edge in to the right.
Learn the one that puts it in to the left.
Solve the middle layer.
Solve the first two layers three times in a row.
Learn the sequence for the yellow cross, and get it.
Get the yellow cross from any starting position.
Learn the sequence that puts the last corners in place.
Solve the whole cube with the sheet in front of you.
Solve the whole cube with nothing in front of you.
Solve it from three different scrambles in one sitting, under five minutes each.
Solve it in under three minutes, and teach somebody the white cross.

tracks.about: The cube looks impossible and is not: it is seven short patterns learned one at a time, and the first one takes an evening. A few minutes a day and within a month you solve it every time, which is a thing people will ask you to do for the rest of your life. You need a cube, about five pounds, and nothing else.

tracks.name: Chess
tracks.line: Setting the board to teaching a beginner.

steps.test: Set the board up correctly and name every piece.
steps.note: White square on the right, and the queen goes on her own colour.

steps.test: Know how every piece moves.
Play one full game to the end.
Castle, and say why you did it.
Take a piece with a pawn the way pawns actually take.
Say the value of each piece and stop giving them away for nothing.
Play five whole games in one week.
Checkmate with a queen and a king against a lone king.
Checkmate with only a king and a rook.
Spot a fork before you play into one.
Win a game against somebody who is genuinely trying.
Open the same way three games running and notice what changes.
Get your pieces out and your king safe in the first ten moves, every time.
Solve ten mate-in-one puzzles.
Solve ten mate-in-two puzzles.
Play a whole game without losing a piece for nothing.
Win a game by a plan you had before it started.
Lose a game and say afterwards where it actually went wrong.
Beat an adult who plays properly.
Teach a complete beginner until they can play a full game.

tracks.about: Chess is a language, and the rungs teach it the way a language is learned: the moves, then a few ideas, then games against people. A few months in you can hold your own against most people who play, and you will have taught somebody else. A board, or a free app.

tracks.name: Memory
tracks.line: Six digits to a hundred.

steps.test: Memorise a six-digit number and say it back a minute later.
Memorise a phone number and say it back an hour later.
Say your own address and two phone numbers from memory, with nothing in your hand.
Memorise a five-item shopping list and buy it with no list in your hand.
Learn the names of five people you met today, and use them tomorrow.
Turn five words into five daft pictures in your head, and say them back.
steps.note: The dafter the picture the better it sticks. That is not a trick, it is how memory actually works.

steps.test: Walk through your own house in your head and name ten places, in order.
steps.note: Front door, hall, kitchen. Always the same ten, always the same order. This is your memory palace.

steps.test: Put five things in those first five places, and say them back.
Put ten things in ten places, and say them back.
Say those same ten back the next morning.
Memorise twenty digits of pi.
Memorise a four-line verse, and say it a week later.
Memorise fifteen things in order.
Learn the first ten cards of a shuffled deck, in order.
