categories.name: Speaking and people
categories.line: Strangers, the stage, listening, hard things, humour, teaching.

tracks.name: Meeting people, part one
tracks.line: From a smile to a second conversation, in twenty small steps.

steps.test: Smile at three people you pass today, with your eyes on theirs for a second.
steps.note: That is the whole rung. Count them on your fingers. Most people look at the ground; you are already doing the rare thing.

steps.test: Say good morning, or hello, to three people you pass, and mean it.
steps.note: Out loud, not a nod. A dog walker, somebody at the bus stop, the person on the till. If one does not answer, that is theirs, not yours; the count is what you said.

steps.test: Thank somebody by their name today: read the badge, or ask it.
steps.note: "Thanks, Claire." The name changes the whole thing. If nobody wears a badge, "Sorry, what is your name?" is the rung.

steps.test: Ask a stranger the time, or whether this is the right road for somewhere.
steps.note: You already know the answer; the point is the asking. Pick somebody standing still. One sentence, a thank you, done.

steps.test: Ask somebody for directions to a place you can name, and listen to the whole answer.
steps.note: "Excuse me, do you know the way to the library?" Let them finish, say the first turn back to them, thank them.

steps.test: In a shop, ask where something is, then ask one more question about it.
steps.note: "Where is the honey?" then "Is that one any good?" You do not have to buy anything. A library, a market stall or a garden centre counts just as well as a shop.

steps.test: Give one honest compliment to a stranger.
steps.note: Their dog, their garden, their coat, how they handled a child. Say it and move on; do not wait for anything back. It has to be true.

steps.test: Keep a conversation with somebody you do not know going for one minute.
steps.note: Three questions will do it: where are you from, what brings you here, what is good round here. Bus stops, queues and dog walks are where these happen.

steps.test: Ask somebody for a recommendation: a book, a walk, a podcast, a place.
steps.note: "What is the best walk round here?" People love being asked. Write the answer down; you will use it on rung eighteen.

steps.test: Phone a shop or business and ask one simple question.
steps.note: Opening hours, or do they stock a thing. Under a minute. Write the question down before you dial. If you never phone anywhere, this is a bigger rung than it looks, and it counts double in your own book.

steps.test: Phone somewhere with a slightly bigger ask.
steps.note: Can they order something in, hold something for you, or could a small group visit one afternoon. You are enquiring, not demanding; a no is a fine answer and the rung is still done.

steps.test: Send a message to somebody whose work you enjoy, saying the one thing it did for you.
steps.note: An author, a maker, a podcaster, a musician. An email, or a message wherever they are. Three sentences, no ask, no link. Most of them are never told; you will be remembered.

steps.test: Send the same kind of message to somebody local.
steps.note: A shop, a club, a coach, a band, the people who run the market. "Just to say Saturday was brilliant, thank you for running it." Local people answer.

steps.test: Talk to a neighbour you have never properly spoken to.
steps.note: Their name, how long they have been here, that is enough. Over the fence, at the bins, at the car. Say your own name first.

steps.test: Ask somebody about themselves and listen for two minutes without talking about you.
steps.note: "How did you get into that?" Then only questions. Two minutes is longer than you think; most people have never been listened to that long.

steps.test: Ask a cheerful, slightly odd question somewhere, and see what happens.
steps.note: "Do you ever get people asking to bring a picnic in here?" or "Has anybody ever proposed in this shop?" Respectful, smiling, one minute. The discovery is that nobody minds and most people enjoy it.

steps.test: Do one useful thing for a stranger today.
steps.note: Hold a door, carry a bag to a car, tell somebody the queue is shorter next door, pass on a recommendation of your own. Small and real.

steps.test: Get one person's name and a way to reach them, with a reason.
steps.note: "I will send you that walk." "Let me know when the market is on again." A number, an email, a handle. The reason is what makes it natural. Somebody from rungs eight, nine or fourteen is ideal.

steps.test: Send what you said you would send, within a day.
steps.note: The walk, the book title, the photo. Short, friendly, no questions. This is the rung almost nobody does, and it is the one that makes you somebody people remember.

steps.test: Have a second conversation with somebody you met on this ladder.
steps.note: Same person, another day. "Did you try that walk?" If it goes well, suggest something: a coffee, the market, the children at the park, a talk you both want to hear. That is a friend beginning. Part two starts here.

tracks.about: Twenty small steps from a smile to a second conversation with somebody you did not know a month ago. Nothing here needs money or a café; the shop rungs need no buying and the calls take a minute. It is written for the person who finds this genuinely hard, so the first rungs are tiny and the later ones are where the friends come from.

tracks.name: Meeting people, part two
tracks.line: From one small thing together to a room full of people you brought together.
tracks.about: Part one got you talking to people; part two turns talk into friends. Reconnecting, inviting, hosting a pot of tea, organising the walk, running a small regular thing, and finally putting on an event of your own. Nothing needs money: tea at yours, a bench, a park. It ends by counting the people you could call on a bad day.

steps.test: Send a one-line message to three people you have not spoken to in a year.
steps.note: "Saw this and thought of you." "Hope the new job is going well." No ask, no catch-up demand. Some will answer this week; that is enough.

steps.test: Ask somebody you met in part one to do one small thing together.
steps.note: A walk, the market, a look at that view you were told about. Twenty minutes is plenty. Costs nothing.

steps.test: Learn and use the name of everybody you meet this week.
steps.note: Say it back straight away, use it once in the conversation, and once at the end. Write them down that night.

steps.test: Introduce two people to each other who did not know each other.
steps.note: "You two should meet, you both…" That sentence is the whole rung, and people remember who did it.

steps.test: Ask somebody for help with something small, and accept it.
steps.note: A hand with a box, a lift, an opinion, a recipe. Asking for help is the fastest road to a friend there is.

steps.test: Say yes to the next invitation you would normally turn down.
steps.note: The thing you would have made an excuse for. Go, stay an hour, then leave if you want to. Count it.

steps.test: Turn up at the same regular thing twice in one week.
steps.note: A run, a class, a market, a service, a group. The second time in a week is when you stop being a visitor.

steps.test: Have a proper conversation with somebody twenty years older than you, and one with somebody twenty years younger.
steps.note: Ask them about their week. Most people only ever talk to their own age.

steps.test: Ask three people what they are working on, and follow up with one of them within a week.
steps.note: "How did the thing go?" A week later, unprompted. Almost nobody does this; you will be remembered for it.

steps.test: Invite one person for a walk, a picnic, or a cup of tea at yours.
steps.note: Tea at home costs nothing. A sandwich on a bench is a picnic. The invitation is the rung, whether or not they can make it.

steps.test: Tell somebody something true about yourself that you usually keep back.
steps.note: Not a confession; a real thing. What you are afraid of, what you want, what you were like at fifteen. It is how acquaintances become friends.

steps.test: Be the one who organises: pick the day, the place, and the time, and tell people.
steps.note: Three people or more. Most gatherings never happen because nobody names a day. Name it.

steps.test: Host two or three people for a simple meal or a pot of tea.
steps.note: Soup and bread is a meal. A pot of tea and a packet of biscuits is enough. The place from the Home ladder is ready in ten minutes.

steps.test: Reconnect with an old friend and meet in person.
steps.note: Somebody you were close to and drifted from. A message, then a walk. The first ten minutes are awkward and then they are not.

steps.test: Do a favour that costs you an hour.
steps.note: Help somebody move something, mind a child, fix a bike, sit with somebody's parent. An hour of yours, given properly.

steps.test: Start a small regular thing and run it three times.
steps.note: A weekly walk, a game night, a Sunday call, a Saturday parkrun with two others. Three weeks running. After three it exists.

steps.test: Ask for an introduction to somebody you would like to meet, and follow it through.
steps.note: "Do you know anyone who…?" Then a message the same day it is offered, and the meeting inside a fortnight.

steps.test: Go somewhere alone where you know nobody, and leave with one name and a way to reach them.
steps.note: A talk, a club night, a fair, a class. The rung is the name, not the hour.

steps.test: Put on a small event of your own: six people or more.
steps.note: A picnic, a games afternoon, a talk in your front room, a walk with a flask at the end. You choose the day and you tell people. Then it happens.

steps.test: Write down the names of the people you could call on a bad day.
steps.note: If the list is longer than it was when you started part one, both ladders worked. That list is the point of all of it. From here a facilitator, and the network you build on purpose.

steps.test: Tell a joke well enough that somebody laughs.
Tell it again to somebody else and get the same laugh.
Learn five jokes and land all five.
Tell one that dies, and carry on cheerfully.
steps.note: Everybody who is funny has died in front of people. It is the entry fee, not the failure.

steps.test: Make somebody laugh with something you thought of yourself.
Notice what actually made people laugh today, and write it down.
Say the funny thing you thought of instead of keeping it in.
Make a joke about yourself, not about somebody else.
Get a laugh out of a room of five.
Write down ten things you find funny and find what they share.
Write a joke of your own with a proper ending.
Tell three of your own and land two.
Do a funny voice or an impression somebody recognises.
Do two minutes of your own material to a group.
Handle somebody heckling you without losing the room.
Do a sketch or an improv scene with somebody else.
Make somebody laugh who was having a rotten day.
Do five minutes and keep it going.
Get a laugh without saying anything at all.
Run a comedy night and keep it going.

tracks.name: Teaching
tracks.line: One thing to a whole session.

steps.test: Teach one person one thing you can do.
Watch them do it, and say nothing while they get it wrong.
steps.note: Taking it off them to show them again is the commonest mistake in teaching.

steps.test: Teach it well enough that they can still do it a week later.
Break something hard into steps and write the steps down.
Teach it in that order and see where they got stuck.
Change the order because of where they got stuck.
Teach two people at once.
Teach three people at once.
Answer a question you did not know the answer to, honestly.
Teach somebody who did not want to learn it.
Run a whole session for younger children.
Teach an adult something they could not do before.

tracks.name: Saying it yourself
tracks.line: From four, beside you. Your name, a hello, a please, a thank you, a question, a story.

steps.test: Say your name and how old you are to somebody you have not met, looking at them.
Say hello first to somebody you know, before they say it to you.
Say goodbye and their name when you leave.
Ask for something in a whole sentence with a please in it, instead of pointing.
Say thank you to the person at the shop, loud enough that they hear it.
Answer a grown-up who asks you a question, without hiding behind anybody.
Ask a grown-up a question you really want the answer to, and listen to all of it.
Tell somebody you do not want to, in words, instead of crying.
Say sorry to somebody yourself, in your own words.
Order your own food or drink while somebody stands beside you.
Tell somebody something that happened today, with a beginning, a middle and an end.
Tell it to somebody who was not there, so that they understand it.

tracks.name: Meeting people
tracks.line: From a name you never asked for to a room where people know you.

steps.test: Ask one person you already know how they are, and listen to the whole answer.
Learn the name of somebody you see often and have never asked.
Use their name the next time you see them.
Have a conversation with a stranger that lasts two minutes.
Ask somebody what they do, and one real question about it.
Find out one thing about somebody that you could ask after next time.
Go somewhere you know nobody, and stay a full hour.
Introduce yourself to three people while you are there.
Ask somebody for their number or their address so you can follow up.
Follow up within two days. A sentence is enough.
steps.note: Almost nobody does this, which is exactly why it works. The meeting is not the thing. The message afterwards is the thing.

steps.test: Ask one of them to meet again — a coffee, a walk, a call.
Go to that second meeting.
Go to the same thing three times, so that people start to know your face.
Introduce two people to each other who ought to know each other.
Ask somebody for an introduction to a person they know.
Volunteer for something where you know nobody.
Ask somebody further on than you for half an hour of their time.
Keep a list of people you have met and one thing about each.
Do somebody a good turn with nothing in it for you, and never mention it.
Be the person who brings somebody new into the group.

categories.name: Making and building
categories.line: Wood, cloth, clay, drawing, knots, electronics, machines, code.

tracks.name: Make something, part one
tracks.line: From a ten-minute drawing to a thing somebody asks where you bought.

steps.test: Draw one thing in front of you for ten minutes, mostly without looking at the paper.
steps.note: A mug, a hand, a plant. It will look wrong; that is the point. Keep it.

steps.test: Tie three knots you can name, and undo them.
steps.note: A reef knot, a bowline, a clove hitch. Rope, a shoelace, a phone cable will all do.

steps.test: Fold a paper aeroplane that flies across a room.
steps.note: Any paper. Fold, throw, adjust, throw again. The adjusting is the making.

steps.test: Draw the same thing every day for five days and keep all five.
steps.note: Same mug, same chair. Lay the five out in a row and see what happened.

steps.test: Make something from a cardboard box.
steps.note: A house, a mask, a shelf, a castle. Scissors and tape. It has to stand up.

steps.test: Sew two pieces of cloth together by hand, ten even stitches.
steps.note: Any two scraps. Even matters more than small.

steps.test: Take ten photographs of one ordinary thing until one is good.
steps.note: A cup, a doorway, a puddle. Move, wait for the light, try again. Keep the one.

steps.test: Build something that stands on its own from what is in the recycling.
steps.note: A tower, a bridge, a creature. It stands without your hand for one minute.

steps.test: Draw a face that looks like the person.
steps.note: Somebody sitting still for ten minutes, or a photo. Eyes halfway down the head, not at the top.

steps.test: Shape one thing from wood, clay, or a bar of soap.
steps.note: A spoon, a bird, a bowl. A knife and a bar of soap is enough for a first carving.

steps.test: Make a simple circuit: a battery, a wire, and a bulb or buzzer.
steps.note: A pound-shop kit, or a lemon, two different coins and a small LED. Light comes on: done.

steps.test: Take a broken thing apart and see how it worked.
steps.note: A clock, a toaster, a toy. Unplugged. Lay the parts out in order.

steps.test: Draw a room in perspective, the lines meeting at one point.
steps.note: Dot in the middle, floor and ceiling lines running to it. Then the furniture.

steps.test: Make a gift by hand and give it.
steps.note: A card, a small carving, a drawing framed, a jar of something. Given, not kept.

steps.test: Mend one thing with glue, thread, or a screw so it works again.
steps.note: A chair, a book, a bag strap, a toy. Working is the test.

steps.test: Write your name beautifully twenty times, until the last one is good.
steps.note: A proper pen, slow. Compare the first and the twentieth.

steps.test: Make a kite, a boat, or a rocket, and fly, float, or launch it.
steps.note: Paper and string, a bottle and a cork, a balloon on a straw. It has to actually go.

steps.test: Follow written instructions to build something with more than twenty steps.
steps.note: A model, flat-pack furniture, a recipe with stages. Every step, in order, no skipping.

steps.test: Design something on paper first, then make it.
steps.note: A drawing with sizes, then the thing. Notice where the drawing was wrong.

steps.test: Make one thing good enough that somebody asks where you bought it.
steps.note: That is the bar. Part two is a craft you keep.

tracks.about: Making, tried from every side: drawing, knots, paper, card, cloth, a photograph, soap carving, a circuit, a thing taken apart, a gift made and given. By the end one thing you made is good enough that somebody asks where you bought it. Scraps, tape and what is in the recycling.

tracks.name: Wood
tracks.line: Sanding to furniture.

steps.test: Sand a piece of wood properly smooth.
Sand it again with a finer paper and feel the difference.
Measure a length twice and mark it once.
steps.note: Every ruined piece of wood was measured once.

steps.test: Saw a cut roughly where you marked it.
Saw a straight cut you would be happy to show somebody.
Saw a cut square, checked with a set square.
Drill a hole where you meant it, right through, without splitting the wood.
Drive a screw in flush, without the head chewing up.
Make something from two pieces joined together.
Glue and clamp a joint that holds when it is dry.
Cut a piece to fit a gap you measured, first go.
Draw a plan first, with the sizes on it.
Build exactly what the plan said.
Cut and fit a proper joint — a halving or a housing.
Sharpen a blade and cut with it before and after.
Finish something with oil or wax so it looks finished.
Build something that has to bear weight, and stand on it.
Fix a mistake instead of starting again.
Build a piece of furniture somebody uses every day.
Teach a younger child to saw safely.

tracks.name: Cloth and thread
tracks.line: Threading a needle to clothes you would wear.

steps.test: Thread a needle on your own.
Tie a knot in the end that will not pull through.
Sew a running stitch along a drawn line.
Sew a line of even stitches, all the same length.
Sew on a button that holds when it is pulled.
Sew a seam joining two pieces of cloth.
Mend a rip in something you would still wear out.
Take up a hem and have it stay up.
Darn a hole in a sock or a jumper.
Sew a straight seam on a machine.
Cut cloth to a paper pattern.
Sew a bag you would actually use.
Put in a zip or a drawstring that works.
Press a seam flat and see how much better it looks.
Make a cushion cover or an apron somebody uses.
Fix somebody else's clothes for them.
Alter something that did not fit until it does.
Make something from a pattern, all the way through.
Make a piece of clothing you would wear out of the house.
Teach somebody to sew a button on, and watch them do it.

tracks.name: Knots and rope
tracks.line: One knot to a rope bridge.

steps.test: Tie a knot that does not come undone when pulled.
Tie a reef knot, and say how it differs from a granny.
Tie a bowline.
Tie a bowline round your own waist.
Tie a clove hitch onto a post.
Tie all three from memory with nobody prompting you.
Tie a figure of eight and a taut-line hitch.
Undo a knot that has been loaded hard, without cutting it.
Lash two poles together so they hold your weight.
Whip or tape the end of a rope so it stops fraying.
Build a structure from poles and lashings that holds a person.
Teach three knots to somebody until they can do them blind.

tracks.name: Clay and carving
tracks.line: A pinch pot to something on a shelf.

steps.test: Make a pinch pot that holds water.
Make one with even walls all the way round.
Roll a coil and build a pot from coils.
Join two pieces of clay so they do not crack apart.
steps.note: Score both faces and wet them. Clay that is only pressed together always comes apart.

steps.test: Make something recognisable out of clay.
Make the same thing twice and make the second one better.
Let something dry slowly without it cracking.
Carve a stick into a useful shape with a knife, safely.
steps.note: Always cut away from yourself, and know where the blade goes if it slips.

steps.test: Whittle a point, a notch and a flat face.
Carve a butter knife you would put on a table.
Carve a spoon you would eat with.
Sand and oil something you carved.
Make a set of three things that match.
Make something with a lid that fits.
Decorate a piece so it looks decided rather than accidental.
Fire or bake something so it lasts.
Repair something you broke, visibly and on purpose.
Make something to a size somebody asked for.
Make something somebody puts on a shelf and keeps.
Teach somebody a pinch pot, hands off, all the way through.

tracks.about: Clay is the most forgiving material there is; if it goes wrong you squash it and start again. From a pinch pot to a bowl you eat from, in a few months of an hour at a time. A bag of air-drying clay is a few pounds and needs no kiln.

tracks.name: Drawing
tracks.line: Recognisable, then good.

steps.test: Draw something and have somebody name it without being told.
Draw the same thing three times and pick the best one.
Draw for ten minutes a day for five days.
Draw something in front of you without lifting the pencil off the paper.
steps.note: It will look strange. It is about looking, not about the drawing.

steps.test: Draw an object by starting with the simple shapes underneath it.
Draw a cube, a cylinder and a ball so that they look solid.
Shade a ball so it looks round, with the light coming from one side.
Draw the same object twice, lit from two different sides.
Draw your own hand, from life.
steps.twist: Draw the hand you draw with, using the other one.

steps.test: Draw the chair you are sitting on, with the legs going the right way.
Draw the gap around an object instead of the object.
steps.note: Draw only the shape of the empty space. Your eye stops guessing and starts looking.

steps.test: Fill a whole page with small drawings of one thing.
steps.twist: Half of them with the other hand.

steps.test: Draw for ten minutes a day for two weeks without missing a day.
Copy a drawing you admire, line for line.
Draw a face with the eyes halfway down the head, not near the top.
steps.note: Almost everybody puts the eyes too high. Halfway down is right, and it fixes a face on its own.

steps.test: Draw a face from a photograph.
Draw the same face again and get the eyes level and the right size.
Draw somebody sitting in front of you, in ten minutes.
Draw somebody you know, and have a third person say who it is.
Draw something somebody asks to keep.

tracks.about: Drawing is looking, written down, and it can be learned like handwriting. The rungs go from ten minutes of drawing a mug to a face that looks like the person. A week of practice makes a difference you can see on the page, and that page is proof you can show anybody. A pencil and paper.

tracks.name: Electricity
tracks.line: One bulb to your own circuit board.

steps.test: Light one bulb with a battery and two wires.
Draw the circuit you just made, as a diagram.
Build a circuit with a switch that works.
Make one where the bulb is dimmer, and say why.
Build one where two things happen at once and explain why.
Wire two bulbs in series, then in parallel, and say what changed.
Use a meter to measure volts across something.
Find a break in a circuit with the meter instead of guessing.
Say what a resistor is for and pick the right one for an LED.
Solder a joint that holds and conducts.
Solder five in a row that all work.
Build a circuit on stripboard from a diagram.
Make a light come on when it gets dark.
Get a microcontroller to blink one light.
Get it to read a button and do something different.
Get it to read a sensor and act on what it reads.
Put it in a box with the wires tidy inside.
Build something that does a job somebody actually wanted.
Fix it when it breaks, without starting again.
Build something other people use, and keep it working.

tracks.name: Machines and code
tracks.line: An idea out loud to something strangers use.

steps.test: Describe an idea for an app out loud, in three clear sentences.
Write down what it should do, in five lines, on paper.
Draw the screens on paper before writing a single word of code.
Make a web page that says your name, and open it in a browser.
Add a button that changes the words when you press it.
Change the colours and the type until it looks like something you would show somebody.
Make a page that adds two numbers you type in.
Break it on purpose, read the error message, and fix it.
steps.note: Reading errors is the whole job. The message almost always says exactly what is wrong.

steps.test: Make it remember what you typed after you close the page.
Ask an AI for a piece you do not understand, then change it to do something else.
Make a list you can add to and delete from.
Put it on the internet with a real address.
Send the address to one person and watch them use it without helping.
Fix the first thing they got stuck on.
Make it work on a phone as well as on a computer.
Add one thing they asked for.
Write down in one sentence what it does, so a stranger would understand.
Let a second person use it with you out of the room.
Change something and put the new version up without breaking the old one.
Have one person use it more than once, because they wanted to.

tracks.name: Photography
tracks.line: A photo to an exhibition.

steps.test: Take a photo where you can tell what it is of.
Take one where the thing you meant is actually in focus.
Get closer, and take it again.
steps.note: Nearly every bad photograph is a photograph taken from too far away.

steps.test: Take one with the light coming from behind you, not behind the subject.
Take one where nothing is growing out of anybody's head.
Take a photo of a person that looks like them.
Take one somebody asks for a copy of.
Take twenty of one thing and pick the best three, and say why.
Take one at the hour before sunset and see the difference.
Put the subject somewhere other than dead centre, on purpose.
Take a photo indoors that is not dark and blurry.
Take one of something moving, sharp.
Take one of the same place in two different lights.
Edit one lightly and keep the original.
Take a set of five that clearly belong together.
Print one and hold it in your hand.
Print and frame one.
Give a printed photograph to the person in it.
Photograph an occasion so that the family keeps the pictures.
Put on a small exhibition of your own photographs.

tracks.name: Scissors
tracks.line: From four, beside you. Cutting, and cutting where you meant to.

steps.test: Open and shut the scissors ten times with nothing in them.
Hold them the right way round, thumb on top, and show somebody.
Cut a piece of paper in two, any way you like.
Snip all along the edge of a piece of paper to make a fringe.
Cut along a straight line somebody drew for you.
Cut a square out.
Cut along a curvy line, all the way, without leaving it.
Cut out a circle and hold it up.
Cut out a shape and turn the paper instead of the scissors.
Fold paper, cut, and open it out to see what happened.
Cut out three shapes and stick them down to make a picture.
Tell somebody what your picture is, while they look at it.

tracks.name: Crayons
tracks.line: From four, beside you. Colouring in, then drawing what you see.

steps.test: Colour one shape in and stay inside the line.
Colour it all the way in, with no white bits left.
Colour a whole picture, every part of it, with more than one colour.
Press hard for a dark colour and softly for a pale one.
Draw a circle that joins up where it started.
Draw a square and a triangle.
Draw a person with a head, a body, two arms and two legs.
Give the person a face, and say who it is.
Draw your house.
Draw somebody standing outside your house.
Draw something that happened today.
Tell the story of your picture to somebody while they look at it.

categories.name: Music and voice
categories.line: Singing, an instrument, rhythm, songs, whistling, reading music.

tracks.name: Play, part one
tracks.line: From a song sung alone to a five-minute show for two people.

steps.test: Sing one whole song out loud, alone, start to finish.
steps.note: In the car, the shower, the kitchen. All the verses you know.

steps.test: Clap a rhythm back to somebody, and have them clap yours.
steps.note: Four beats, then eight. A table and two spoons if hands are boring.

steps.test: Learn one coin or card trick well enough to fool yourself in a mirror.
steps.note: A coin vanish, or the trick where the chosen card comes to the top. Ten minutes a day for three days.

steps.test: Throw and catch one ball a hundred times without dropping it.
steps.note: A rolled sock counts. Same height every throw; that is the whole secret of juggling.

steps.test: Whistle a tune somebody can name.
steps.note: Cannot whistle? Hum it, and whistling is a rung in the Music room when you want it.

steps.test: Stand on one leg for a minute, then the other.
steps.note: Eyes on one spot. Then, when it is easy, eyes shut.

steps.test: Learn a three-line joke and tell it to somebody.
steps.note: Short, clean, told slowly. The pause before the last line is the joke.

steps.test: Do one trick for one person.
steps.note: The trick from rung three. If they see how it works, that is how you learn where to look.

steps.test: Juggle two balls in one hand, or three balls for three throws.
steps.note: Socks again. Three throws and a drop still counts.

steps.test: Dance for a whole song with nobody watching.
steps.note: Curtains closed if you like. All the way to the end of the song.

steps.test: Play five notes on any instrument that make a tune somebody recognises.
steps.note: A keyboard app on a phone counts. Ode to Joy is five notes. An instrument you own is better.

steps.test: Skip ten times in a row.
steps.note: A rope, a washing line, a length of anything. Ten without a stumble.

steps.test: Learn a second trick and do both, one after the other, for somebody.
steps.note: Two tricks is an act. Say something between them.

steps.test: Sing with another person, both of you singing.
steps.note: Any song you both know. Out loud, together, to the end.

steps.test: Do a cartwheel, a handstand against a wall, or a forward roll.
steps.note: On grass or a carpet. Whichever you have never done, or not for twenty years.

steps.test: Make up a game with rules and play it with somebody.
steps.note: A cup, a coin, a hallway. Write the rules down in three lines.

steps.test: Play a whole tune for one person.
steps.note: Start to finish, mistakes and all. The instrument from rung eleven.

steps.test: Juggle three balls for ten throws.
steps.note: This is the one people remember learning. A month of a few minutes a day.

steps.test: Be somebody else for ten minutes: a voice, a hat, a face painted on.
steps.note: A character with a name. Children are the best audience for this one.

steps.test: Put on a five-minute show for two or more people.
steps.note: A song, a trick, a joke, a tune. Introduce it. Bow at the end. Part two is a real act.

tracks.about: Songs, tricks, juggling, dancing, a joke, a tune on anything, a cartwheel, a character with a hat. Twenty rungs of play that end in a five-minute show for two people. Socks for juggling, a phone keyboard for the tune, and no audience until you are ready.

tracks.name: Singing
tracks.line: A voice warm-up to singing in front of people.

steps.test: Sing one whole song out loud where somebody can hear you.
Do a voice warm-up in the morning, three days running.
Hum a note somebody plays or sings, and match it.
Match five notes in a row.
Do a voice warm-up every morning for one week.
Sing a whole song in tune, on your own, to one person.
Sing standing up, breathing from low down instead of your shoulders.
Sing the same song louder without it going shouty.
Learn a second song properly, words and all.
Do a voice warm-up every morning for thirty days.
Sing a song to a group.
Sing one round with somebody else.
Hold your own line while somebody sings a different one.
Sing a harmony line with somebody else.
Sing something unaccompanied, with nothing to hide behind.
Learn a song in another language.
Sing three songs from memory, back to back.
Sing something to somebody who needed cheering up.
Lead a song that everybody joins in with.
Get somebody who says they cannot sing to sing one whole song.

tracks.about: Everybody can sing; most people have just never been allowed to. The rungs go from a song sung alone to one sung for people, in tune, with your own voice. Nothing to buy. This one changes how you feel about yourself faster than almost any other.

tracks.name: An instrument
tracks.line: One note to playing for people.

steps.test: Get one clear note out of an instrument.
steps.note: Any instrument. A tin whistle costs less than a takeaway and five notes gets you a tune.

steps.test: Play three different notes cleanly, one after another.
Play five notes in a row without a squeak or a buzz.
Play a five-note tune anybody recognises.
Play that tune three times in a row without a mistake.
Play a whole tune from beginning to end.
Play a tune in time with a beat — a metronome, or your own foot.
steps.note: In time matters more than fast. Slow and steady beats quick and lumpy, every time.

steps.test: Learn a second tune from scratch, on your own, with nobody teaching you.
Take the bar you keep getting wrong, play it slowly twenty times, and get it right.
steps.note: This is the actual skill, and almost nobody is taught it. Not playing the tune — fixing the one bar. Slow enough that it is never wrong, twenty times, then speed up.

steps.test: Play three tunes from memory.
Practise ten minutes a day for two weeks without missing a day.
Play a whole tune for one person, in the room with you.
Work a short tune out by ear, with nobody showing you the notes.
steps.note: Something you can hum. Find the first note, then the next. It takes longer than you think and it changes how you hear music.

steps.test: Learn a tune from written music, or from tab, on your own.
Play with somebody else, in time.
Play a tune all the way through for somebody without stopping, mistakes and all.
steps.note: Everybody hears the stop. Almost nobody hears the wrong note.

steps.test: Learn the beginner version of a song you actually like.
steps.note: The simple arrangement, not the record. Every song has one and it is not cheating.

steps.test: Play that song end to end, three times, without stopping.
Play it from memory, with nothing in front of you.
Play it for two or three people, and show one of them the first line.

tracks.about: One clear note, then five that make a tune, then a whole song played for somebody who knows it. It does not matter which instrument: a keyboard app on a phone will carry you through the first rungs, and a real instrument after that. This is the ladder for playing a song people recognise, for people, by ear or from the page.

tracks.name: Rhythm
tracks.line: Clapping in time to holding a beat for others.

steps.test: Clap in time with a song, all the way through.
Keep a steady beat on a drum for one minute.
Keep it for two minutes without speeding up.
steps.note: Everybody speeds up. Recording yourself is the fastest way to find out that you do.

steps.test: Clap a rhythm somebody gives you, back at them, correctly.
Clap on the offbeat while somebody claps on the beat.
Count a bar of four out loud while you play it.
Play a rhythm in three, and one in four, and hear the difference.
Play two different rhythms with your two hands.
Keep time with a metronome for three minutes.
Hold the beat while other people play over it.
Stop and come back in on the right beat.
Lead a drum circle.

tracks.name: Whistling
tracks.line: One note to a whole tune.

steps.test: Whistle one clear note.
Whistle two notes, one after the other.
Whistle up and down, high to low.
Whistle a tune somebody can name.
Whistle it in tune, checked against the real thing.
Whistle three tunes properly.
Whistle loudly with your fingers.
Teach somebody who cannot whistle to whistle.

tracks.name: Writing a song
tracks.line: Two lines to a song people sing.

steps.test: Write two lines that rhyme and mean something.
Write four lines about one thing that actually happened.
Say them out loud and cut every word that is not needed.
Write a whole verse.
Put a tune to it, even a simple one.
Write a chorus that says the one thing the song is about.
Sing the verse and the chorus to one person.
Change one line because of what they said.
Write a second verse that moves the story on.
Get the whole thing under three minutes.
Play or sing it the same way twice.
Write it down so somebody else could play it.
Record it, however roughly.
Listen back and fix the one thing that is wrong.
Write a whole song and perform it.
Write one for somebody, about them.
Give it to them.
Write a second song without waiting to feel like it.
Write one somebody else asks to hear again.
Write one the group sings without you starting it.

tracks.name: Reading music
tracks.line: Naming notes to sight-reading.

steps.test: Name every note on a line of written music.
Name the notes in the spaces and on the lines of the treble clef.
Clap a written line of rhythm, in time.
Say the note names of a simple tune out loud, in order.
Play a five-note written line on an instrument.
Read and clap crotchets, minims and quavers.
Play a written line in time with a beat.
Find middle C on a keyboard and point to it on the page.
Play a whole eight-bar tune from the page.
Read the time signature and count yourself in.
Play a tune you have never heard, from the page, slowly.
Read sharps and flats, and play them right.
Play a tune in a key with one sharp in it.
Name the notes in the bass clef.
Play a written line with your left hand.
Play a tune with a repeat, and a first and second ending.
Write out a four-bar tune you made up, so somebody else could play it.
Have somebody play what you wrote, and hear that it is right.
Sight-read a simple tune you have never seen, first try, slowly.
Sight-read a simple tune at proper speed, in front of somebody.

tracks.name: Dance
tracks.line: One step to leading the floor.

steps.test: Learn one dance step and do it in time.
Do it without counting out loud.
Learn three steps and put them together.
Dance in front of one other person.
Learn a whole short dance and do it with somebody.
Hold a frame with a partner and move without treading on them.
Lead, or follow, and let the other one do the opposite.
Dance a ceili dance properly with a set.
Learn a second set dance.
Dance at something where other people were watching.
Keep going after a mistake instead of stopping.
Learn a dance from another country.
Dance to music you have never heard before.
Ask somebody to dance.
Dance with somebody much older than you.
Make up a dance of your own.
Teach it to one person.
Teach it to two people and get them dancing it together.
Get somebody up who said they do not dance.
Lead the dancing at a group evening.

tracks.name: A song all the way through
tracks.line: From four, beside you. One song, sung whole, then sung to somebody.

steps.test: Sing one song all the way through with somebody singing beside you.
Sing it all the way through on your own, with nobody helping.
Sing it without forgetting any of the words.
Clap the beat while somebody else sings it.
Sing it and clap the beat at the same time.
Sing it as loud as you can.
Sing it so quietly that only the person next to you can hear.
Sing it fast, then sing it slow.
Sing it to somebody who has never heard you sing it.
Learn a second song all the way through.
Make up a new verse and sing that too.
Sing your song to a whole roomful of people.

categories.name: Magic and performance
categories.line: Card tricks, coins, sleight of hand, mind reading, mime, puppets.

tracks.name: Card tricks
tracks.line: One trick to a whole act.

steps.test: Do one card trick that works, on one person.
steps.note: A self-working one out of a book counts. Start where it cannot go wrong.

steps.test: Do the same trick three times without fumbling it.
Shuffle a deck properly, twice, without dropping any.
Cut the deck one-handed.
Learn a false cut that looks like a real one.
Force a card so the person is sure they chose freely.
Control a chosen card to the top of the deck.
Do a trick that genuinely fools an adult.
Do a trick and never say what is about to happen.
steps.note: Announcing it gives them somewhere to look. Say nothing and they cannot follow the method.

steps.test: Learn a double lift.
Do three tricks in a row without a mistake.
Do a trick with the cards in somebody else's hands.
Do one with a deck that is not yours.
Do a trick with your own patter, in your own words.
Do one where you never touch the cards at all.
Perform to four people standing around you.
Have a trick go wrong and finish anyway.
Build a routine where each trick leads into the next.
Perform a five-minute card act for a group.
Teach somebody one trick until they can fool a third person with it.

tracks.about: Card tricks are small performances: a secret, a story, and a moment when somebody's face changes. Each rung is one trick learned until it is smooth, then done for a person. By the end you have a five-minute act you can do at any table. Any pack of cards.

tracks.name: Coin tricks
tracks.line: Vanishing one to the whole routine.

steps.test: Make a coin vanish and reappear.
Palm a coin and let somebody look at your hand.
Do a French drop so nobody sees it.
Do it slowly enough that it looks natural.
steps.note: Speed hides nothing. What hides it is doing the fake exactly like the real thing.

steps.test: Look at your empty hand, not at the hand with the coin.
Vanish a coin and show both hands empty.
Produce a coin from behind somebody's ear convincingly.
Make a coin travel from one hand to the other.
Do three coin moves in one routine.
Do a routine with a borrowed coin.
Make a coin go through a table.
Do a routine with your own patter.
Do it standing, with people close.
Do it surrounded, with people watching from all sides.
Vanish four coins one at a time.
End on a production of something bigger than a coin.
Perform it twice in a row to the same person without them catching it.
Do a coin routine for a group.
Keep the method to yourself when somebody asks.
Teach somebody the French drop until they can fool you.

tracks.about: A coin vanish is the oldest trick there is and still the best, because everybody has a coin. The rungs build a few sleights until your hands do them without you, then put them in front of a person. Practise in front of a mirror; the mirror is the audience until you are ready.

tracks.name: Mind reading
tracks.line: One guess to a proper effect.

steps.test: Do a trick where you name a card somebody chose.
Do it without saying how clever it was.
Do one that works on two people in a row.
Learn to force a word or a number.
Do a prediction you wrote before they chose.
Read somebody's body language and guess right three times.
Ask a question that tells you the answer without them noticing.
Do an effect where you never touch anything.
Take longer over it than feels comfortable.
steps.note: Mind reading that is instant looks like a trick. Mind reading that seems to cost you something looks real.

steps.test: Get one wrong on purpose and then get it right.
Do a full mind reading effect with a story around it.
Do it on somebody who came in wanting to catch you.
Do one where the method is invisible even on a second showing.
Say plainly that it is a trick, and still have it land.
Do one that uses something of theirs.
Do a two-person effect with somebody helping you.
Perform three effects to a group and keep the method secret.
Take a guess with nothing to fall back on, and be wrong gracefully.
Build a ten-minute set that builds to one big finish.
Never use it to make somebody feel foolish.

tracks.name: Mime and clowning
tracks.line: One gesture to holding a room silently.

steps.test: Mime one action so clearly that somebody names it.
Mime three in a row and have all three named.
Do the invisible wall convincingly.
Do the rope pull.
Keep the wall in exactly the same place for a whole minute.
steps.note: The whole illusion is that the invisible thing does not move. One slip and it is gone.

steps.test: Mime carrying something heavy, then something light.
Tell a whole tiny story with no words.
Make somebody laugh without saying anything.
Mime a whole conversation with a person who is not there.
Do a walking-on-the-spot walk.
Perform a two-minute silent piece.
Run a mime game for younger children.

tracks.name: Puppets
tracks.line: Making one to putting on a show.

steps.test: Make a puppet out of a sock or a paper bag.
Give it a voice and keep the voice the same for two minutes.
Make it look at things, and at people.
steps.note: Where the puppet looks is what makes it alive. Nothing else comes close.

steps.test: Make it breathe while it is not talking.
Have it talk to one person and get an answer.
Make a puppet with moving parts.
Make a second puppet with a different voice.
Have the two of them talk to each other.
Write a short puppet story with a beginning and an end.
Perform it to two people.
Build a stage and run a proper show.
Run a puppet show younger children ask for again.

tracks.name: Circus skills
tracks.line: Spinning a plate to a routine.

steps.test: Spin a plate or a hoop and keep it going for ten seconds.
Keep it going for thirty seconds.
Keep a hoop spinning round your waist for thirty seconds.
Get a diabolo or devil sticks going at all.
Keep a diabolo or devil sticks going for thirty seconds.
Keep it going for a whole minute.
Do ten keepy-uppies with a football.
Do twenty-five keepy-uppies.
Spin a hoop on your arm and move it to the other arm.
Learn one trick with clubs, poi or a hoop.
Do that trick five times out of five.
Learn a second trick.
Throw and catch one club.
Learn a trick that goes wrong in front of people and recover from it.
Put two tricks together without stopping in between.
Put three circus tricks into one routine.
Do the routine to music, in time.
Perform it to five people.
Perform your routine at a day out.
Teach somebody their first trick until they can do it on their own.

categories.name: Food and the kitchen
categories.line: Knife skills, cooking, baking, growing, preserving, hosting.

tracks.name: Real food, part one
tracks.line: For grown-ups. From one honest look at a label to an eight-hour eating window.

steps.test: Read the ingredients of everything you eat today. Change nothing.
steps.note: Just read. If you cannot picture an ingredient growing, or being made in a kitchen, it is one to notice. Today is looking, not fixing.

steps.test: Drink only water, tea, coffee or herbal tea for a whole day.
steps.note: No fizzy drinks, no juice, nothing sweetened. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose today and count it. Already done is still done, and it is the ground the rest stands on.

steps.test: Eat one meal slowly: fork down between mouthfuls, taste every one.
steps.note: Twenty minutes for a plate. Notice when you are full; it arrives earlier than the empty plate does.

steps.test: Swap one thing in one meal for something more real.
steps.note: Cereal for eggs, crisps for nuts or cheese, a sauce from a jar for butter and salt, white bread for a plate of vegetables. One swap, one meal.

steps.test: Nothing to eat for the first three hours after waking.
steps.note: Water, tea or coffee are fine. If you already skip breakfast, count it. Notice that hunger comes in waves and passes.

steps.test: Nothing to eat in the three hours before you sleep.
steps.note: Finish dinner, close the kitchen. Herbal tea if you want something. Most people sleep better for it the very first night.

steps.test: A whole day without snacks: meals only, as many as you like.
steps.note: Three meals, or two, or four; the rule is nothing between them. Snacking is the habit most worth breaking, so this is a big rung.

steps.test: A day sweetened only by honey, fruit, or nothing.
steps.note: No sugar, no sweeteners, no syrups. If you already live like this, do it on purpose and count it. Read the labels; sugar hides under twenty names.

steps.test: A day where nothing you eat has more than five ingredients on its label.
steps.note: Food with no label (meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, fruit, butter) counts as zero. This is the rung that empties the biscuit tin.

steps.test: Cook one meal from real food only.
steps.note: Meat, fish or eggs; vegetables; butter, cream or olive oil; salt. Nothing from a packet with a list on it. It can be simple: eggs, spinach and butter is a meal.

steps.test: Both edges in one day: nothing for three hours after waking, nothing for three hours before bed.
steps.note: Rungs five and six together. You have done each already; today they meet.

steps.test: A twelve-hour window: first bite and last bite twelve hours apart.
steps.note: Eight to eight, nine to nine. Most people are nearly there already; this makes it deliberate. Water and tea outside the window are fine.

steps.test: A day where every carbohydrate is a vegetable or a piece of fruit.
steps.note: No bread, pasta, rice, potatoes, cereal or sweets. Plenty of everything else: meat, fish, eggs, cheese, butter, vegetables. Eat enough of the real things and you will not be hungry.

steps.test: Skip one meal on purpose and notice what actually happens.
steps.note: Not a snack instead; nothing until the next meal. Hunger rises, peaks, and goes. Write down what you noticed.

steps.test: Two big meals and nothing else, for one day.
steps.note: Make them proper meals, plates full of real food. This is how most people ate for most of history.

steps.test: Do one food shop buying only real food.
steps.note: Nothing that needs its label read. Meat, fish, eggs, dairy, vegetables, fruit, nuts, butter, olive oil. Look at the trolley at the end.

steps.test: Three days in a row with no snacks.
steps.note: Rung seven, held. By the third day the pull between meals has mostly gone.

steps.test: A ten-hour window: first bite to last bite in ten hours.
steps.note: Nine to seven, or ten to eight. Move the edges to suit your day; the width is the rung.

steps.test: Sixteen hours without eating, once.
steps.note: Dinner at seven, nothing until eleven the next morning. Water, tea and coffee throughout. Sleep does most of it for you.

steps.test: An eight-hour window for a full day: sixteen hours off, eight on.
steps.note: Two or three real meals inside the eight hours, nothing outside them. That is the far end of this ladder. Past here is part two; and if you have a health condition or take medicine, a doctor before you go further.

tracks.about: For grown-ups. Twenty rungs from one honest look at a label to an eight-hour eating window, in an order that never jumps. If a rung is already how you live, you do it on purpose that day and it counts. Real food, fewer snacks, a bit of space between meals; nothing extreme until the very end, and a doctor before going further if you take medicine.

tracks.name: Real food, part two
tracks.line: For grown-ups. From an eight-hour window to a way of eating that is yours.
tracks.about: Part one changed single days; part two makes it a week at a time and then a month. Real breakfasts, meals you cooked, no snacks for five days, a week of twelve-hour windows, then ten, then eight; a real-food kitchen, a whole chicken or a pot of beans used up, and one quiet day of twenty-four hours without food. Anybody on medicine, pregnant, diabetic, or under eighteen asks a doctor before the long ones. It ends with you writing down how you eat now.

steps.test: A week where every breakfast is real food, or no breakfast at all.
steps.note: Eggs, meat, fish, yoghurt, fruit, nuts, butter; or nothing until lunch. No cereal, no toast, no bars. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose and count it.

steps.test: Cook three real meals in one week.
steps.note: Meat or fish or eggs, vegetables, a fat you can name, salt. Nothing from a packet with a list. Three, on three different days.

steps.test: Five days running with no snacks.
steps.note: Meals only, as many as you need. By day five the pull between meals has mostly gone.

steps.test: A week without sugar, honey included; fruit is fine.
steps.note: Read every label. Sugar hides under twenty names. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose and count it.

steps.test: A twelve-hour eating window every day for a week.
steps.note: Eight to eight, nine to nine. Seven days in a row. Water, tea and coffee outside the window are fine.

steps.test: Make one thing you usually buy.
steps.note: Bread, yoghurt, stock, a sauce, pickles, granola without the sugar. Once, properly, and taste the difference.

steps.test: Eat a big plate of vegetables with butter or olive oil as a whole meal.
steps.note: Roasted, steamed, fried, whatever you like; a lot of them; fat on top. Notice that it is a meal.

steps.test: Three days running where every carbohydrate is a vegetable or a piece of fruit.
steps.note: No bread, pasta, rice, potatoes, cereal, sweets. Plenty of everything else. Eat enough and you will not be hungry.

steps.test: Cook a whole chicken, a whole fish, or a pot of beans from dry, and use all of it.
steps.note: The carcass becomes stock, the leftovers become tomorrow. This is how food was cooked for most of history.

steps.test: A ten-hour window every day for a week.
steps.note: Nine to seven, ten to eight. Move the edges to fit your days; keep the width.

steps.test: A day of two meals, no snacks, both cooked by you.
steps.note: Proper plates. Real food. Nothing between.

steps.test: Read one book, or listen to one long talk, on fasting or real food by a doctor or scientist who has studied it, and write down three things.
steps.note: One who has treated patients or run studies, not a seller of plans. Three things you did not know, in your own words.

steps.test: Sixteen hours off, eight on, three days running.
steps.note: Dinner at seven, first bite at eleven. Sleep does most of it. Water, tea and coffee in the gap.

steps.test: Keep a real-food kitchen for a week: nothing in it with more than five ingredients.
steps.note: Clear the cupboards first. What has no label counts as zero. Everybody in the house eats better without deciding to.

steps.test: Eat only what you cooked yourself for three days.
steps.note: Nothing bought ready, nothing from a café or a van. A flask and a box when you are out.

steps.test: Twenty-four hours without eating, once, on a quiet day.
steps.note: Dinner to dinner. Water, tea and coffee throughout; rest; nothing heavy planned. Not if you are pregnant, diabetic, on medicine, or under eighteen: a doctor first, always.

steps.test: A month without sugar.
steps.note: Thirty days, fruit allowed, honey not. After a month the sweet things you used to want taste like what they are. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose and count it.

steps.test: Cook a real-food meal for other people and say nothing about it being healthy.
steps.note: Roast chicken, vegetables in butter, a good salad, cheese and fruit after. Let them enjoy it. The word healthy ruins a dinner.

steps.test: Sixteen hours off, eight on, for a full week.
steps.note: Seven days. This is the far end of the ladder and most people find, by now, that it is simply how they eat.

steps.test: Write down how you eat now, what changed, and what you will keep.
steps.note: One page. That page is your way of eating, and it is yours to defend. From here a facilitator, if you want to go further, and a doctor beside you if you do.

tracks.name: Knife and board
tracks.line: From buttering bread properly to preparing a whole meal, and teaching a younger one.

steps.test: Butter a slice of bread properly, right to the edges.
how: Soft butter, not fridge-hard. Leave it out for half an hour first.
Spread from the middle outwards, right to every edge and corner.
No tearing the bread.
steps.note: The smallest possible knife job, and the one that teaches a light hand. Spread a hard butter and you tear the bread; that is the whole lesson in one slice.

steps.test: Learn the claw grip, with your fingertips tucked under.
how: Curl the fingers of your holding hand so the knuckles stick out and the fingertips hide behind them.
The flat side of the blade rests against your knuckles and slides along them.
Practise it on a carrot with somebody watching before you speed up at all.
steps.note: This one grip is why professional cooks can chop fast and still have ten fingers. Learn it before anything else and you never have to unlearn a bad habit.

steps.test: Cut a flat side onto a round vegetable first so it cannot roll.
how: Take a slice off one side of the onion, carrot or potato.
Turn it onto that flat side. Now it sits still.
Every round thing gets this treatment, every time.
steps.note: Rolling vegetables cause most kitchen cuts. This takes two seconds and removes the problem entirely.

steps.test: Cut something soft — a banana, a mushroom, a tomato — with the claw grip.
how: Slow. Speed comes from not stopping, never from moving fast.
Let the knife do the work — a sharp knife needs almost no pressure.
Fingertips tucked the whole time.
steps.note: Soft things show you whether the knife is sharp: if a tomato squashes rather than slices, the knife is blunt and that is more dangerous than a sharp one.

steps.test: Peel a vegetable without taking half of it away.
how: Peeler away from you, long strokes, light pressure.
Turn the vegetable rather than moving your hand about.
Look at the peelings — thin ribbons, not chunks.
steps.note: The peelings are the evidence. Thick peelings are money in the bin, and on a potato most of the good is just under the skin anyway.

steps.test: Chop an onion without help.
how: Top off, leave the root end on — it holds the whole thing together.
Halve it through the root, peel, flat side down.
Cuts towards the root but not through it, then across. It falls into dice.
steps.note: The onion is the test everybody is measured by, and the root-end trick is the whole secret. Once you can do an onion you can do anything on a board.

steps.test: Cut everything for one dish to roughly the same size.
how: Look at the biggest piece and the smallest piece before it goes in the pan.
Same size means everything is cooked at the same moment.
Take an extra minute rather than fixing it later.
steps.note: This is the actual difference between a decent home cook and a poor one, and it has nothing to do with recipes. Even pieces cook evenly. That is most of cooking.

steps.test: Prepare all the vegetables for a whole meal before anything goes in the pan.
how: Everything chopped, in bowls or piles, before the heat goes on.
Board wiped and clear before you start cooking.
It will take longer than you think the first time.
steps.note: Getting everything ready first is what stops a meal turning into a panic. It also means you can cook things that need your attention rather than only things that wait for you.

steps.test: Sharpen a knife, and cut the same vegetable before and after.
how: A cheap steel or a pull-through sharpener, or the back of a ceramic mug in a pinch.
Same angle each stroke, both sides evenly.
Cut a tomato before and cut one after.
steps.note: A blunt knife needs force, slips, and is how people get cut. A sharp knife is the safe one. Almost every kitchen in the country has only blunt ones.

steps.test: Wash, dry and put away your knife and board properly, every time, for a week.
how: By hand, dried immediately, never left in the sink for somebody to reach into.
Never in the dishwasher — it ruins the edge and the handle.
Board scrubbed and stood on its edge to dry.
steps.note: A knife left in a sink of water is the classic way somebody else gets hurt. This rung is about the person who washes up after you.

steps.test: Chop for somebody else who is cooking, at their pace.
how: Ask what size they want things and do it that way rather than your way.
Keep ahead of them so the pan never waits.
Clear your board as you go.
steps.note: Being the useful pair of hands in somebody else's kitchen is a social skill as much as a knife one, and it gets you fed in a lot of houses.

steps.test: Teach a younger child to chop safely.
how: Sitting down, at a table, with something soft and a small knife.
The claw grip first, the flat side second, and never anything else until both are automatic.
Your hand over theirs for the first few cuts, then your hands behind your back.
steps.note: Children are far better at this than adults expect and far safer once shown properly. The ones who are never taught are the ones who get hurt at fifteen.

tracks.about: Almost everything that gets called cooking is actually chopping, and almost nobody is ever taught how. A fortnight of this and a meal takes half as long and costs half as much, because real ingredients are cheaper than prepared ones and it is the chopping you were paying to avoid. It also happens to be the safest thing in the kitchen to learn properly and the most dangerous to pick up by accident.

tracks.name: Cooking a meal
tracks.line: From a cold breakfast to putting a hot meal in front of eight people.

steps.test: Make yourself a cold breakfast and clear it away afterwards.
how: Anything that needs no heat: eggs boiled the night before, yoghurt, fruit, cheese, oatcakes.
Eat it sitting down rather than standing up.
Everything washed, dried and put away before you leave the kitchen.
steps.note: Clearing away is half of this ladder and the half people skip. A cook who leaves a wreck behind stops getting to cook.

steps.test: Make a hot drink safely for yourself and somebody else.
how: Kettle filled above the element, lid down, handle turned in.
Pour slowly, away from you, with the cup on the worktop rather than in your hand.
Ask them how they take it rather than guessing.
steps.note: The first hot thing you handle. Handle turned in, pour on the worktop — two habits that prevent almost every kitchen scald.

steps.test: Boil an egg exactly the way you like it, twice running.
how: Water at a gentle boil, egg in, timer on. Six minutes runny, eight soft, ten hard.
Write down the time that worked.
Do it again two days later using your own number.
steps.note: Cooking is timing more than anything else. This is the smallest possible lesson in it: same time, same result, every time.

steps.test: Read a recipe all the way through before you start.
how: Every line, including the last one, before you touch anything.
Note the bits that need waiting — resting, rising, soaking, marinading.
Check you actually have everything.
steps.note: Almost every kitchen disaster is a recipe read one line at a time. Two minutes of reading saves the meal where the last step turns out to be 'leave overnight'.

steps.test: Get everything out, chopped and weighed before the pan goes on.
how: Every ingredient in its own bowl or pile, in the order it goes in.
Pans out, utensils out, bin within reach.
Only then turn the heat on.
steps.note: This is how every professional kitchen in the world works and it is why they are calm. Cooking is easy once the chopping is behind you.

steps.test: Make beans on toast with both parts ready at the same moment.
how: Work backwards: the toast takes two minutes, the beans take four. Beans first.
Butter on the plate and the table set before either is ready.
Hot food on a warm plate.
steps.note: The humblest possible lesson in timing two things, and it is exactly the same skill as getting a roast and its vegetables to land together.

steps.test: Cook pasta and a sauce and get them together hot.
how: Sauce on first, pasta into properly salted boiling water second.
Taste the pasta a minute before the packet says.
Drain, then straight into the sauce pan and toss — never sauce sitting on top.
steps.note: Salting the water and finishing the pasta in the sauce are the two things that separate a decent plate of pasta from a sad one, and both are free.

steps.test: Fry something without burning it or leaving it raw.
how: Pan properly hot before anything goes in — a drop of water should dance.
Do not crowd the pan. Two batches beats one steamed mess.
Leave it alone. Turn it once, when it lets go of the pan by itself.
steps.note: Turning things over and over is the commonest mistake there is. A thing that is stuck is not ready to turn; when it is ready, it releases.

steps.test: Taste as you go, and change it — more salt, or something sharp.
how: Taste before it goes on the plate, every single time.
Flat and dull usually means salt. Heavy and rich usually means something sharp: lemon, vinegar, mustard.
Add a little, stir, taste again.
steps.note: This is the rung that makes you a cook rather than a recipe follower. Nobody can taste your food from a page in a book.

steps.test: Cook a hot meal for yourself, start to finish.
how: Something real: meat or fish or eggs, a vegetable, something to cook it in.
Everything ready first, taste before serving, sit down to eat it.
Clear the kitchen afterwards.
steps.note: A whole meal on your own is the middle of this ladder. If this is already routine for you, cook something you have never cooked before and count that.

steps.test: Clean as you go, so the kitchen is nearly clear when you sit down.
how: Wash each thing while the next thing cooks.
Bin, cloth and hot soapy water within reach from the start.
The rung is what the kitchen looks like when the food goes on the table.
steps.note: This is the habit that decides whether cooking feels like a pleasure or a chore, and it costs no extra time at all — only different timing.

steps.test: Cook a hot meal for your family.
how: Something you have cooked before rather than a first attempt.
Ask beforehand what nobody will eat, so you are not surprised.
Plates warm, everything landing together, table laid.
steps.note: Feeding people is the oldest way there is of saying something you might not say out loud. This rung is worth more than the four above it.

steps.test: Cook the same meal again, better.
how: Write down one thing you would change before you forget it.
Cook it again within a fortnight with that one change.
Ask whether they noticed.
steps.note: Cooking the same thing three times beats cooking three different things. The second and third times are where the skill actually appears.

steps.test: Time three things so they are all ready together.
how: Write the times backwards from when you want to eat.
The longest thing goes on first. Everything else fits around it.
One timer per thing if you need it.
steps.note: This is the whole difficulty of cooking a meal, in one rung. Once you can do this with three things, a Christmas dinner is only the same problem with eight.

steps.test: Cook a meal out of whatever happened to be in the house.
how: Look at what you have first, then decide, rather than deciding then shopping.
Eggs, onions, a tin of something and whatever vegetable is going over is a meal.
No shopping trip allowed.
steps.note: This is where cooking starts saving you real money and real waste. It is also the skill that means you are never stuck.

steps.test: Cook for somebody who cannot eat something, and get it right.
how: Ask exactly what they cannot have, and whether it is a preference or a medical matter.
Read the labels on anything from a packet — it hides in sauces, stock and bread.
Clean board, clean pan, clean knife if it is serious.
steps.note: Being cooked for safely is rare enough that people remember who did it. Take it seriously and ask rather than assuming.

steps.test: Cook a roast, with the vegetables, all ready together.
how: Work backwards from the time you want to eat, on paper.
Meat rests for fifteen or twenty minutes — that is when the vegetables finish and the gravy happens.
A cheap cut cooked slowly beats an expensive one cooked badly.
steps.note: The roast is the traditional test and it deserves its reputation: six things, one oven, one moment. The resting time is the trick that makes it possible.

steps.test: Cook three courses and get them all to the table hot.
how: Pudding made first and left. Starter prepared cold or nearly cooked.
Main the only thing actually happening while people are in the house.
Written plan on the worktop.
steps.note: Doing the work in advance is the whole answer. Three courses is not three times the cooking, it is one course cooked while people are there and two done that morning.

steps.test: Cook a meal for eight people.
how: Choose something that scales and waits: a stew, a curry, a big tray bake, a pot of soup and good bread.
Cook it the day before if you can — most of these are better for it.
Count the plates, forks and chairs before the day.
steps.note: Numbers are not the hard part. Choosing a dish that forgives being held for half an hour is the whole skill of cooking for a crowd.

steps.test: Cook for the whole group at a day out.
how: A big pot of something, or a fire and something to grill, or a proper picnic you actually made.
Plan for it being cold, wet, and later than intended.
Bring more than you think, and something hot to drink.
steps.note: Feeding people outdoors is the oldest version of this and the one nobody forgets. It is also the end of the ladder: you can now feed anybody, anywhere.

tracks.about: Being able to feed yourself and other people well, from real ingredients, without a recipe in your hand. This is the most immediately useful ladder in the school: it saves real money every week, it is the practical half of Real food, and a person who can cook is welcome everywhere. It goes from boiling an egg to a roast and three courses, in about three months of cooking a few times a week — which you were going to do anyway.

tracks.name: Baking
tracks.line: From weighing accurately to a loaf of your own, and selling what you made.

steps.test: Weigh five things accurately on a scale, to the gram.
how: Bowl on the scale, zero it, then add. Zero it again for the next thing.
Get it exact rather than close. Baking is the one place where close is not good enough.
No scale? Kitchen scales are a few pounds second hand and every charity shop has one.
steps.note: Cooking forgives, baking does not. Everything above this rung depends on the weighing being honest.

steps.test: Bake something from a packet mix, exactly as it says.
how: Read it all the way through first. Then follow it to the letter.
Oven on early — it takes fifteen minutes to get properly hot.
Set a timer and check five minutes before it goes off.
steps.note: A packet mix takes all the decisions away so that you learn the oven, the tin and the timing without anything else to go wrong.

steps.test: Line and grease a tin so nothing sticks.
how: Butter the tin, then a circle of baking paper in the bottom, then butter that too.
For a loaf tin, a long strip up and over both ends acts as handles.
No paper? Butter and a dusting of flour, tapped out.
steps.note: More home baking is ruined at the turning-out stage than at any other. Two minutes of lining saves the whole thing.

steps.test: Bake something by following a written recipe on your own.
how: Everything weighed and lined up before you start.
Follow it exactly, even the bits you would change.
Write on the recipe afterwards what you noticed.
steps.note: Follow it exactly once before you ever improvise. You cannot tell what a change did unless you know what the original does.

steps.test: Rub butter into flour until it looks like breadcrumbs.
how: Cold butter, cut into small cubes, straight from the fridge.
Fingertips only, lifting the mixture up and letting it fall as you rub.
Stop when it looks like coarse breadcrumbs — a few bigger lumps are fine.
steps.note: Cold hands and cold butter. This one technique is the base of scones, shortbread, crumble and pastry, so it is worth ten minutes of practice.

steps.test: Make scones or shortbread that come out right.
how: Handle the dough as little as possible — the less you work it the lighter it is.
Hot oven, high shelf, and do not open the door for the first ten minutes.
Cut straight down with the cutter, no twisting, or they rise crooked.
steps.note: The first thing you will make that people ask for again. It is also the quickest: twenty minutes from a cold kitchen to something on a plate.

steps.test: Know when something is done without cutting it open.
how: A skewer into the middle comes out clean. A sponge springs back when pressed.
Bread sounds hollow when you knock the bottom of it.
Colour first, then the test. Pale means underdone whatever the timer says.
steps.note: Ovens all lie by ten or twenty degrees. Learning the tests rather than trusting the timer is what makes your baking work in anybody's kitchen.

steps.test: Bake a sponge that rises.
how: Butter and sugar beaten until genuinely pale and fluffy — a good five minutes.
Eggs added a little at a time so it does not split.
Flour folded in gently at the end. Beating here knocks the air out.
steps.note: A risen sponge is air, and the air went in during the beating. This is the rung that teaches why a method is in the order it is in.

steps.test: Bake something twice, and make the second one better.
how: Write down one change before you forget: five minutes less, a little more salt, a hotter oven.
Same recipe, one change only, within a fortnight.
Note which was better.
steps.note: One change at a time is the only way to learn anything from your own baking. Two changes and you will never know which did it.

steps.test: Make a dough and knead it for ten full minutes.
how: Timer on. Ten minutes is much longer than it feels — most people stop at three.
Push it away with the heel of your hand, fold it back, turn it a quarter, repeat.
It goes from a shaggy lump to smooth and springy. That change is what you are looking for.
steps.note: Kneading is the whole of bread and there is no shortcut worth having. Ten minutes of it is also a remarkably good way to be in a bad mood less.

steps.test: Make a loaf of bread from flour, water, salt and yeast.
how: Four ingredients only. Nothing else belongs in a loaf.
Knead ten minutes, rise until doubled, knock back, shape, rise again, bake hot.
It costs about thirty pence and takes fifteen minutes of actual work spread over an afternoon.
steps.note: A shop loaf has a label with twenty things on it. Yours has four. This one rung is the whole argument of Real food, made edible.

steps.test: Make a loaf where the crumb is even all the way through.
how: Knock the air out properly before the second rise, and shape it tightly.
Do not let the second rise go too far — it should spring back slowly when pressed.
Cut it only when it is cool, however hard that is.
steps.note: Big holes at the top and dense at the bottom is the classic second loaf. Proper shaping and not over-proving is the fix.

steps.test: Bake something with a filling that does not leak.
how: Cold pastry, cold filling, and seal the edges with a wet finger and a fork.
Cut a hole or two in the top so the steam has a way out.
Do not overfill. Everybody overfills.
steps.note: Leaks come from steam with nowhere to go. A couple of slits in the lid is the difference between a pie and a tray to scrub.

steps.test: Ice or decorate something so it looks like it was meant to.
how: Completely cold before any icing goes near it, or it slides off.
A thin first coat to catch the crumbs, then the real coat on top.
Simple and neat beats elaborate and messy every time.
steps.note: Looking deliberate is mostly patience: cold cake, thin first coat, one colour done neatly. It doubles the pleasure for the person receiving it.

steps.test: Bake something without looking at the recipe.
how: Pick the thing you have made most often.
Write the recipe out from memory first, then bake it and check.
Whatever you got wrong is the bit you never actually learned.
steps.note: Having one thing in your head that you can make in anybody's kitchen with no book is worth more than twenty recipes you can follow.

steps.test: Bake for somebody's birthday.
how: Ask what they actually like rather than baking what you like making.
Make it the day before so you are not rushing.
Bake a small test version first if it is a new one.
steps.note: A baked thing made by a person is one of the few gifts nobody has ever had too many of, and it costs about three pounds.

steps.test: Work out what a batch costs you to make.
how: Weigh the flour, butter, sugar and eggs you used and price each from the receipt.
Add something for the electricity and the paper.
Divide by the number of pieces.
steps.note: This is where baking meets Money and value, and the numbers usually surprise people in both directions. You cannot price anything until you know this.

steps.test: Bake to order for somebody else, to exactly what they asked for.
how: Write down what they asked for and read it back to them.
Agree the day and the time before you agree anything else.
Deliver it when you said, not when it is convenient.
steps.note: Somebody else's specification is a different job from your own baking. Getting the brief right, and on time, is most of what being paid for anything is.

steps.test: Price what you baked and sell it to people who are not related to you.
how: Cost plus your time, then a real price, written on a card.
A stall, a car boot, a school fair, a sign at the gate, a message to the street group.
Say the price out loud without apologising for it.
steps.note: The nerve is not in the baking, it is in saying the number. That is the rung. Ten pounds earned from something you made changes how you see your own hands.

steps.test: Teach somebody to bake one thing, start to finish, hands off.
how: Your hands behind your back. Say it, do not do it.
Let them make the mistakes — the crooked scones teach more than your perfect ones.
They take the whole batch home.
steps.note: Hands off is the hard part and the whole rung. Something somebody made themselves, badly, with you beside them, is what makes them a baker.

tracks.about: Baking is chemistry that you get to eat, and unlike cooking it rewards exactness rather than judgement, which makes it the better one to learn with children. The ladder goes from a packet mix to a proper loaf of bread from flour, water and salt — which costs about thirty pence and beats anything in a shop — and ends by selling what you made to somebody who is not related to you, which is a different kind of nerve entirely.

tracks.name: Cooking on fire
tracks.line: Toast on a stick to a whole meal outdoors.
