steps.test: Toast something on a stick over a fire and eat it.
Wait for embers instead of cooking on flames.
steps.note: Flames burn the outside and leave the middle raw. Embers are what you actually cook on.

steps.test: Cook an egg or a sausage over a fire without burning it.
Bake a bread twist on a stick.
Wrap something in foil and cook it in the embers.
Keep a fire steady at cooking heat for twenty minutes.
Cook a one-pot meal over a fire for two people.
Set up a pot so it hangs or stands steady over the heat.
Cook two things at once over the same fire.
Wash up outdoors and leave no trace of any of it.
Cook a full meal outdoors for six.
Run the fire and the food for a whole day out.

tracks.name: Growing
tracks.line: One seed to feeding people.

steps.test: Plant a seed and keep it alive for a month.
Water it without drowning it, and say how you knew.
Grow something fast — cress, radishes — and eat it.
Grow something you then eat, that took longer than a month.
Find out what your soil is like and what suits it.
Dig a bed or fill a pot properly and plant it out.
Sow seed in a tray and prick the seedlings out.
Keep a patch weeded every week for a month.
Lose a crop, work out why, and say what you would do differently.
steps.note: Everybody who grows anything kills things. The ones who get good are the ones who work out why.

steps.test: Grow three different things through a whole season.
Harvest something at the right moment, not too early or too late.
Grow something from a cutting rather than a seed.
Make compost and put it back on the ground.
Grow something over winter.
Save seed and grow next year's from it.
Grow enough of one thing to make a whole meal from it.
Grow enough to give some away.
Keep a note through a season of what worked and what did not.
Plant something that will not be ready for a year.
Run a growing patch for the group.

tracks.name: Keeping food
tracks.line: Jam to a full store cupboard.

steps.test: Make jam that sets.
Sterilise the jars properly before you fill them.
Label and date everything you put away.
Make a second batch that sets better than the first.
Pickle something in vinegar.
Eat it a month later and say whether it worked.
Freeze a harvest so it is still good in three months.
Dry herbs or fruit until they keep.
Make a chutney.
Ferment something — sauerkraut, kefir, a sourdough starter.
Keep a starter or a ferment alive for a month.
Salt or cure something.
Bake with something you preserved yourself.
Cook a whole meal using three things you put away.
Preserve a glut that would otherwise have been thrown out.
Fill a shelf with things you made that keep.
Know which of them is safe how long, and why.
Throw out something that went wrong, without arguing with yourself.
Give away a box of it and have people ask for more.
Teach somebody to make one thing that keeps.

tracks.name: Feeding people
tracks.line: Laying a table to hosting an evening.

steps.test: Lay a table properly for everybody.
Put something on the table that nobody asked for — flowers, a candle.
Serve a meal and make sure everybody has what they need.
Ask everybody what they cannot eat, before you plan anything.
Plan a meal for six on paper before cooking it.
Write the timings backwards from when you want to sit down.
steps.note: Start from the moment the plates hit the table and work back. Everything else is guessing.

steps.test: Cook something the day before so there is less to do on the day.
Get everybody sitting down within ten minutes of when you said.
Introduce two guests to each other with something they have in common.
Notice the person saying least, and bring them in.
Cook and host a meal for people who are not family.
Do it to a budget and come in under.
Have something go wrong and say nothing about it.
Feed somebody who turned up unexpectedly.
Host somebody new to the area, on their own.
Get somebody else to help, and let them do it their way.
Host an evening with a reason to it — a birthday, a leaving, a welcome.
Sit down and eat with them instead of hovering in the kitchen.
Send everybody home with something.
Host an evening people ask you to do again.

tracks.name: In the kitchen
tracks.line: From four, beside you. Hands washed, then stirring, spreading, cracking and making.

steps.test: Wash your hands properly before you touch any food.
how: Warm water, soap, and long enough to sing something short.
Backs of the hands and between the fingers, not just the palms.
Dry them on a towel, not on your clothes.
steps.note: Start every single session with this and it becomes automatic within a fortnight. Do it yourself beside them rather than telling them to.

steps.test: Put an apron on by yourself.
how: Over the head first, then the ties.
A tea towel tucked in at the neck works perfectly well as an apron.
Let them struggle with the ties for a while before you help.
steps.note: The apron is the signal that this is a proper job, not playing. Children take the whole session more seriously with one on.

steps.test: Stir something in a bowl until it is all mixed and nothing is left at the bottom.
how: A big bowl on a damp cloth so it does not spin.
Show them how to go round the bottom edge where it hides.
Let them check by lifting the spoon and looking.
steps.note: Give them the checking as well as the stirring. A child who has been shown how to tell when a job is done will do it properly without being watched.

steps.test: Pour from a small jug into a bowl without spilling it.
how: Small jug, half full. Both hands.
Slow and close — hold the jug low, near the bowl.
Practise with water at the sink first, where spills do not matter.
steps.note: Practising with water first is the trick for all of this. Ten free goes at the sink is worth more than one careful go with the eggs.

steps.test: Spread butter on a slice of bread, right to the edges, without tearing it.
how: Soft butter, left out beforehand. Hard butter tears the bread and they get cross.
A round-ended knife, spreading from the middle outwards.
Look at the corners together at the end.
steps.note: The corners are the standard, and it is a standard a four-year-old can see for themselves. That is what makes it a good first job.

steps.test: Peel a banana or a satsuma all by yourself.
how: Start the satsuma peel for them with your thumbnail, then hands off.
A banana opens more easily from the bottom than the stalk end.
Their fruit to eat afterwards.
steps.note: Let them finish it even when it takes three minutes and makes a mess. Finishing it themselves is the entire rung.

steps.test: Crack an egg into a bowl.
how: Tap it firmly on the flat worktop, not on the edge of the bowl — it shatters less.
Both thumbs in the crack, open it over the bowl.
Use a separate small bowl so a bad one does not spoil the mixture.
steps.note: The small bowl is how you let them do it without any risk to the meal, which means you can say yes rather than 'not this time'.

steps.test: Pick the bits of shell out.
how: A bigger piece of shell picks up a small one far more easily than fingers do.
Look properly rather than quickly.
Their job to say when it is clear.
steps.note: Fixing your own mistake without anybody being cross about it is a small, important lesson, and this is the safest possible place to learn it.

steps.test: Weigh something on the scales and say the number out loud.
how: Bowl on, zero it together, then spoon it in slowly.
Let them stop at the right number rather than you saying stop.
Numbers on a scale are real numbers doing a real job.
steps.note: This is reading, counting and a bit of chemistry, and none of it feels like a lesson. It is also the first rung of the Baking ladder.

steps.test: Make a sandwich and give it to somebody to eat.
how: Their choice of filling, within reason.
Cut it however they think is best.
They carry it and hand it over themselves.
steps.note: The handing-over is the important half. Making something that another person actually eats is the first time a child feeds somebody, and they know it.

steps.test: Wipe the table and put your things in the sink afterwards.
how: Damp cloth, and show them the crumbs they missed rather than doing it after them.
Everything they used goes in the sink or the dishwasher.
Apron off and hung up last.
steps.note: Clearing up is part of the job, not a punishment at the end of it. Start it at four and it is never a battle at fourteen.

steps.test: Help make one whole thing for everybody's tea.
how: Pick something with jobs they can genuinely do: a tray bake, a crumble, soup, buns.
Tell everybody at the table who made it.
Let them serve it out.
steps.note: Say their name out loud when the food goes on the table. Being useful to the whole family, publicly, is what they are actually after.

tracks.about: For a child of about four and upwards, with a grown-up beside them. Children want to be in the kitchen long before we let them, and a four-year-old can genuinely stir, pour, peel a satsuma, crack an egg and make a sandwich for somebody else. Every rung here is a real job that actually needed doing, which is the whole point: children can tell the difference between helping and being given something to keep them busy.

categories.name: Money and business
categories.line: Handling it, earning it, selling, running something, investing.

tracks.name: Money and value, part one
tracks.line: From writing down what you spend to being paid three times for one thing.

steps.test: Write down every penny you spend today.
steps.note: On paper or the notes app. No changing anything; just seeing it.

steps.test: Write down, roughly, what came in this month and what went out.
steps.note: One page. Two numbers and the gap between them is more than most people ever look at.

steps.test: Name three things you own that somebody would pay for.
steps.note: Not the house. A bike, a coat, a tool, a book, a game. Write a price beside each.

steps.test: Sell one thing you no longer need, for any price.
steps.note: An online listing, a car boot, a friend. Given away does not count; a pound does. The point is asking for money and getting it.

steps.test: Ask for a better price on one thing, politely.
steps.note: "Is that your best price?" at a market, on a phone contract, on anything second-hand. A no costs nothing.

steps.test: Cancel one thing you pay for and do not use.
steps.note: A subscription, a membership, a service. If there is nothing to cancel, count it and enjoy that.

steps.test: Write down one skill you have that somebody would pay for.
steps.note: Everybody has one. Tidying, driving, baking, explaining a phone, fixing a bike, minding a dog. Write it as an offer: "I can … for …".

steps.test: Make one thing that could be sold.
steps.note: A card, a loaf, a poster, a small repair, a jar of something. Made, finished, and you would take money for it.

steps.test: Offer one thing to one person for money.
steps.note: An hour of help, a bake, a lift, a lesson. A no is a fine answer; the rung is the offer, said out loud.

steps.test: Earn one pound you did not have this morning.
steps.note: Any honest way. Most people go years without earning a single pound outside their job.

steps.test: Find out properly what three people you know do for a living.
steps.note: What they actually do all day, what is hard, what pays. Ask; people like being asked.

steps.test: Set one money goal with a number and a date, written down.
steps.note: "£200 by the end of next month, from things I make or do." Small and real beats big and vague.

steps.test: Put aside a tenth of anything that comes in this week, before you spend.
steps.note: A jar, a separate account, an envelope. The oldest money habit there is. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose today and count it. Already done is still done.

steps.test: Ask for something you want at work or in a deal: more, better, or sooner.
steps.note: A day off, a rate, a discount, a start date. Ask once, plainly, then stop talking.

steps.test: Price one thing you could sell, from what it costs you to what people pay.
steps.note: Materials, time, what the shop charges. Write the number down and say it out loud without flinching.

steps.test: Sell that thing three times.
steps.note: Three different people, or the same one thrice. Now you know it sells.

steps.test: Read one book, or listen to one long talk, by somebody who has actually made money.
steps.note: Not a guru: a person who built and ran something. One, all the way through.

steps.test: Spend nothing for one whole day.
steps.note: Not a penny. Notice how often the hand goes to the pocket. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose today and count it. Already done is still done.

steps.test: Write a one-page plan for something you could run.
steps.note: What it is, who it is for, what it costs, what it earns, what you would do first. One page, no more.

steps.test: Get paid by three different people for the same thing.
steps.note: That is a business, however small. Part two grows it.

tracks.about: Money made and money kept, in twenty rungs that start with writing down what you spent today and end with three different people paying you for the same thing. Selling one thing, asking for a better price, an offer said out loud, a tenth put aside. Small, real, and most of it is nerve rather than knowledge.

tracks.name: Handling money
tracks.line: Naming coins to a weekly shop.

steps.test: Name every coin and note when somebody holds one up.
Count out one pound in three different ways.
Work out what two things cost together, before the till says.
Pay for something yourself and check the change is right.
Say what something costs in a whole hour of somebody working.
Give correct change from a five-pound note, five times running.
Compare two sizes of the same thing and say which is better value.
Write down every penny you spend for one week.
Look at that week and say where it actually went.
Keep a written record of money in and out for a month, and balance it.
Plan a week's shopping on paper with a budget on it.
Do a full weekly shop to that budget and come in under it.

tracks.name: Earning
tracks.line: One job to paying somebody else.

steps.test: Do one real job and be paid for it.
Agree what the job is and what it pays, before you start.
steps.note: Agreeing afterwards is how people end up feeling cheated on both sides.

steps.test: Finish it properly even though nobody was watching.
Do a job for somebody outside your own family.
Ask somebody if they need anything done.
Do the same job for the same person twice.
Turn up on time, three times running.
Say how much you charge, out loud, without apologising for it.
Do a job badly, own it, and put it right for nothing.
Hold a paid job around the place for a season, and turn up for it.
Save half of everything you earn for a month.
Work out what an hour of your time is worth right now.
Turn ten pounds into thirty pounds honestly, and show your working.
Find a second way of earning that is not selling your hours.
Get somebody to come back to you because of the last job.
Ask for more than you asked last time, and get it.
Turn down a job that was not worth doing.
Get somebody else a job you could not do.
Pay another person a fair share for their part in something you ran.
Give some of what you earned away, on purpose.

tracks.name: Selling
tracks.line: One thing to one person, to a real product.

steps.test: Sell one thing to one person.
Say what it is and what it costs, in one sentence.
Sell something to three people in one day.
Run a stall with real money and real change.
Hear no five times and keep going.
steps.note: Selling is mostly hearing no. The ones who are good at it stopped minding.

steps.test: Ask somebody what they were actually looking for, before offering anything.
Sell to ten people you have never met.
Work out what a thing costs you before you price it.
Price something so it sells, and defend the price when asked.
Put the price up and find out what happens.
Write down what you sold and what you made.
Handle somebody being unhappy with what you sold, and put it right.
Say no to a sale that would not have been fair.
Get somebody to buy a second time.
Ask a customer why they bought it, and listen.
Change what you sell because of what they told you.
Sell something you made yourself.
Get somebody to recommend you to somebody else.
Make something strangers buy more than once.
Teach somebody else to make their first sale, and let them do the talking.

tracks.name: Running something
tracks.line: A plan on paper to being asked back.

steps.test: Imagine you are putting on a games afternoon for six children. Write down five things you would have to sort out before the day.
steps.note: There is no right list. A room, a start time, a helper, which games, what to drink, what happens if it rains. Anything that would go wrong if nobody thought of it counts. The point is writing it down before the day, which is most of running anything.

steps.test: Ask three people whether they would actually come.
Run one part of an outing yourself.
Make a list of everything that has to happen, in order.
Put a name against every item on that list.
steps.note: A job with no name against it does not get done. That is the whole of organising.

steps.test: Ask somebody to do one of them, and let them.
Set a date and tell people.
Work out what it costs before it starts.
Organise a small event for the group and make it happen.
Deal with one thing going wrong on the day.
Thank everybody who helped, by name.
Write down afterwards what you would change.
Run the same thing again, better.
Make an event cover its own costs with nobody topping it up.
Find out what people actually want first, then do that.
Run something where you were not the one at the front.
Hand a job to somebody who had never done it.
Cancel or change something when it was the right call.
Run something for people outside the group.
Run something people ask you to do again.

tracks.name: Making money grow
tracks.line: Saving to understanding it.

steps.test: Save for four weeks without spending any of it.
Say what you are saving for, out loud.
Put money somewhere you cannot get at it easily.
Explain what interest is, in your own words, correctly.
Work out what a pound a week becomes in a year.
Work out what it becomes in ten years with interest on top.
steps.note: This one sum has changed more lives than any other in this room.

steps.test: Save for three months without touching it.
Buy something, improve it, and sell it for more.
Do that twice and work out what you actually made.
Explain what a share in a company actually is.
Explain what a bank does with your money.
Say what inflation does to money in a tin under the bed.
Explain the difference between a debt that pays you and one that costs you.
Track a small investment for one month and explain what happened.
Watch it go down and not sell.
Track it for six months and explain what happened.
Say what you would never put money into, and why.
Spot something that was too good to be true, and walk past it.
Set aside a fixed share of everything that comes in, every time.
Teach a younger child what saving and interest mean.

tracks.name: Negotiating
tracks.line: Asking to a fair deal.

steps.test: Ask for something you want, out loud, in a full sentence.
Ask, and then stop talking.
steps.note: The silence after the ask does the work. Filling it is how people talk themselves down.

steps.test: Swap something with somebody so you are both pleased.
Decide the number you will not go past, before you start.
Ask for a better price and get one.
Ask for something extra instead of money off.
Ask somebody what they need out of it, before saying what you want.
Ask a question instead of arguing back.
Get somebody to name their number first.
Say a number, out loud, and let it stand.
Walk away from a deal that was not good enough.
Go back the next day and get it anyway.
Find the thing that costs them little and is worth a lot to you.
Sort out a disagreement where both sides end up content.
Negotiate with somebody you will have to deal with again.
Give something away in a deal, on purpose, and say why.
Negotiate a bill or a subscription down, from your chair.
Say no and keep the relationship.
Negotiate something real on behalf of somebody else.
Become somebody people want to deal with again.

categories.name: Beauty and buildings
categories.line: Why one street feels good and another does not. Shapes, proportion, arches, and your own town.

tracks.name: Looking at buildings
tracks.line: Noticing, then being able to say why.

steps.test: Point at a building you think is pretty and one you think is ugly, and say which is which.
Say one reason why. Any reason counts, including a feeling.
Find two buildings on the same street and say which you would rather live in, and why.
Count the windows on a building and say whether they are evenly spaced.
Look at a building at eye level and say what a person walking past actually sees.
Find a building with a front door that looks like it means it.
Find one where the top, the middle and the bottom are clearly different.
Photograph three you like and three you do not.
Find one thing the three good ones share.
Find one thing the three bad ones share.
Walk somebody round and show them the good and the bad, and have them see it too.
Write down, in your own words, five rules for what makes a building good.

tracks.name: Proportion
tracks.line: Why some shapes feel right and others do not.

steps.test: Fold a piece of string exactly in half by eye, then check it.
Look at two rectangles and say which one feels nicer to you. There is no wrong answer.
Divide a line into three equal parts by eye, then measure and see how close you got.
Draw a square by eye and check it with a ruler.
Draw a house and put the door at a size that looks right for a person.
Measure a door, a chair and a step, and say what they all have in common.
steps.note: They are all sized off a human body. Almost everything that feels right is.

steps.test: Find something around you about one and a half times as long as it is wide.
Find something twice as long as it is wide, and say which shape you prefer.
Learn what the golden ratio is, roughly, and find one thing close to it.
Draw the same window three sizes and say which suits the wall.
Look at a room and say whether the ceiling is too low, too high, or right.
Find a building where one part is clearly the wrong size, and say which.
Draw a front of a building with everything in proportion to the door.
Space five windows evenly across a drawn wall, by eye.
Change one proportion in your drawing and see the whole thing change.
Draw the same building twice, once well proportioned and once badly.
Show both to somebody and see if they pick the same one you would.
Find a good proportion in something that is not a building at all.
Lay out a page, a poster or a garden using a proportion on purpose.
Draw the front of a building where every part looks right beside every other part.

tracks.name: Shapes and geometry
tracks.line: Circles, squares, tiles and solids.

steps.test: Find a circle, a square and a triangle in the room you are in.
Draw a circle freehand that somebody else agrees is properly round.
Draw a square and check its corners against the corner of a page.
Draw a triangle with all three sides the same, using a compass.
Make a shape that tiles, and fit six of them together with no gaps.
Find out which regular shapes tile and which cannot.
Step a compass around a circle six times and have it close exactly on itself.
Cut and fold paper into a solid shape that stands up.

tracks.name: Symmetry and pattern
tracks.line: Repeats, mirrors, and why they calm a room.

steps.test: Fold paper, cut a shape, open it out, and see the two halves match.
Find three symmetrical things around you.
Find something almost symmetrical and say what spoils it.
Draw the missing half of a face or a building so both sides match.
Make a pattern that repeats six times without a mistake.
Make one that repeats by turning instead of by mirroring.
Find a repeating pattern somewhere in your town.
Find a symmetrical building and a lopsided one, and say which feels calmer.
Find a building that is symmetrical on purpose except in one place.
Design a tile of your own.
Repeat it in every direction and fix whatever does not line up.
Design a tile that still works when you repeat it in every direction.

tracks.name: Arches and columns
tracks.line: The old ways, and why they were used.

steps.test: Find an arch somewhere near you and stand underneath it.
Build an arch out of blocks that stands up on its own.
Take the middle stone out and watch what happens.
steps.note: That is the keystone. Nothing holds until it is in, and everything holds once it is.

steps.test: Point out the three parts of a column — the base, the shaft and the top.
Say in your own words why an arch holds more weight than a flat beam.
Find a round arch and a pointed one and say which is older.
Find a column, an arch and a dome all in one day.
Explain to somebody younger why old buildings were built this way.

tracks.name: Your own town
tracks.line: Reading the place you actually live.

steps.test: Walk down your street and count the buildings you like.
Find the oldest building near you and say what is different about it.
Find out what your street was before it was houses.
Find a place where two different times sit side by side.
Draw a map of one street with the good buildings marked on it.
Find a spot in your town that feels good to stand in.
Say what makes it so — the width, the light, the noise, the edges.
Find a spot that feels bad to stand in, and say what would fix it.
Find where people naturally stop and stand, and say why there.
Find the one thing you would change about your town if you could change one.
Tell somebody who could do something about it.
Take somebody round and show them the town the way you now see it.

categories.name: The classical mind
categories.line: Logic, the big questions, the great stories, and one beautiful thing a day.

tracks.name: Spotting a bad argument
tracks.line: Telling a good argument from a loud one.

steps.test: Notice somebody changing the subject instead of answering, and say so afterwards.
Say what is wrong with "everybody does it, so it must be fine".
Say what is wrong with "he is wrong because he is an idiot".
Tell the difference between a reason and a feeling, in one argument.
Say what somebody would have to show you to change your mind.
steps.note: If nothing could change your mind, it was never an argument. It was a loyalty.

steps.test: Spot an argument that attacks the person instead of the point.
Spot one that says a small thing must lead to a disaster.
Spot one where somebody argues against a thing nobody said.
Spot three different bad arguments in a week and write down what was wrong with each.
Name five kinds of bad argument and give a real example of each.
Find a bad argument on your own side.
Say what you actually believe and what your reason is, separately.
Say back somebody else's argument so well that they agree that is it.
Then say why you still disagree.
Notice a number being used to prove something it does not prove.
Notice when something is true and irrelevant.
Point one out kindly, in the moment, without making anybody feel small.
Lose an argument on purpose because the other person was right.
Hold two possible answers open for a whole week without settling.
Teach somebody younger how to tell a good argument from a loud one.

tracks.name: Asking the good question
tracks.line: The Socratic habit, at any age.

steps.test: Ask why three times in a row about the same thing and see where you end up.
Ask somebody what a word really means, and keep going until it is clear.
Take a word like fair or brave and give an example and a non-example.
Ask a question you genuinely do not know the answer to.
Ask one that cannot be answered yes or no.
Ask a question and wait five full seconds for the answer.
steps.note: Most people fill the silence in two. The answer that was coming never arrives.

steps.test: Ask somebody how they came to think that.
Ask questions for five whole minutes without giving your own opinion once.
Ask the question everybody is avoiding.
Ask a question that helped somebody work something out themselves.
Change your own mind out loud, because of an answer somebody gave you.
Run a question with a group and keep everybody talking.

tracks.name: The big questions
tracks.line: Philosophy, done out loud, from about five upwards.

steps.test: Say what you think the word good means, in your own words.
Answer this and give a reason: is it ever right to tell a lie?
Say what you think fair means, and give a case where it is hard.
If every plank of a ship is replaced one by one, is it still the same ship? Say why.
Say whether you are the same person you were at five, and why.
Argue properly for the opposite of what you actually believe.
Say what you would do in a case where both choices are bad.
Say whether something can be beautiful if nobody ever sees it.
Say what you think a good life is, in three sentences.
Ask an older person the same question and listen to all of it.
Read a page of a philosopher and say one thing you agreed with and one you did not.
Read a second one who disagrees with the first.
Say which of them you think is right, and what it would take to be sure.
Sit with a question for a whole week without answering it.
Write a page on what you believe and why.
Have somebody take it apart, and thank them.
Change one line of it, honestly.
Discuss a big question with somebody much younger, at their level.
Notice one of these questions turning up in an ordinary day.
Run a proper discussion for the group and let the best answer win, even if it is not yours.

tracks.name: The great stories
tracks.line: Myths, fables, and the books people keep reading.

steps.test: Listen to a whole myth or fable and say what happened.
Say what the story was actually about, underneath the events.
Say what the person in it wanted, and what stopped them.
Learn one myth well enough to tell it.
Tell it from memory to somebody else.
Read three of Aesop and say what each one is for.
Find a fable that you think is wrong.
Read a whole book that people have been reading for hundreds of years.
Say why you think people kept reading it.
Find the same idea turning up in two different old stories.
Find one turning up in something made this year.
Read a story from a place you know nothing about.
Learn the names of five gods or heroes and what each stood for.
Say which character in an old story you are most like, and why.
Read a second old book, longer than the first.
Argue that an old story got something wrong.
Tell an old story to somebody who has never heard it.
Read one aloud to the younger ones, doing the voices.
Read the same story again a year later and notice what changed.
Give somebody a book that mattered to you, and talk about it after.

tracks.name: Words and where they come from
tracks.line: Latin and Greek, the useful way.

steps.test: Learn what one word root means and find two English words that use it.
steps.note: Aqua means water: aquarium, aqueduct. That is the whole exercise, with a root of your own.

steps.test: Learn three roots.
Learn five roots.
Find a word in the room that uses one of them.
Learn ten roots and what they mean.
Learn five prefixes — un, re, pre, sub, trans.
Learn five endings and what they do to a word.
Break a long word into its parts and guess what it means.
Work out a long word you have never seen before, from its parts alone.
Do that with five words in one day.
Learn twenty Latin or Greek words and use them correctly.
Find where three English words came from, and be surprised by one.
Find two words that look related and are not.
Learn the Latin or Greek behind five things in a hospital or a courtroom.
Read one line of Latin or Greek and say what it means.
Read a motto on a building or a coin and translate it.
Learn thirty roots.
Guess a word in another European language from its root, and be right.
Explain to somebody why a word means what it means.
Teach somebody to break a long word into its parts.

tracks.name: One beautiful thing a day
tracks.line: Looking on purpose, and keeping what is worth keeping.

steps.test: Find one beautiful thing today and say why it is.
Find one that nobody else would have noticed.
Do it every day for a week.
Write each one down.
Find one in something ordinary — a tool, a doorway, a pavement.
Find one made by a person, and one not made by anybody.
Do it every day for a month and write each one down.
Start a commonplace book and copy the first thing worth keeping into it.
Keep it for a month.
Learn one piece of music, one poem or one painting well enough to describe it from memory.
Show somebody something beautiful they had been walking past for years.
Read back a month of your own list and pick the best one.

tracks.name: Thinking on your own
tracks.line: A walk, a question, and no screen.

steps.test: Walk or sit for ten minutes with nothing to look at, thinking about one thing.
Say afterwards what you worked out.
Do it three times in one week.
Go for a walk with no phone at all.
Sit for twenty minutes with one question and nothing else.
Write down what you actually think about something, a page of it.
Write it without looking anything up first.
steps.note: Find out what you think before you find out what everybody else thinks. It is much harder afterwards.

steps.test: Read what somebody else thinks about it, after.
Write a page every week for a month.
Change your mind on paper, and write down what changed it.
Notice a thought you have had a hundred times and never examined.
Work something out on a walk that you could not work out sitting down.
Spend a whole day with no screen at all.
Be bored for an hour without reaching for anything.
Write down the thing you have been avoiding thinking about.
Decide something you have been putting off, and write down why.
Say one thing you believe that the people around you do not.
Write a page every week for three months.
Read back your own pages from two months ago.
Keep it going for a whole season.

categories.name: Nerve
categories.line: Small brave things, done on purpose, until they stop being brave. The later levels are for older ones and adults.

tracks.name: Asking out loud
tracks.line: From the time of day to the thing you actually want.

steps.test: Ask a stranger the time, or for directions you do not really need.
Ask a second stranger the same day.
Ask for something small in a shop — a bag, a glass of water, what they would recommend.
Ask somebody to repeat something you did not catch.
Ask for help carrying, reaching or finding something.
Ask politely for a discount, and take no cheerfully.
Ask somebody for a recommendation and then act on it.
Ask somebody for a favour you would normally talk yourself out of asking for.
Ask, and then say nothing until they answer.
Ask somebody for their time — half an hour of it — and say what for.
Ask for something you genuinely want, from somebody who could actually say yes.
Take somebody else out and get them to do their first ask.

tracks.name: Walking in
tracks.line: Rooms where you know nobody.

steps.test: Walk into a room where you know nobody, and stay.
Stay for a full twenty minutes before you let yourself leave.
Say hello to one person in that room.
Go somewhere new on your own and buy one thing.
Join a class or a group where everybody already knows each other.
Sit down with people you have never met and start a conversation.
Go back a second time, when the first time was awkward.
Turn up to something on your own, having told nobody you were coming.
Eat somewhere on your own without a phone in front of you.
Go to something where you are the only one of your kind in the room.
Learn one person's name and remember it a week later.
Bring somebody who would never have gone on their own.

tracks.name: On the phone
tracks.line: The call you would rather send a message about.

steps.test: Make one phone call you would rather have sent a message about.
Phone a shop and ask whether they have something.
Write down the one sentence you will open with, then ring.
steps.note: One sentence, not a script. It is only the first ten seconds that anybody dreads.

steps.test: Phone and book something — a table, an appointment, a slot.
Phone somebody you have been meaning to ring for weeks.
Phone somewhere expensive and ask real questions about what they do.
Leave a voicemail that says who you are and what you want.
Phone to sort out something that went wrong, politely, and get it put right.
Stay pleasant with somebody who was not.
Ask to speak to somebody who can actually decide.
Phone a stranger to ask for information, advice or an introduction.
Make five calls in one day that you had been putting off.

tracks.name: Getting told no
tracks.line: Collecting refusals until they stop stinging.

steps.test: Ask for something you are fairly sure will be refused, and be refused.
Notice that nothing at all happened afterwards.
Collect three noes in a week, on purpose.
Ask for something silly and get a no with a smile.
Collect ten noes.
Ask one more question after a no, instead of walking off.
Ask why not, and get an actual reason.
Turn a no into a yes by asking a different way.
Get a no from somebody whose opinion you care about.
Ask the same person again, later, after something changed.
Count your noes for a month and notice you stopped minding.
Take somebody else out collecting noes.

tracks.name: Speaking up on the spot
tracks.line: No warning, no notes.

steps.test: Say something out loud in a group of people you do not know.
Answer a question you were not expecting.
Ask a question at a talk or an event, in front of everybody.
Say your name and one sentence about yourself to a room.
Start your answer before you have finished working it out.
Stand up and thank somebody publicly, in a room.
Speak for one minute with no warning at all.
Speak for two minutes with no warning at all.
Say "I do not know" in front of people and carry on.
Speak up when something is wrong and nobody else has.
Disagree with somebody in front of a room.
Take a microphone you were not expecting to be handed.

tracks.name: Not minding what people think
tracks.line: Harmless, cheerful, and entirely your own business.

steps.test: Wear something you would normally think twice about, for a whole day.
Hum or sing out loud somewhere people can hear you.
Say hello to three strangers in one walk.
Sit alone in a cafe for an hour with no phone out.
Dance where people can see you.
Do something harmlessly odd in public and stay for the reaction.
Ask a question that everybody else thinks is obvious.
Be the first to clap, or the first onto a dance floor.
Say what you actually like, when it is not the fashionable answer.
Do something enthusiastically in front of people too cool for it.
Notice a worry about what people think, and do it anyway.
Do the thing you have been putting off purely because of what people would think.

categories.name: Negotiation
categories.line: Almost everything is flexible — the price, the terms, the timing. Most people simply never ask.

tracks.name: Asking for a better price
tracks.line: From asking at home to shifting a printed price tag.

steps.test: Ask somebody at home for something you want, and give one good reason why.
Find out what somebody else pays for something you pay for.
Ask, in a shop or at a market, whether that is the best they can do.
Ask a second time somewhere else the same day.
Get three different prices for the same thing before you buy anything.
Ask what it would cost if you bought two.
Ask what it would cost in cash, or today.
Get money off by asking, then write down the exact words that worked.
Ask somebody who does not look like they can move the price.
Ask for the person who can.
Ask about something second-hand and settle in the middle.
Get a better price on something that had a printed price tag on it.

tracks.name: Asking for more instead of less
tracks.line: Value is easier to move than price.

steps.test: Ask for something extra that costs them nothing — a bag, more sauce, a longer look.
Ask twice in one day.
Ask for a free upgrade somewhere, pleasantly, and take no cheerfully.
Ask what comes with it before you ask what it costs.
Get something added in for nothing — delivery, a case, a longer guarantee.
When the price will not move, ask what else they can do instead.
Write down three things you would rather have than money off.
Ask for one of those three.
Ask for more of somebody's time rather than more of their money.
Get an upgrade on something that actually mattered — a seat, a room, a service.
Say what you would need to make it a yes, and let them find it.
Show somebody else that asking for more is easier than asking for less.

tracks.name: From your chair
tracks.line: The bills you have never once questioned.

steps.test: Find one thing your household pays every month and work out what it costs in a year.
Look up what a brand new customer pays for that same thing.
Write down the number you want before you ring.
Phone them and ask, plainly, whether that is the best they can do.
Ask to be put through to somebody who can actually change it.
Say you are thinking of leaving, and mean it.
Get a rate, a fee or a bill reduced by asking for it.
Go through every regular bill you have in one afternoon.

tracks.name: Terms, not just the price
tracks.line: The price is often the least flexible part.

steps.test: Think of the last thing you bought that cost more than a coffee. Say two things about that deal that were not the price.
steps.note: How long it will last. Whether you could take it back. When you had to pay. A deal is never only the number.

steps.test: Ask when it could arrive, and whether sooner is possible.
Ask what happens if it goes wrong.
Read the part everybody skips, once, all the way through.
Ask for longer to pay, or to pay in parts.
Ask for a better guarantee or a longer window to change your mind.
Ask who does the work, and when.
Get something written down that had only been said.
Improve a deal without the price changing at all.
Say what matters most to you, and trade the rest.
Spot a term that was worse than the price, and change it.
Explain to somebody why the price is usually the last thing to move.

tracks.name: Being willing to walk away
tracks.line: The quietest strength there is.

steps.test: Before you next buy one thing, write down the most you will pay for it. Then do not go above it.
Work out what you will do instead if there is no deal.
steps.note: Knowing your other option is what makes walking away possible. Without one you are only pretending.

steps.test: Leave something in a shop that you wanted, because it was not right.
Say "that is more than I want to spend", and then stop talking.
Sleep on a decision you wanted to make on the spot.
Say you will think about it, and actually leave.
Walk away from a deal, and be glad about it afterwards.
Have somebody come back to you with a better offer after you left.
Say no to a thing you could afford and did not need.
Walk away from a deal with somebody you liked.
Notice when you are about to buy because you feel rushed, and stop.
Walk away from something you really wanted, because the terms were wrong.

tracks.name: Both sides pleased
tracks.line: The deals people come back for.

steps.test: Swap something with somebody so that you are both happy.
Ask somebody what they actually need before you say what you want.
Say back their side before you argue yours.
Find one thing that costs you little and is worth a lot to them.
Give that away first, without being asked.
Do a deal where the other person clearly got something they wanted too.
Tell somebody something that weakened your own position, because it was true.
Split a difference instead of winning it.
Settle a disagreement so both people came away with most of it.
Let somebody else have the last word on something small.
Do a deal with somebody you will have to see every week.
Go back and fix a deal that turned out unfair on them.
Do a deal that somebody thanks you for afterwards.
Turn down a better offer because you had already given your word.
Broker something between two other people.
Keep a relationship intact through a deal that did not happen.
Have somebody recommend you to somebody else.
Do a second deal with the same person.
Say what you would not do, out loud, before the talking starts.
Become somebody people want to deal with again.

categories.name: You belong here
categories.line: Fine shops, grand rooms and expensive things — so you never again decide somewhere is above you.

tracks.name: Your town, part one
tracks.line: From a street you have never walked to being greeted by name.

steps.test: Walk one street in your own town that you have never walked.
steps.note: Ten minutes. Look up: the upper floors are where the old town still is. If you have walked every street, walk one at a different time of day.

steps.test: Learn the names of five streets or places you pass every week.
steps.note: Say them out loud as you pass. Most people can name three streets in the town they have lived in for years.

steps.test: Say hello to the person who runs one shop, stall or café you pass often, by name if you can.
steps.note: No need to buy anything. "Morning, I walk past every day and never say hello." That is the whole rung.

steps.test: Find out one thing about your town's history and tell somebody.
steps.note: Why the name, what the oldest building was for, who the statue is. One fact, told once.

steps.test: Walk into a building you have never been in and look around for two minutes.
steps.note: A library, a town hall, a church, a hotel lobby, an auction house. You are allowed. Nod to somebody, look, leave.

steps.test: Sit somewhere public for fifteen minutes and just watch who comes and goes.
steps.note: A bench, a square, a station, the steps of somewhere. A bench costs nothing and a café is not required.

steps.test: Find three groups that meet in your town and write them down.
steps.note: A choir, a club, a parkrun, a class, a market, a men's shed, a mums' group. The library notice board, a search, or asking somebody.

steps.test: Ask somebody local for their best recommendation.
steps.note: A walk, a view, a shop, a person worth knowing. "You've lived here a while, what should I not miss?"

steps.test: Pick up litter for ten minutes on one street and leave it better.
steps.note: A bag and, if you have them, gloves. Nobody will thank you and that is rather the point.

steps.test: Go to one thing that is on, and stay half an hour.
steps.note: A market, a match, a talk, a service, a fair, a carol concert. Pick one that is free.

steps.test: Find out who actually runs things in your town.
steps.note: The council, your councillor, the group behind the events, who owns the big empty building. Names, written down.

steps.test: Send one message of thanks to a local person or group for something they run.
steps.note: The market, the run, the choir, the litter pick. Three sentences. Local people answer.

steps.test: Walk into somewhere you feel you do not belong and ask one question.
steps.note: A fine shop, a golf club reception, a grand hotel. "Is the restaurant open to non-residents?" Smile, thank them, go.

steps.test: Introduce yourself to a neighbour two doors further than you have ever gone.
steps.note: Your name, how long you have been here. In a flat, the floor above or below counts.

steps.test: Go to one group's meeting once. Say your name. Stay to the end.
steps.note: One from rung seven. Free ones exist everywhere: a run, a choir, a walking group, a class at the library.

steps.test: Offer to help at one thing.
steps.note: Set out chairs, hand out water, tidy up, hold a banner. "Do you need a hand with anything?" is the whole rung.

steps.test: Go back to the same group a second time.
steps.note: The second visit is when people start to remember you. Say your name again anyway.

steps.test: Bring somebody with you to something local.
steps.note: A friend, a child, a neighbour. Being the one who knows what is on is a kind of belonging.

steps.test: Learn ten local names.
steps.note: The butcher, the postie, the librarian, the coach, the people at the bus stop. Write them down; use them.

steps.test: Be greeted by name by three people on one walk through town.
steps.note: Nothing to put on, nothing to organise. When it happens, you belong here. Part two builds something for the town.

tracks.about: Your own town, walked, learned, and joined. From a street you have never walked to a meeting you went back to twice, to being greeted by name on one walk through. Free things only; no group needs paying for and no shop needs buying from.

tracks.name: From where you are sitting
tracks.line: All of this can start today, at home.

steps.test: Look up a grand building near you that is open to the public, and find its opening times.
Look up the real price of something you would never normally price.
Look up what one night somewhere very good actually costs.
Find out that something you assumed was closed to you is not.
Phone a dealership and ask two questions about a model.
Phone a fine hotel and ask what is included in a room.
Email somewhere you assume would never reply.
Ask a real question in it, not a polite one.
Book a viewing, a tasting or a trial of something.
Put a date in the diary for something you have always put off.
Tell one person you are going.
Book something in advance that you would normally have talked yourself out of.

tracks.name: Fine shops
tracks.line: Looking properly, and being helped.

steps.test: Walk into an expensive shop and look at three things properly, without hurrying.
Stay long enough that somebody comes over.
Let an assistant come over, and tell them what you are looking at.
Ask what the difference is between two of them.
Ask to try something on — a watch, a coat, a jacket.
Try on something far beyond what you would ever spend, and look in the mirror.
Say thank you and leave without buying, and without apologising.
Go back to the same shop a second time.
Ask somebody who works there what they would choose, and why.
Spend half an hour somewhere expensive without buying and without apologising.
Learn one real thing about how the good ones are made.
Take somebody who would never have gone in on their own.

tracks.name: Cars
tracks.line: Sitting in it is free.

steps.test: Look up a car you like and read what it actually costs.
Find out what it costs to run, not just to buy.
Walk into a dealership and look at one car, unhurried.
Let somebody come and talk to you about it.
Sit in it, adjust the seat, and stay there a few minutes.
Ask the questions you actually want answered.
Ask what people usually get wrong about it.
Say plainly that you are not buying today, and stay anyway.
Book a test drive.
Take the test drive.
Work out what it would take to be able to buy it, honestly, on paper.
Take somebody else for their first look.

tracks.name: Grand rooms
tracks.line: Most of them are open, and most people never check.

steps.test: Find out which grand buildings near you are open to the public.
Go into one of them.
Walk into a fine hotel lobby and sit down for ten minutes.
Use the lavatory in a very grand building, and take your time.
Visit the city hall, the courthouse, a gallery or a cathedral, and look up.
Sit through part of a public court hearing or a council meeting.
Have a coffee somewhere far smarter than you would normally.
Ask a member of staff a question in one of those places.
Go to a talk, a recital or an opening you were not invited to but could attend.
Go to an event in a building you had assumed was not for you.
Stay to the end, instead of leaving early.
Eat alone in a good restaurant, with no phone on the table.

tracks.name: Carrying yourself
tracks.line: Not shrinking is a physical habit.

steps.test: Walk into a room with your head up and make eye contact with one person.
Stand with your shoulders back and your weight even, for one whole conversation.
Walk slower than you want to across a room.
steps.note: Hurrying is what says you do not think you should be here. Nothing else says it as loudly.

steps.test: Take up your full space — do not shrink, and do not hurry through.
Sit down properly instead of perching on the edge.
Let somebody serve you without apologising for the trouble.
Say what you want without softening it into a question.
Take a compliment with a thank you, and nothing after it.
Stop saying sorry for things that are not your fault, for one whole day.
Hold a silence in a conversation instead of filling it.
Shake hands properly and say your own name clearly.
Look at the person you are speaking to for the whole sentence.
Wear something you feel good in, deliberately, to something ordinary.
Ask for what you want in a room where you feel out of place.
Introduce yourself to the most senior person in the room.
Disagree with somebody more important than you, calmly.
Walk in late, on purpose, and sit down without apologising.
Make somebody else feel like they belong, in a room where you barely do.
Notice one place where you no longer feel out of place at all.
Notice that you have stopped feeling out of place, and say when it changed.

tracks.name: The story you tell yourself
tracks.line: Testing the thing you assume would happen.

tracks.name: A home that works, part one
tracks.line: From a made bed to a place that is ready for anybody in ten minutes.

steps.test: Do one whole room properly: cleared, cleaned, everything with a place.

steps.test: Make a first-aid kit that would actually help.

steps.test: Deal with the pile: every letter and paper opened, filed, or binned.
steps.note: One sitting. Three piles: act, keep, bin. The bin pile is bigger than you think.

steps.test: Make one thing for the home.
steps.note: A shelf, a frame, a cushion, a hook, a bird box. Made by you, in use.

steps.test: A full week with the place tidy every night before bed.
steps.note: Ten minutes each night. By the seventh night it takes five.

steps.test: Have somebody round, and be ready in ten minutes.
steps.note: Tea, a clear table, a chair to sit in. When ten minutes is enough, the place works. Part two makes it beautiful.

tracks.about: A home that works: the bed, one drawer, the sink dry, one thing fixed, the stopcock found, five things given away, and on to a whole room done properly and a week of tidy nights. It ends with somebody round and ten minutes to be ready. Renting counts exactly the same.

categories.name: Focus and calm
categories.line: Stillness, attention, sleep, fasting, gratitude, doing hard things.

tracks.name: Stillness, part one
tracks.line: From two quiet minutes to a morning that begins the right way, seven days running.

steps.test: Sit still for two minutes, eyes closed, and count your breaths.
steps.note: Lose count, start again. Two minutes is longer than you think and shorter than you fear.

steps.test: Write down three things you are grateful for tonight.
steps.note: Small ones are best: the kettle, a text, the weather holding.

steps.test: Look at one beautiful thing for five full minutes.
steps.note: A tree, a painting, a face, the sky. Five minutes without looking away.

steps.test: Eat one meal with no screen, no book, no phone.
steps.note: Just the food and whoever is there. Notice how long the meal actually takes.

steps.test: Sit still for five minutes.
steps.note: Same as rung one, longer. A timer, so you are not the one watching the clock.

steps.test: Do the hard thing first tomorrow, before anything else.
steps.note: The call, the email, the task you keep moving. Decide tonight what it is.

steps.test: Thank somebody for something they did a long time ago.
steps.note: A teacher, a parent, an old friend. A message or a call. Most people never hear it.

steps.test: Read one page of something old and wise, and copy out one line.
steps.note: Marcus, the Psalms, Epictetus, a proverb book. One line, by hand, kept.

steps.test: Ten minutes of stillness.
steps.note: Sitting, breathing, nothing else. The mind will wander; bring it back, that is the exercise.

steps.test: A whole day without complaining out loud.
steps.note: Catch yourself, stop, say something else. Most people do not last until lunch the first time.

steps.test: Write one page on what a good life would be, for you.
steps.note: Not the money. The days, the people, the work, the place. By hand if you can.

steps.test: A full day without news or social media.
steps.note: Notice what you reach for instead. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose today and count it. Already done is still done.

steps.test: Forgive one small thing and let it go.
steps.note: Nobody needs to know. Say it in your head, then stop bringing it up, even to yourself.

steps.test: Fifteen minutes of stillness, three days running.
steps.note: Same time each day works best. Morning, before the phone.

steps.test: Every day for a week, write down one thing you were given for nothing.
steps.note: Sight, a friend, the sea, a language, a joke. Seven days, seven things.

steps.test: Do something kind that nobody will ever know about.
steps.note: Not even the person. Pay for the next coffee, clear a neighbour's leaves, leave a book on a bench.

steps.test: Sit with a hard feeling for ten minutes without fixing it.
steps.note: No phone, no food, no distraction. Just notice it. It changes on its own.

steps.test: Twenty minutes of stillness.
steps.note: This is where it starts to feel like something you would miss.

steps.test: Tell one person, to their face, what you are grateful to them for.
steps.note: In person, not a message. Short. Watch what it does to them.

steps.test: Seven mornings running that begin with stillness, gratitude, and the hard thing first.
steps.note: Ten minutes still, three things written, then the hard thing. A week of it is a different life. Part two goes further in.

tracks.about: Two minutes still, then five, then twenty. Three things written down at night, one beautiful thing looked at properly, a day without complaining, a hard feeling sat with. It ends with a week of mornings that begin the right way. Nothing to buy and nothing to believe; just sitting, noticing, and the hard thing first.

tracks.name: Sleep
tracks.line: From going to bed without a fight to running your own rest and fixing somebody else’s.

steps.test: Go to bed at the time you said you would, three nights running.
how: Decide the time in the morning, not at eleven at night.
Set an alarm for going to bed, not only for getting up.
Three nights, written down and ticked off.
steps.note: The hard part of bedtime is never the bed, it is stopping whatever you are doing. An alarm at the start of the evening does the deciding for you.

steps.test: Get up at the same time three days running.
how: Same time every one of the three, including any day off.
Feet on the floor and curtains open within a minute of the alarm.
Whatever time you went to bed.
steps.note: The waking time is the lever, not the bedtime. Fix when you get up and your body sorts out when you fall asleep, usually within a week.

steps.test: Get daylight on your face in the first hour of the morning, every day for a week.
how: Outside, not through a window. Ten minutes is plenty.
Even a grey morning outdoors is many times brighter than any indoor room.
Walk to the shop, stand in the garden, walk somebody to school.
steps.note: This is the strongest and cheapest thing on the whole ladder. Morning light is what sets the clock that decides when you feel sleepy fourteen hours later.

steps.test: Keep screens out of the last half hour before bed, for a week.
how: Phone on charge in another room, or at least across the room.
A book, a bath, tidying, talking, drawing — anything that is not a lit rectangle.
Seven nights.
steps.note: It is the endless scrolling more than the light: a screen never reaches the end of itself, so it never lets you stop. A book has pages that run out.

steps.test: Go to bed at your time seven nights running.
how: Same time, including at the weekend.
Start the last half hour early enough that the time is actually possible.
Seven nights, ticked off.
steps.note: A week is where this stops taking willpower. After about five nights the sleepiness starts arriving on its own, which is the whole point.

steps.test: Notice how you feel after a bad night, and say so out loud.
how: Name it plainly to somebody: short-tempered, foggy, weepy, hungry.
Do it on the day, not afterwards.
No excuses attached to it, just the fact.
steps.note: Joining up a bad night with a bad day is what makes anybody bother to fix their sleep. Children in particular have usually never been told the two are connected.

steps.test: Get up at the same time seven days running.
how: Every day, including Saturday and Sunday.
Curtains open, outside within the hour.
If you had a bad night, get up anyway — the lie-in is what keeps the cycle going.
steps.note: The weekend lie-in is what undoes most people. Two late mornings is the same as flying two time zones west and back every single week.

steps.test: Make your room properly dark and properly cool for a week.
how: Cover or turn off every little light: standby lamps, chargers, clocks.
Cooler than feels right — a window open, one fewer blanket.
A cheap blackout blind or even a towel over the curtain rail works.
steps.note: Dark and cool are the two conditions your body is actually waiting for. An hour of work on your room pays back every night for years.

steps.test: Keep screens out of the last full hour before bed, for a fortnight.
how: Phone charging in another room overnight. Buy an alarm clock if that is what it takes.
Decide what the hour is for before you need it: a book, a bath, a walk, a jigsaw.
Fourteen nights.
steps.note: Most people find the hour itself becomes the best part of the day within a fortnight, which nobody expects when they start.

steps.test: Have the same last twenty minutes every night for a fortnight.
how: Same order every night: teeth, room ready, curtains, a few pages, light off.
Boring on purpose. The sameness is the medicine.
Fourteen nights of the identical routine.
steps.note: A routine works because it stops being a decision. Children are given one and grown-ups think they have outgrown it; they have not.

steps.test: Find out how many hours you actually need, by trying it.
how: A week where you go to bed at the same time and wake without an alarm.
Write down the hours each night and how the day went.
A holiday week or a quiet week is the time to do this.
steps.note: Almost everybody guesses wrong about their own number. Knowing it means you can plan a week properly instead of hoping.

steps.test: Run your own rest for a month, and then help somebody else fix theirs.
how: A month of your own times, your own routine, nobody reminding you.
Then sit down with somebody and go through it: waking time, morning light, dark room, last half hour.
Give them the one that will help them most, not all four at once.
steps.note: One change at a time is how you help somebody. The waking time and the morning light are the two that do most of the work, so start them there.

tracks.about: Sleep is the one thing that makes every other ladder in the school easier, and it is the easiest of all of them to fix, because almost all of it comes down to a handful of habits that cost nothing: the same waking time, daylight in the morning, a dark cool room, and the last half hour away from a screen. It works the same way for a child of six and an adult of forty, which is why this ladder is written for both.
