Sit with something uncomfortable instead of fixing it straight away.
Help somebody else through the moment they want to quit.

tracks.name: Noticing the good
tracks.line: One thing to a habit.

steps.test: Say one good thing about today, out loud, at tea.
Do it three days running.
Do it every day for a week.
Say one that is about a person, not a thing.
Thank somebody properly, to their face, for something specific.
Thank somebody who is never thanked for it.
Find something good on a day that was bad.
Write down three each night for a week.
Write a thank-you letter that somebody keeps.
Do the daily one for thirty days.
Read back a month of them.
Start it at a table where nobody was doing it.

tracks.name: Fasting
tracks.line: For grown-ups. From a comfortable sixteen hours to thirty-six, done properly.
tracks.warn: Adults only past step five. Not if you are pregnant, diabetic, underweight, still growing, on medication that needs food, or have ever had trouble with eating. Children stop at step four — going without snacks is theirs; going without meals is not.

steps.test: Go sixteen hours with nothing but water, tea or black coffee, and work a normal day inside it.
how: Dinner at seven, nothing until eleven the next morning. Sleep does most of it.
No milk, no sugar, no sweeteners — they end the fast in your head even when they barely do in your body.
Do it on an ordinary working day, not a quiet one.
steps.note: You have done sixteen hours before; this rung is doing it while life carries on around you. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Drink a large glass of water with a pinch of salt in it during a fast.
how: A good pinch of ordinary salt in a pint of water, drunk over an hour.
Do it at the point in the fast where you usually start feeling flat.
Costs nothing and you already have both ingredients.
steps.note: Most of what people call hunger past about eighteen hours is thirst and salt, not food. This one trick removes most of the headaches people blame fasting for.

steps.test: Sit through one wave of hunger without eating, and time how long it lasted.
how: When it arrives, look at the clock and write the time down.
Do something with your hands until it passes, then write that time down too.
Most waves are fifteen to twenty minutes.
steps.note: Hunger comes in waves and goes again whether you eat or not. Watching one arrive and leave is the single most useful thing on this ladder, because after it you stop believing hunger is an emergency.

steps.test: Go eighteen hours, water only.
how: Dinner at seven, nothing until one the next day.
Water, black tea, black coffee, herbal tea. Nothing else.
Plan what you will do at the hour it gets hard — a walk is the best answer.
steps.note: Eighteen is where sixteen stops being mostly sleep and starts being a decision. The salt water from rung two matters here.

steps.test: Take a walk in the middle of a fast rather than sitting through it.
how: Twenty minutes, outside, at the hour you would normally be eating.
Notice that the hunger is quieter while you are moving.
Any weather, any route.
steps.note: Moving while fasted feels wrong and is not. A walk is the cheapest and fastest way to send a wave of hunger away, and it fills the time the meal used to take.

steps.test: Do eighteen hours on three separate days in one week.
how: Three days, with ordinary eating in between. Not consecutive.
Same edges each time so your body knows what is coming.
Write the three days down and tick them off.
steps.note: Repetition is what makes this comfortable. The third one is always much easier than the first, and it is the rung where fasting stops being an event.

steps.test: Break a fast properly: a real meal, eaten slowly, not a feast.
how: Eggs, fish, meat, vegetables, butter. Something you cooked.
Eat it slowly, and stop at comfortably full rather than stuffed.
Nothing sweet as the first thing that goes in.
steps.note: Almost everybody undoes a good fast in the twenty minutes after it. How you break it matters more than how long it was.

steps.test: Go twenty hours, water only.
how: Dinner at seven, nothing until three the next afternoon.
Salt in your water once during the day.
Keep busy through the early afternoon — that is the hard hour.
steps.note: Twenty hours means one proper meal in a day. That is how a great many people have eaten for most of history and it is not an extreme thing.

steps.test: Do a full day on one meal, and make that meal a proper one.
how: One plate, real food, enough of it. Not a small plate.
Eat it at the time that suits your day, and nothing else all day.
Eat until you are properly full — this is not about eating less at the meal.
steps.note: The mistake here is a small meal, which leaves you hungry and cross and convinced fasting does not suit you. One big honest plate is the rung.

steps.test: Go twenty-four hours, from one evening meal to the next.
how: Seven in the evening to seven the next evening.
Water, salt, black tea and coffee. A walk in the afternoon.
Plan the meal at the end before you start, so you are not deciding while hungry.
steps.note: Evening to evening is much easier than it sounds because you sleep through a third of it and eat on both days. You did one of these in Real food part two — this is doing it deliberately.

steps.test: Do twenty-four hours on an ordinary working day, not a quiet one.
how: A normal day of work, people and demands, with nothing to eat in it.
Do not tell everybody. This is not a performance.
Water and salt, and a walk at lunchtime instead of lunch.
steps.note: Finding out that you can work, think and be civil to people on an empty stomach removes a fear most people carry all their lives.

steps.test: Notice what you actually feel when you say you are hungry, and write down three words for it.
how: Do it in the last few hours of a fast.
Bored? Tired? Cold? Sad? Thirsty? Out of habit? Be specific.
Three words, written down.
steps.note: A good half of what gets called hunger turns out to be something else with a name. Naming it is what lets you answer it properly instead of with food.

steps.test: Do twenty-four hours twice in one fortnight.
how: Two full days, a week apart.
Same shape both times so you can compare them.
Write down which was easier and why.
steps.note: Twice tells you whether the first one was a fluke. For nearly everybody the second is markedly easier, which is the point of doing it.

steps.test: Go twenty-eight hours.
how: Evening meal, then through the next day, then sleep, then break it in the morning.
Salt water twice across the day.
Keep the day gentle — light work, walking, nothing heavy.
steps.note: Past twenty-four hours the hunger usually gets quieter rather than louder, which surprises everybody the first time.

steps.test: Sleep through part of a fast, and notice how you sleep.
how: Go to bed inside a fast rather than breaking it at dinner.
Write down in the morning how you slept and how you woke.
Warm room, extra blanket — you will feel the cold more.
steps.note: Some people sleep beautifully fasted and some sleep badly. Knowing which you are is worth more than any general advice about it.

steps.test: Go thirty-two hours.
how: Evening meal to the following morning, through a full day and a night.
Salt and water properly. Do not skip this — it is what keeps your head clear.
Stop if you feel genuinely unwell rather than merely uncomfortable. That is not failure, that is sense.
steps.note: Knowing the difference between uncomfortable and unwell is the real skill of this ladder. Uncomfortable you can sit through; unwell you eat.

steps.test: Do something you would normally need a meal for, while fasted.
how: A long walk, a day out with the children, a hard morning's work, a hill.
Water and salt with you.
Break the fast properly afterwards with a real meal.
steps.note: This is the rung where the point of the whole thing lands: your day stops being organised around the next meal, and that is a freedom you keep.

steps.test: Plan and cook the meal that will break your longest fast, before you start it.
how: Decide it, shop for it, and have it ready in the fridge.
Meat or fish, vegetables, butter or olive oil. Nothing sweet, nothing from a packet.
Write down the time you will eat it.
steps.note: Decisions made while hungry are bad decisions. Making this one in advance is what stops thirty-six hours ending in a takeaway.

steps.test: Go thirty-six hours, and break it with the meal you planned.
how: Evening meal, a full day, a night, and then breakfast the second morning.
Salt and water throughout, a walk each day, gentle work.
Eat slowly when you break it. Stop at comfortably full.
steps.note: Thirty-six hours done properly and broken properly is the far end of this ladder. Going further than this is a thing to do with a doctor, not with an app.

steps.test: Write down your own rules for fasting, and the ones you will not break.
how: How often, how long, and on which days of your week.
The stop rules: unwell rather than uncomfortable, ill, pregnant, on new medicine.
Who you would tell before a long one.
steps.note: The ladder ends where Real food ended: with your own written way of doing it rather than somebody else's. Rules you wrote while clear-headed are the ones that hold when you are not.

tracks.about: Real food part two took you to a sixteen-hour window and one twenty-four hour fast. This ladder is the craft of going further: what to drink, how to keep working through it, what to do when you feel rough, and — the part nearly everybody gets wrong — how to break a long fast without wrecking the good of it. It costs nothing; it is the only thing in the school that saves you money while you do it. If you are pregnant, underweight, diabetic, on medication, or have any history of disordered eating, this ladder is not for you. Talk to a doctor first.

categories.name: Creating order
categories.line: Clear it, mend it, give it away, clean the forgotten places. A life flows when the place is in order.

tracks.name: The bedroom
tracks.line: Where the day starts and ends.

steps.test: Clear every surface in the bedroom and put back only what you used this week.
Make the bed properly every morning for a week.
Empty the box by the door: bin it, give it, or find each thing a real home.
Get everything off the floor.
Clean the bedroom to a close look: under the bed, the skirting, the corners, the light switch.
Wash the bedding, the pillow covers, and the curtains or blind.
Take out anything that is not for sleeping or dressing.
Sit in the finished room for ten minutes with nothing in your hands and notice how it feels.

tracks.name: The desk
tracks.line: One clear surface to think at.

steps.test: Clear the desk to bare wood, wipe it, and put back the three things you use every day.
Every loose paper into one pile, then through it once: bin, file, or act on it today.
Sort the drawers: one drawer for what you use, everything else out.
Tame the cables: unplug what is not used, coil and label the rest.
Put one thing on it that you are glad to look at.
Sit down and check the chair and the screen are at the right height.
Set the desk each evening for the morning: a clear surface and one thing ready. Do it for a week.
Work a whole session at the clear desk and notice the difference.

tracks.name: The wardrobe
tracks.line: Only clothes you are glad to put on.

steps.test: Take every piece of clothing out and put it on the bed. All of it.
Try on anything you are unsure about. Keep only what fits now and what you are glad to wear.
Bag the rest today: give it, sell it, or bin what is worn out.
Put back what stays so you can see every piece at once.
Mend, or take to be mended, anything kept with a button, a hem or a zip gone.
Put the out-of-season things somewhere else entirely.
Work out what you are actually missing, and write the list.
Dress for a week from the finished wardrobe and count how many mornings were quicker.

tracks.name: Broken things
tracks.line: Fix it or let it go.

steps.test: Walk the whole house with a notebook and list every broken thing.
Fix three small things from the list today.
For each thing you will not fix, decide today: bin it, or take it to be repaired this week.
Take the ones for repair out of the house.
Fix one thing that needs a part or a tool: order the part, get the tool, do it.
Fix something you have walked past for a year.
Replace what has to be replaced, rather than leaving the gap.
Fix or remove the last thing on the list.
Notice one thing that broke because it was never maintained.
Do the one maintenance job that would stop it happening again.
Fix something for somebody else in the house.
Keep a page for broken things and clear it every Sunday for a month.

tracks.name: Giving away
tracks.line: What no longer serves you can serve somebody.

steps.test: Fill one bag with things you have not used in a year. Today.
Take it to a charity shop, a friend, or a giving box the same day.
Do the kitchen: gadgets, mugs, tins past their date. One bag out.
Do the books, games and hobby things you have finished with. Pass them on.
Do the bathroom cupboard and the medicine box.
Do the shed, the garage or the loft corner you avoid.
Give away one thing that is good and that you like, to somebody who will use it more.
Ask each person in the house to fill one bag too.
Sell one thing rather than keeping it "just in case".
Let go of one thing you kept only because it cost money.
Keep the bag by the door and add to it for a fortnight.
A month on, count what you missed.

tracks.name: The phone and the inbox
tracks.line: The clutter you carry in your pocket.

steps.test: Delete every app you have not opened in a month.
Delete the screenshots and the junk photos from the last month.
Unsubscribe from twenty emails you never read.
Turn off every notification that is not a person talking to you.
Get the inbox to empty once: archive, delete, or act.
Clear the home screen to one page of what you use.
Put the two apps that eat the most time off the first page.
Back up the photographs you would be sick to lose.
Sort one year of photographs and delete the near-duplicates.
Cancel one subscription you had forgotten you pay for.
Check where you are still signed in, and sign out of what you do not use.
Keep the inbox at empty by the end of each day for a week.

tracks.name: The forgotten places
tracks.line: Behind, under, on top of, and inside.

steps.test: Clean the windows, inside and out, in one room.
Wash or wipe the blinds and the curtain rail.
Clean behind and under the sink, and the bin itself.
Empty and wipe the fridge, shelf by shelf, and bin what is past.
Clean the oven, or the thing in the kitchen you have been avoiding.
Wash the curtains, or take them to be cleaned.
The top of the cupboards, the light shades, and the skirting all the way round: one room.
Move the furniture and clean what was under it.
Clean the front door, the handle and the step.
Do the one place in the house nobody has looked at in years.
Descale, empty or change the filter on something that needed it.
Do one forgotten place every week for a month.

tracks.name: Keeping it
tracks.line: Order that stays.

steps.test: Everything you own has a home: choose one for the five things that never get put away.
Put those five things away in their homes tonight.
Ten minutes every evening putting the day back. Do it for three days.
Do it for a week.
Clear one surface every single evening for a week.
One in, one out: for a week, nothing new comes in without something going.
One in, one out for a month.
A Sunday reset: half an hour that puts the whole place right. Do one.
Do four of them, one a week.
Put things away where they live rather than where they will do.
Stop a pile before it starts, three times in one week.
Walk the whole house with a close look. Where has clutter crept back? Deal with it today.
Find the one spot that always goes wrong, and change what it is for.
Get everybody in the house to keep one shared surface clear for a week.
Deal with the post the day it arrives, for a fortnight.
Leave a room right when you leave it, every time, for a week.
Keep the place in a state you are glad to walk into for a month.
Do a reset after something disrupted it — illness, visitors, a bad week.
Notice that putting things away has stopped needing a decision.
Keep the place in a state you are glad to walk into for three months.

tracks.name: Your own things
tracks.line: From four, beside you. Shoes, cover, clothes, books, and one box put right.

steps.test: Put your shoes side by side by the door, the same way round.
Hang your coat up on a hook.
Pull the cover up straight on your bed when you get out of it.
Put your clothes in the wash basket at bedtime, without being asked.
Put the books back on the shelf the right way up.
Put the lids back on the pens and the tops back on the tubs.
Empty one box of toys onto the floor and put every single one back in.
Find a home for one thing that never had one.
Put away what you were playing with before the next thing comes out.
Do that for a whole afternoon.
Tidy your room with somebody, and stay until it is finished.
Do all of it one whole day without anybody reminding you.

journey.name: Easy wins
journey.line: Every one of these is a decision rather than a skill. Minutes each, nothing to buy, nothing to learn first. Most people are surprised they had never done them.

journey.name: Courage, worth and asking
journey.line: Deliberately early. Once you can ask for things, walk into anywhere and hear no without flinching, a great many things that looked like they cost money turn out not to. This stage quietly changes what everything after it is worth.
